questions.question_text: The writer uses 'numbered sensitivity' to refer to
questions.passage: Time was when boys used to point guns and say “Bang! Now the aim real guns and shoot one another. Nearly 4,200 teenagers were killed by firearms in 1990. Only motor vehicle accidents kill more teenagers than firearms and the firearms figures are rising. The chance that a black male between the ages of 15 and 19 will be killed by a gun has almost tripled since 1985 and almost doubled for males’ according to the National Centre for Health Statistics. Who could disagree with Health and Human Services Secretary, Donna Shalala, when she pronounced these statistics ‘frightening and intolerable? In the shameful light of this ‘waste of this young lives ‘ in Ms Shalal’s words an often asked questions seems urgently due to be raised again; would less violence on television the surrounding environment for most children and young adults make violence in actual life less normal, less accepted, less horrifying? It may be difficult to prove exact correlation between the viewer of fantasized violence and the criminal who act out of violence after turning off the set. But if the premise of education is granted that good models can influence the young then it follows that bad models can have an equivalent harmful effect. This is the reasonable hypothesis held by 80 percent of the of the respondents to a recent time mirror poll who think that violent entertainment is ‘harmful’ to society Witness enough mimed shootout, see enough ‘corpses ‘fall across the screen, and the taking of human life seems no big deal. Even if a simple casual relationship cannot be established between watching violence and acting it out, is not this numbered sensitivity reason enough for cutting back on the overkill in films and TV? From: The Christian Science Monitor, April 16-22, 1993 P.20, Boston MA

options.option_a: deadening of the capacity to feel
options.option_c: heartlessness on the part of actors

questions.explanation: The phrase 'numbered sensitivity' is a likely mishearing or typo of 'numbed sensitivity,' referring to the desensitization caused by repeated exposure to violence in media. The writer argues that even without a direct causal link between media violence and real-life violence, the loss of emotional responsiveness (deadening of sensitivity) to violence is a compelling reason to reduce its portrayal. Option A ('deadening of the capacity to feel') directly aligns with this interpretation. The passage emphasizes how repeated exposure to fictional violence reduces the perceived gravity of real-life violence, supporting the idea of 'numbed sensitivity.'
questions.common_mistake: Option B ('objectionable behaviour') might be incorrectly chosen if the reader focuses on the broader issue of violence rather than the specific metaphor of 'sensitivity.' Similarly, Option D ('unreasonable violence') could be selected if the reader misinterprets the phrase as a direct reference to media content rather than its psychological effect.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements can be implied from the passage?
questions.passage: You would think that the common cold should be easy to study, but it is not so easy as it looks. Colds often seem to spread from one person to another, so it is often assumed that the must be infectious, but there are some puzzling observations which do not fit in with this theory. An investigator in Holland examined some eight thousand volunteers from different areas and came to the conclusion that in each of the group the colds all appeared at the same time transfer of infection from case to case could not account for that. Yet at the common cold research unit in Salisbury the infection theory has been tested out, two series of about two hundred people each were inoculated, one with salt-water and the other with secretions from known cold victims. Only one of the salt-water group got a cold, compared with seventy-three in the other group. In the British Medical journal the other day, there was a report of a meeting. The common cold fact and fancy’ at which one of Miles Howard: the Spectator the speakers reported a study of colds made in cirencester over the last five years. Three hundred and fifty volunteers had kept diary records of their colds and an average each had seven every year, with an annual morbidity of seventy days. So nearly one fifth of our lives is spent in more or less misery, coughing and sneezing. Some widely held beliefs about the common cold have turned out to be true. It seems that old people are just as liable to colds as the young. Sailors in isolated weather ships have just as many colds while onboard and not in contact with the outside world as when in shore. It is a truism that common illness pose more problems than the rare. The rare disease is by comparison much easier to handle. There are not so many cases and all of them have been intensively studied. Someone has red up all the literature about the disease and published a digest of it. There will be more facts and fewer fancies

options.option_a: People catch more colds in winter
options.option_b: The origin of colds is inconclusive
options.option_c: People catch more colds in warm weather.
options.option_d: People catch colds equally in warm and cold weather.

questions.explanation: The passage discusses conflicting evidence regarding the causes of the common cold. While the infection theory is supported by the Salisbury study (73 cases in the infected group vs. 1 in the control), the Holland study observed simultaneous colds in groups, challenging the infection transfer theory. This contradiction implies that the origin of colds remains inconclusive. The passage does not mention seasonal patterns (options A, C, D), making them unsupported. The correct inference is that the origin of colds is inconclusive.
questions.common_mistake: Assuming the passage supports seasonal patterns (A/C/D) due to prior knowledge, but the text provides no such information.

questions.question_text: comprehension passage IIIThe expression, 'not in memory but expectation' used in the passage inmplies
questions.passage: Young men have strong passions, and tend to tend to gratify them in indiscriminately. Of the bodily desire, it is the sexual by which they are most swayed and in which they show absence of self-control. They are changeable and fickle in their desires, which are violent while they last, but quickly over their impulse are keen but not deep-rooted, and are like sick people’s attacks of hunger and thirst. They are hot-tempered and quick-tempered, and apt to give way to their anger, bad temper often gets the better of them, for owing to their love of honor they cannot bear being slighted, and are indignant if they imagine themselves unfairly treated. While they love honor, they love victory still more, for youth is eager for superiority over others and victory is one form of this. They love both more than they love money which they indeed love very little, not having yet learnt what it means to be without it. They look at the good side rather than the bad, not having yet witnessed many instances of wickedness. They trust others readily, because they have not yet been cheated. They are sanguine, nature warms their blood as though with excess wine and besides that they have as yet met with few disappointments’ their lives are mainly spent not in memory but in expectation for youth has a long future before it and a short past behind it on the first day of one’s life one has nothing at all to remember, and can only look forward. They are easily cheated owing to the sanguine disposition just mentioned. Their hot tempers and hopeful disposition make them more courageous than older men are, the hot temper prevents fear and the hopeful disposition creates confidence, we cannot feel fear so long as we are feeling angry, and any expectation of good makes us confident. Aristotle’s youth and old –age, p 197
questions.explanation: The expression 'not in memory but expectation' implies that young men are more focused on their future rather than dwelling on their past experiences. This is because they have a long future ahead of them and a short past behind them. The phrase suggests that young men are more optimistic and hopeful, looking forward to what is to come rather than reflecting on what has already happened. This is in line with the description of young men as 'sanguine' and having a 'hopeful disposition'.
questions.common_mistake: Some students may interpret the phrase as implying that young men are not concerned with the present, but this is not the correct interpretation. The correct interpretation is that they are more focused on the future.

Since the passage focuses on the final, binding legal instrument, 'an Act' (option A) is the correct answer. A 'bill' (option D) is a draft proposal, not the enacted law itself.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'a bill' with 'an Act' due to their related but distinct roles in the legislative process.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 26 to 30 choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the lettersboat
questions.explanation: The word 'boat' has a long 'o' sound, which is also present in the word 'bought'. This sound is often referred to as the 'close-mid back rounded vowel' sound. In phonetics, this sound is represented by the symbol /oʊ/. The correct answer is 'bought' because it is the only option that has the same vowel sound as 'boat'. The other options, 'board', 'go', and 'glory', have different vowel sounds.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the 'o' sound in 'boat' with the 'o' sound in 'go' or 'glory', which are different vowel sounds. Another common mistake is not paying close attention to the vowel sound in each option and choosing an answer based on the similarity in spelling rather than sound.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 30, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters underlined.air
questions.explanation: The word 'air' has the vowel sound /eə/ (as in 'bear' or 'pair'). The correct option is 'heir' (A), which shares the same vowel sound as 'air' (/eə/). 'Her' (B) has the /ɜː/ sound, 'hear' (C) has the /iː/ sound, and 'fire' (D) has the /aɪ/ sound, none of which match the vowel sound in 'air'.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'hear' (C) with 'air' due to the presence of 'ei' in both, but 'hear' has a long 'ee' sound (/iː/), not the same as 'air'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 30, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters underlined.Pleasure
questions.explanation: The underlined vowel sound in 'Pleasure' is the 'ea' sound, which is also found in 'plenary'. This is because the 'ea' sound in 'pleasure' is pronounced as /iː/ (ee sound), similar to the pronunciation of 'plenary'.
questions.common_mistake: Students may confuse the vowel sound in 'pleasure' with the one in 'oleat', which has a different vowel sound.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 30, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters underlined.thunder
questions.explanation: The underlined vowel sound in 'thunder' is the 'under' sound, which is pronounced as /ʌndər/. The correct option that has the same vowel sound is 'defer', which also has the /ʌ/ sound. This is because 'defer' is pronounced as /dɪˈfɜːr/, where the 'e' is pronounced as /ɜː/ but the preceding 'e' is pronounced as /ɪ/ and the 'e' after the 'r' is pronounced as /ɜː/ but the preceding 'e' is pronounced as /ɪ/ but the 'e' in 'defer' is pronounced as /ɪ/ but the 'e' in 'under' is pronounced as /ʌ/.
questions.common_mistake: Students may confuse the vowel sound in 'thunder' with other options that have different vowel sounds, such as 'prefer' which has the /ɪ/ sound or 'differ' which has the /ɪ/ sound.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 30, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters underlined.tear (noun)
questions.explanation: The underlined vowel sound in 'tear' is /ɪər/ or /ɪr/. The option that has the same vowel sound is 'care' which also has the /ɪər/ or /ɪr/ sound. Therefore, the correct answer is option_b.
questions.common_mistake: Students may confuse the vowel sound in 'tear' with other words that have different vowel sounds, such as 'pear' or 'hear'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In questions 31 and 32, choose from the options the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters underlined.thought
questions.explanation: The underlined 'th' in 'thought' represents the voiceless dental fricative sound /θ/, as in 'think'. Among the options, 'theatre' (option A) also contains the 'th' combination pronounced as /θ/ in British English. 'Taught' (B) ends with a /t/ sound, 'weather' (C) has the voiced dental fricative /ð/, and 'fate' (D) lacks a 'th' sound entirely.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the 'th' in 'weather' (voiced /ð/) with the 'th' in 'thought' (voiceless /θ/), or mispronouncing 'theatre' as starting with a /t/ sound in some dialects.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In questions 31 and 32, choose from the options the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters underlined.caliph
questions.explanation: The underlined consonant sound in 'caliph' is /l/. Among the options, 'perhaps' is the word that has the same /l/ sound.
questions.common_mistake: Students may confuse the /l/ sound with other consonant sounds such as /p/ or /t/.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 33 to 36, select the word that has the same pattern of stress as the given wordENORMOUS
questions.explanation: The word ENORMOUS has the stress pattern of EN-o-RO-mus. Among the given options, SOLUTION has a similar stress pattern of SO-lu-TION. The other options do not match the stress pattern of ENORMOUS.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the stress patterns of words, especially when they are not familiar with the correct pronunciation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 33 to 36, select the word that has the same pattern of stress as the given wordHONOUR
questions.explanation: The word HONOUR has a stress pattern of /ˈhɒnər/ (HON-our). This means that the first syllable is stressed. Among the given options, the word 'human' has a similar stress pattern of /ˈhjuːmən/ (HUE-man), where the first syllable is also stressed. Therefore, the correct answer is option_c: 'human'.
questions.common_mistake: Students may mistakenly choose option_a: 'hotel' because it has a similar sound to 'honour', but the stress pattern is different. The correct stress pattern for 'hotel' is /ˈhoʊtəl/ (HO-tel), where the second syllable is stressed.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 33 to 36, select the word that has the same pattern of stress as the given wordQUALITY
questions.explanation: The word 'QUALITY' has a stress pattern of /ˈkwɒlɪti/ (KWOL-i-tee). This pattern is similar to 'guarantee' /ˈɡærənti/ (GAR-uh-nee), which has the same stress pattern of emphasis on the first syllable.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the stress patterns of words with similar sounds or syllable counts, but fail to consider the actual emphasis in each word.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 33 to 36, select the word that has the same pattern of stress as the given wordEDUCATION
questions.explanation: The word 'EDUCATION' has a stress pattern of ED-u-CAT-ion. To find the word with the same pattern, we need to identify the word that has a similar stress pattern. Among the options, 'economics' has a stress pattern of e-CO-nom-ics, which is similar to ED-u-CAT-ion.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the stress patterns of words, especially when they are not familiar with the correct pronunciation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In questions 37 and 38, identify the word that has the stress on the second syllable.
questions.explanation: The word 'reproduce' is pronounced /rɪˈprɒdjuːs/ with stress on the second syllable ('PRO'). Other options have stress on the first syllable: 'always' (/ˈɔːlweɪz/), 'result' (/rɪˈzʌlt/), and 'understand' (/ˌʌndəˈstænd/). Stress placement is critical for distinguishing correct answers in phonetic questions.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing stress patterns in longer words like 'understand' (stress on first syllable) or misidentifying stress in compound words.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In questions 39 and 40, identify the word that has a different stress pattern from the others
questions.explanation: The words 'integral', 'intimate', and 'discourse' all have the same stress pattern, with the stress on the third syllable. However, the word 'accelerate' has a different stress pattern, with the stress on the second syllable. This is because the prefix 'ac-' is unstressed, and the stress falls on the second syllable 'cel-'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the stress patterns of words with similar prefixes or roots, leading to incorrect identification of the word with a different stress pattern.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In questions 39 and 40, identify the word that has a different stress pattern from the others
questions.explanation: The words 'navigate', 'legislate', and 'liberate' all have the stress pattern /næv-ig-eɪt/, /lɛd-ɪ-seɪt/, and /lɪb-ə-reɪt/ respectively. However, the word 'envelop' has a different stress pattern, /ɪn-ˈvɛl-əp/, with the stress on the second syllable.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the stress patterns of words with similar prefixes or roots.
related_topics: Phonetics and Phonology in English Language

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of questions 41 to 62,fill each gab with the most appropriate option from the list provided.Without our relentless campaigns we might .... sure if victory in the race for the National Assembly
questions.explanation: The sentence requires a third conditional structure to express a hypothetical past situation. The correct form after 'might' is 'have + past participle.' 'Never have been' (option A) fits this structure, as 'sure' is an adjective requiring the verb 'to be' in past participle form ('been'). Options B, C, and D incorrectly use base form verbs or incorrect tenses.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the base form of the verb with the past participle after modal verbs like 'might.'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of questions 41 to 62,fill each gab with the most appropriate option from the list provided.We are all hungry, we ..... anything to eat since morning
questions.explanation: The sentence requires the present perfect tense ('haven't had') to indicate an action (not eating) that started in the past (since morning) and continues to the present. 'Since morning' signals a duration from a specific past time to the current moment, which aligns with the present perfect structure. Options A and B use past tenses that do not account for the ongoing relevance of the action. Option D ('never had') incorrectly uses an absolute negative ('never') incompatible with 'since morning'.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing present perfect with past simple due to the phrase 'since morning', or misinterpreting 'never' as a suitable alternative.
related_topics: Use of 'Since' and 'For' in Time Clauses

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedTo check desertification in the arid zones ..... trees should be planted
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'drought-resistant' because it is the standard term used to describe plants or trees that can survive in arid conditions without perishing. 'Drought-resistant' refers to the ability to withstand drought, which aligns with the goal of checking desertification. 'Drought-proof' implies complete immunity, which is unrealistic. 'Drought-resisting' is grammatically incorrect as a single adjective (requires a gerund or verb form). 'Drought-effective' is not a recognized collocation.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'drought-resistant' with 'drought-resisting' due to similar phonetics, or incorrectly selecting 'drought-proof' as an overgeneralization.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedThe loquacious young lad reeled off all the names of the players ----
questions.explanation: The phrase 'off hand' means done casually or without prior preparation, which fits the context of the loquacious lad reciting names spontaneously. 'Reel off' implies listing something quickly, often without prior planning, aligning with 'off hand.' Other options like 'at hand' (available) or 'off head' (non-idiomatic) do not fit the context.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'off hand' with 'at hand,' which refers to availability rather than spontaneity.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedI like the character that played the role of a political ---- at the last convention of the party
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'turncoat,' which refers to a person who betrays their cause or side, often by changing allegiance. In the context of a political convention, this term fits as it describes someone who switches political loyalty. The other options are either misspellings or incorrect forms of the word. 'Turnedcoat' is a common distractor but is not the standard term.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'turncoat' with 'turnedcoat' due to the past tense form of 'turn,' but the idiomatic expression requires the singular form 'turncoat.'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedAll the traders in the market saw the women buy ---- the imported suits
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'off' because the phrase 'buy off' is an idiomatic expression that means to buy all of something that is available. In this context, the women bought all the imported suits, leaving none for others. The preposition 'off' is used to indicate that the suits were completely sold out.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'buy off' with 'buy up', which has a similar meaning but is not the best fit in this context. 'Buy up' typically implies buying something in large quantities, but it doesn't necessarily mean buying all of it.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedThe man declared his intention from the ----
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'outset' (A). 'Outset' means the beginning or the start of something, which fits the context of declaring an intention at the start. 'Inset' (B) refers to an inserted part, 'onset' (C) typically denotes the beginning of a problem or event (often negative), and 'offset' (D) means to compensate or move sideways. The sentence requires a word indicating the initial stage, making 'outset' the most appropriate choice.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'outset' with 'onset' due to their similar meanings but distinct contexts (e.g., 'onset' is often used for the start of a problem).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the questions fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedThe Team Manager told us that the race can only be won by -----
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'swift-footed' because the sentence discusses winning a race, which inherently requires speed. 'Swift-footed' directly implies the ability to run quickly. 'Bare-footed' refers to footwear, not speed, while 'flat-footed' and 'tore-footed' are either irrelevant or non-standard terms. Contextual understanding of adjectives describing physical attributes is key here.
questions.common_mistake: Selecting 'bare-footed' due to a literal interpretation of 'foot' in the sentence, ignoring the need for a term related to speed.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedThe Governor rejected the bill and withheld his
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'assent' (option B). In the context of governance, 'assent' refers to formal approval or agreement. When a Governor 'withholds his assent,' it means he refuses to approve a bill. The other options are incorrect: 'accent' relates to pronunciation, 'access' refers to entry or availability, and 'ascent' refers to climbing or rising. The sentence requires a term specific to legislative approval.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'assent' with homophones like 'accent' or 'ascent' due to similar pronunciation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedThe new school is not provided with ---- for science practicals
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'enough equipment' (Option A). 'Equipment' is an uncountable noun and does not take a plural form, making options B and D incorrect. The phrase 'enough equipment' is grammatically correct because 'enough' is used with uncountable nouns to indicate sufficiency. The sentence implies a lack of sufficient resources, so 'enough' is necessary to convey this meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'equipment' (Option C) without 'enough' might be tempting, but the sentence structure requires 'enough' to emphasize insufficiency. Alternatively, pluralizing 'equipment' (Options B and D) is incorrect because it is uncountable.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of questions 41 to 62,fill each gab with the most appropriate option from the list provided.Much as I would love to visit him, i'm afraid -----
questions.explanation: The phrase 'Much as I would love to...' introduces a contrast between a desire and an obstacle. The correct completion must express inability ('I can't') rather than refusal ('I won't') or grammatical errors. 'I can't' (option B) aligns with the speaker's fear of being unable to act on their desire, making it the most appropriate choice.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'can't' (inability) with 'won't' (unwillingness) or overcomplicating the structure with incorrect phrasing like 'I can't be able.'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedllesa witnessed the largest ---- of writers at any convention in recent times
questions.explanation: The sentence refers to the number of writers attending a convention. 'Turnout' means the number of people attending an event, making it the correct choice. 'Turnaround' refers to a reversal or improvement, 'turnover' relates to the rate of replacement or business volume, and 'turn-on' is slang for excitement or stimulation. Only 'turnout' fits the context of attendance.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'turnout' with 'turnover,' which relates to business or personnel changes rather than attendance.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedThe warring faction need words of ------
questions.explanation: The sentence requires a noun to complete the phrase 'words of...' since 'of' typically follows a noun. 'Advice' (option D) is the noun form meaning guidance or recommendations. 'Advise' (A) and 'advises' (C) are verbs, which do not fit the grammatical structure here. 'Adverse' (B) is an adjective meaning harmful or unfavorable, which is irrelevant to the context of providing guidance.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'advise' (verb) with 'advice' (noun). Students may incorrectly select 'advise' due to familiarity with the verb form, ignoring the grammatical requirement for a noun in this context.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedThe politicians were ---- by the press
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'ridiculed' because the press is known to mock or make fun of politicians, which aligns with the meaning of 'ridiculed.' 'Marooned' implies abandonment, 'eclipsed' suggests overshadowing, and 'ostracized' refers to social exclusion, none of which fit the context of press interaction with politicians.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'ostracized' with 'ridiculed' due to similar negative connotations, but 'ostracized' implies exclusion rather than mockery.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedThere are many. --- to her personality
questions.explanation: The word 'facets' refers to distinct aspects or features of a complex entity, making it the most suitable choice to describe the various parts of a personality. 'Moods' (A) relate to temporary emotional states, 'styles' (B) pertain to methods or approaches, and 'faces' (D) is a literal term not typically used metaphorically in this context.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'facets' with 'faces' due to their superficial similarity, even though 'faces' lacks the nuanced meaning required here.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedThere are several ----- in the farmyard
questions.explanation: The sentence requires a general term for the animal. 'Sheep' is the plural of 'sheep' and refers to the animal regardless of age or gender. 'Ewe' refers specifically to an adult female sheep, 'lamb' refers to a young sheep, and 'goat' is a different animal altogether. Since the sentence uses 'several' (a general quantity), the non-specific term 'sheep' is most appropriate.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing specific terms like 'ewe' or 'lamb' with the general term 'sheep'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedAlero called her---- sister
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'younger' because Alero is calling her sister, implying a comparison of age. Since 'younger' is the comparative form of 'young', it is used to describe a person who is younger than another. This is a common usage in English language.
questions.common_mistake: Students may choose 'older' because it is the opposite of 'younger', but it does not fit the context of the sentence.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedWithout our relentless campaigns we might ....... sure of victory in the race for the National Assembly?
questions.explanation: The sentence presents a hypothetical past situation using 'might' to indicate possibility. The correct structure for a third conditional (hypothetical past) is 'might have + past participle.' Here, 'never have been' (option A) fits because it uses the past perfect tense to express that without the campaigns, victory certainty would not have existed. Options B and D use incorrect verb forms ('have never be' and 'be never'), while option C ('never had been') incorrectly places 'had' before 'been' without the auxiliary verb 'have.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing past perfect ('have been') with present perfect ('have be') or omitting the auxiliary verb 'have' entirely.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedHe arrived ---- to see his family leave for the countryside
questions.explanation: The phrase 'in time' is used to indicate that someone arrived just before a specific event occurred. In this context, 'He arrived in time to see his family leave' means he arrived before they left, allowing him to witness the departure. 'Timely' (B) is an adjective and cannot function as a prepositional phrase. 'Late' (C) would imply he arrived after they had already left, contradicting the sentence's intent. 'With' (D) is irrelevant here. The correct structure requires the adverbial phrase 'in time' to convey the intended meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'in time' (just before an event) with 'on time' (punctually) or incorrectly using adjectives like 'timely' in place of adverbial phrases.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of questions 41 to 62,fill each gab with the most appropriate option from the list provided.You can travel on your own ----?
questions.explanation: The sentence 'You can travel on your own ----?' requires a question tag to confirm the statement. The modal verb 'can' in the main clause necessitates the opposite tag 'can't you' to form a grammatically correct question tag. Options A, B, and D use incorrect modal verbs (is, would, should) that do not align with 'can'.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing question tags with other types of questions or mismatching modal verbs (e.g., using 'wouldn't you' instead of 'can't you').

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 41 to 62, fill each gap with the most appropriate option from the list providedOur culture does not allow one to ---- when an elderly person is speaking
questions.explanation: The correct phrasal verb is 'cut in,' which means to interrupt someone while they are speaking. The sentence implies that interrupting an elderly person is culturally unacceptable. 'Cut off' refers to stopping something (e.g., a phone call), 'cut on' is not a standard phrasal verb, and 'cut of' is grammatically incorrect.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'cut in' with 'cut off,' which refers to stopping rather than interrupting.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of questions 41 to 62,fill each gab with the most appropriate option from the list provided.Raffle draws like gambling often end in a ---- for me
questions.explanation: The sentence requires a noun to complete the prepositional phrase 'end in a ----'. 'Loss' (option B) is the correct noun form meaning a negative outcome. 'Lost' (A) is a past tense verb/participle, 'loose' (C) is an adjective/verb, and 'lose' (D) is a verb. The context demands a noun to describe the result of gambling/raffles.
questions.subtopic: Parts of Speech and Word Forms
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'lose' (verb) with 'loss' (noun) due to semantic similarity, or misidentifying the grammatical role required in the sentence.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of questions 63 to 67,select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.If he were here it could be more fun

options.option_a: He did not show up and so the occasion lacked much fun
options.option_b: He was being expected to supply more fun
options.option_c: There was not fun because he was not present
options.option_d: He was expected but did not show up to liven up the occasion.

questions.explanation: The sentence 'If he were here it could be more fun' implies that the person's absence is the reason for the lack of fun. Option D correctly captures this implication by stating that he was expected but did not show up to liven up the occasion. This option requires the reader to infer the consequence of the person's absence, which is a key aspect of coherence and cohesion in language.
questions.common_mistake: Students may mistakenly choose option A, which states that he did not show up and so the occasion lacked much fun. While this option is close, it does not explicitly convey the implication that the person's absence is the reason for the lack of fun.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 63 to 67, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.Though he is our elected representative he often takes a rather jaundiced view of our problem

options.option_a: He takes a rather hazy view of our problems
options.option_b: He takes an unfavourable position concerning our problems
options.option_c: He takes a rather forceful view of our problems
options.option_d: He takes a sickly view of our problems

questions.explanation: The word 'jaundiced' in this context means having a biased or prejudiced view, typically one that is negative or unfavourable. Option B correctly captures this meaning by stating 'He takes an unfavourable position concerning our problems.' The other options misinterpret the term: 'hazy' (A) implies confusion, 'forceful' (C) suggests intensity, and 'sickly' (D) refers to a literal medical condition rather than a metaphorical bias.
questions.common_mistake: Option D is often chosen because 'jaundiced' literally refers to a yellowish skin condition, but the question requires understanding its figurative use to describe a prejudiced attitude.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 63 to 67, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.When I visited Jame I only gave him a congratulatory card on account of his promotion

options.option_a: The only person I visited was James and nobody else
options.option_b: It was only James that I gave a congratulatory card to
options.option_c: All I gave James when I visited him was a congratutory card
options.option_d: All I did when I visited James was give him a congratulatory card

questions.explanation: The sentence emphasizes that the sole action taken during the visit was giving a congratulatory card. The placement of 'only' modifies the verb 'gave,' indicating that no other actions occurred during the visit. Option D correctly captures this by stating that all the speaker did during the visit was give the card. Options A and B misinterpret the focus of the sentence (who was visited vs. what was done). Option C narrows the focus to the item given rather than the action itself.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the focus of 'only' as referring to the item given (card) rather than the action (giving) during the visit.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 63 to 67, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.The events of last Friday show that there is no love tost between the Principal and the Vice-Principal
questions.explanation: The phrase 'no love lost between them' is an idiom meaning there is no affection or goodwill between two people, often implying mutual dislike or hostility. The sentence indicates that the Principal and Vice-Principal have no positive feelings for each other, making option D ('They dislike each other') the correct interpretation.
questions.common_mistake: Option A ('They like each other') is a direct contradiction of the idiom's meaning. Some may misinterpret 'no love lost' literally, assuming it means 'no loss of love,' but the idiom actually conveys the absence of affection.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 63 to 67, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.The politician's inflammatory remarks were heavily criticized.

options.option_a: The politician's rude remarks were heavily criticized
options.option_b: The politician's provocative remarks were heavily criticized
options.option_c: The politicians bombastic remarks were heavily criticized
options.option_d: The politician's tribalistic remarks were heavily criticized.

questions.explanation: The word 'inflammatory' refers to remarks that provoke anger or unrest. 'Provocative' (option B) best captures this meaning, as it implies intent to cause a strong reaction. 'Rude' (A) focuses on impoliteness, 'bombastic' (C) relates to exaggerated language, and 'tribalistic' (D) refers to tribal favoritism, none of which align with 'inflammatory.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'inflammatory' with 'rude' or 'bombastic' due to overlapping connotations of negativity.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThe Governor told the chief that he was only on aroutine tour
questions.explanation: The phrase 'routine tour' implies a visit that is standard, regular, and part of normal duties. Option A ('normal and regular visit') directly aligns with this meaning. Options B and C involve unplanned or impromptu actions, which contradict 'routine.' Option D introduces 'homage,' which is unrelated to the context of a standard visit.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'routine' with 'working visit' in option D, ignoring the inaccuracy of 'homage' in the context.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThe boy was told that he would needseveral morepints of blood if he was to survive
questions.explanation: The phrase 'several more' indicates a moderate number of additional items. 'Many' is the closest synonym as it refers to a large quantity, which aligns with the idea of needing a significant number of additional pints. 'Much' is incorrect because it is used for uncountable nouns, while 'pints' is countable. 'Some' and 'plenty' do not convey the same moderate quantity as 'several'.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'many' with 'plenty' due to both implying a large amount, but 'plenty' suggests excess rather than a moderate number.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThe Principal told the teacher to stopbrow-beatingthe children
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'brow-beat' means to intimidate or pressure someone through aggressive or domineering behavior. In the sentence, the Principal is instructing the teacher to stop intimidating the children. Among the options, 'bullying' (option B) best captures the meaning of aggressive intimidation, while 'pampering' (A) and 'deceiving' (C) are opposites or unrelated. 'Caning' (D) refers to physical punishment, which is not the focus of 'brow-beating.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'brow-beating' with 'caning' due to both involving harsh treatment, but 'brow-beating' emphasizes psychological pressure rather than physical punishment.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsSome actions of the Nigerian youths havealienatedthem from those who weresympatheticto their cause
questions.explanation: The word 'alienated' means to isolate or estrange someone, while 'sympathetic' means having a favorable or kind attitude. Option D ('estranged/well disposed') correctly matches these meanings. 'Estranged' is a direct synonym for 'alienated,' and 'well disposed' aligns with 'sympathetic.' Other options either contradict the original terms (e.g., 'opposed' in option C) or use incorrect pairings (e.g., 'endeared' in option A).
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'sympathetic' with negative terms like 'opposed' or misinterpreting 'alienated' as 'separated' without considering the second part of the phrase.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThe essay topic isnebulous
questions.explanation: The word 'nebulous' refers to something that is vague or unclear in meaning or form. It describes an idea, concept, or object that is not well-defined or is difficult to understand. In this context, the word 'vague' is the nearest in meaning to 'nebulous'. The other options, 'incorrect', 'distinct', and 'clear', do not convey the same meaning as 'nebulous'.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'nebulous' with 'ambiguous', which can also mean unclear, but 'ambiguous' often implies a deliberate attempt to be unclear or misleading, whereas 'nebulous' typically implies a lack of clarity due to a lack of definition or understanding.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThe man was able to persuade hiswillful and obstinatedaughter to follow the career he chose for her
questions.explanation: The italicized words 'willful' and 'obstinate' both describe a person who is determined to have their own way and resistant to change. 'Unyielding' and 'obdurate' (option B) are direct synonyms, as they convey stubbornness and resistance to persuasion. Options A and D focus on positive traits (intelligence, hard work) unrelated to the negative connotations of the original words. Option C introduces unrelated negative traits (odious) that do not align with the context of stubbornness.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'obstinate' with 'arrogant' (option A) or misinterpreting 'willful' as 'hardworking' (option D).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsMr Okon has been described as aneagle-eyededitor
questions.explanation: The phrase 'eagle-eyed' is an idiom used to describe someone with exceptional sharpness of vision or keen observation. 'Clear-sighted' (option B) directly aligns with this meaning, as it refers to having good vision or the ability to perceive details clearly. 'Long-sighted' (C) refers to physical vision correction for distant objects, while 'quick-sighted' (D) is not a standard term. 'Short-sighted' (A) is the opposite of 'eagle-eyed.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'eagle-eyed' with 'long-sighted' due to both relating to vision, but 'eagle-eyed' emphasizes sharpness rather than distance.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsInspite of hergrim situation, the young widow smiled dutifully at the visitors pleasantries
questions.explanation: The word 'pleasantries' refers to polite or friendly remarks, often used to initiate or maintain conversation. In the context of a grim situation (a young widow's mourning), the visitors' 'pleasantries' are likely light-hearted or jocular remarks (D) to ease the tension. While 'condolence messages' (C) might seem plausible, 'pleasantries' is broader and not strictly limited to condolences. 'Jocular remarks' aligns with the idea of polite, perhaps forced, conversation in a somber setting.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'pleasantries' with 'condolence messages' (C) due to the context of mourning, but 'pleasantries' here refers to general polite remarks rather than specific expressions of sympathy.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsI have always believed that my mother is a veryimpassionedwoman
questions.explanation: The word 'impassioned' means full of or characterized by strong emotion or passion. Among the options, 'emotional' (D) is the closest synonym, as it directly relates to experiencing or expressing strong feelings. 'Emotive' (A) refers to the ability to evoke emotions, which is slightly different. 'Impartial' (B) and 'impassive' (C) are incorrect as they mean unbiased and showing no emotion, respectively.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'impassioned' with 'impassive' due to similar prefixes, or selecting 'emotive' as a closer synonym when 'emotional' is more precise.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThe party gathering was thrown into a state ofeuphoriaafter the election result announced
questions.explanation: The word 'euphoria' refers to a feeling of intense happiness or excitement. In the context of the sentence, the party gathering's reaction to the election result is best described as excitement, as it conveys a heightened emotional state. While 'pleasure' is a general term for enjoyment, 'excitement' more accurately captures the intensity and energy associated with euphoria.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'euphoria' with 'pleasure' due to their association with positive emotions, but 'euphoria' implies a stronger, more dynamic reaction.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThe family discussed the crime committed and decided tonail the lie to the counter
questions.explanation: The phrase 'nail the lie to the counter' is an idiom meaning to expose a lie or falsehood publicly. 'Nail' here implies fixing or securing the truth, while 'to the counter' suggests making it visible or known. Option A ('expose it publicly') aligns with this interpretation. Other options either contradict the idiom (B, C) or misinterpret its intent (D).
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the idiom with literal meanings (e.g., interpreting 'nail' as a physical action) or selecting 'seek more advice' (D) due to misunderstanding the context of addressing a lie.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsMy father was at theapogeeof his career when he was retired
questions.explanation: The word 'apogee' refers to the highest point or peak of something. In the context of the sentence, it indicates the father had reached the pinnacle of his career before retiring. Option B ('highest point') directly aligns with this definition. Other options misinterpret the term: 'terminal point' (A) implies an end, 'least productive stage' (C) contradicts the meaning, and 'redundant stage' (D) is irrelevant.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'apogee' with 'perigee' (the opposite term) or misinterpreting it as 'terminal point' due to the context of retirement.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThough David's condition isserioushis life is not in immediate danger
questions.explanation: The word 'serious' in the sentence describes a condition that is severe but not immediately life-threatening. 'Grave' (option D) is the most appropriate synonym, as it conveys a high level of severity without implying immediate danger. 'Nasty' (A) refers to unpleasantness, 'hypertensive' (B) is specific to high blood pressure, and 'dangerous' (C) implies a direct threat, which contradicts the sentence's context.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'dangerous' (C) because it is a direct synonym for 'serious,' but the sentence explicitly states that David's life is not in immediate danger, making 'grave' a better fit.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThat punch by the young boxer proved to befatal
questions.explanation: The word 'fatal' in the sentence means causing death. Among the options, 'deadly' is the most accurate synonym, as it directly conveys the idea of resulting in death. 'Effective' and 'hard' describe the punch's impact but not its lethal outcome, while 'belated' refers to timing, which is irrelevant here.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'effective' or 'hard' with 'fatal' due to their association with strength, rather than the lethal consequence implied by 'fatal'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThe presence of the security men in the area will provide amoment of respitefor the residents
questions.explanation: The phrase 'moment of respite' refers to a brief period of relief or rest. 'Temporary relief' (option D) directly captures this meaning, as 'temporary' aligns with 'moment' and 'relief' matches 'respite.' Options A and B incorrectly imply permanence ('soothing relaxation' and 'enduring reprieve'), while option C shifts focus to 'security,' which is unrelated to the concept of respite.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'respite' with permanent solutions (e.g., 'lasting security') or misinterpreting 'moment' as a prolonged period.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsit is time for all concerned to firstpick to piecesthe strike action before proffering solution
questions.explanation: The phrase 'first pick to pieces the strike action' implies a detailed examination or analysis of the strike action before proposing solutions. 'Critically analyse' (option B) aligns with this meaning, as it involves thorough evaluation. 'Embrace joyfully' (A) and 'commend highly' (D) are positive actions, which do not fit the critical tone. 'Stop abruptly' (C) is unrelated to analysis.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'pick to pieces' with 'pick apart' and misinterpreting it as 'stop abruptly' instead of 'analyze.'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 68 to 84, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsThe new ruler isbig heartedin his dealing with the people
questions.explanation: The phrase 'big hearted' describes someone who is kind, generous, and compassionate. In the context of the sentence, the ruler is portrayed as benevolent in his dealings with the people. Among the options, 'generous' (option A) is the most accurate synonym. 'Cruel' (B) and 'proud' (D) are direct antonyms, while 'soft' (C) is a vague term that does not fully capture the nuance of generosity implied by 'big hearted.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'soft' with 'big hearted' due to the association of 'heart' with softness, but 'soft' lacks the connotation of generosity and kindness central to 'big hearted.'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsThe teacher announced that the class would be making a fleeting to the zoo
questions.explanation: The word 'fleeting' means short-lived or temporary. The opposite of 'fleeting' in the context of a trip's duration would be 'long.' 'Brief' is a synonym of 'fleeting,' while 'routine' and 'guided' do not directly oppose 'fleeting' in meaning. The correct antonym is 'long' (option C).
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'fleeting' with 'brief' (a synonym) instead of identifying 'long' as the true antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsThe project is designed toalleviatepoverty in the country
questions.explanation: The word 'alleviate' means to reduce the severity of a problem. Its antonym in this context is 'exacerbate,' which means to worsen or make a problem worse. 'Tackle' (A) implies addressing a problem, 'eradicate' (C) means to completely eliminate, and 'assuage' (D) is a synonym for 'alleviate.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'eradicate' (C) as the opposite due to its strong action, but it still aligns with reducing a problem rather than worsening it.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsCivil engineering ispredominantlya male profession
questions.explanation: The word 'predominantly' means 'mainly' or 'mostly'. The opposite of this in the context of the sentence would be 'seldom', which means 'rarely' or 'not often'. The other options do not convey the opposite meaning: 'absolutely' implies completeness, 'essentially' refers to the fundamental nature, and 'generally' is similar in meaning to 'predominantly'.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'generally' with 'predominantly' due to their similar meanings, leading to selecting the wrong antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsThe officer said that he knew nothing to thedetrimentof the applicant
questions.explanation: The word 'detriment' means harm or damage. The sentence implies the officer knew nothing that would harm the applicant. The opposite of 'detriment' is 'advantage,' which means benefit. Options A (damage) and B (disfavour) are not direct antonyms, while D (background) is unrelated. Thus, 'advantage' (C) is the correct answer.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'disfavour' (B) with the opposite of 'detriment,' but 'disfavour' relates to lack of favor, not direct harm/benefit.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: When the driver applied the brakes, theyacted up
questions.explanation: The phrase 'acted up' in this context is a phrasal verb that means 'responded well' or 'functioned properly.' While 'acted up' can sometimes mean 'malfunctioned' in mechanical contexts, the sentence implies the brakes worked effectively when the driver applied them. The correct answer is B because the intended meaning here is that the brakes responded well to the driver's action.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'acted up' with 'malfunctioned' due to its literal interpretation in mechanical contexts, leading to incorrect choices like A, C, or D.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsThe striking worker have vowed not to return to work until the decision is rescinded
questions.explanation: The word 'rescinded' means to cancel or revoke a decision. The opposite of this action is 'implemented,' which means to put a decision into effect. The workers want the decision canceled (rescinded), so the opposite would be enforcing it. 'Changed' (A) is not the direct opposite, 'dismissed' (B) is a synonym, and 'incorporated' (D) refers to inclusion rather than cancellation.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'dismissed' (B) with the opposite, as it might seem to mean 'rejected,' but in this context, it aligns with 'rescinded' rather than opposing it.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsIt is rare for a leader and his deputy to see to eye
questions.explanation: The phrase 'see eye to eye' means to agree or share the same opinion. Its opposite is 'disagree,' which directly contradicts the idea of agreement. Options B and C relate to mutual respect and unity of thought (similar to agreement), while D refers to mutual criticism, which is not the direct antonym of agreement.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'reproach each other' (option D) with disagreement, as both involve conflict but are not direct antonyms of agreement.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsCommon sense requires that one should be decorous at formal gathering
questions.explanation: The word in italics is 'decorous'. Decorous means behaving in a way that is socially acceptable and polite. The opposite of 'decorous' is 'impolite', which means behaving in a way that is socially unacceptable and rude. Therefore, the correct answer is option_b.
questions.common_mistake: Students may confuse 'decorous' with 'courteous', which is actually a synonym. They may also think that 'incurious' or 'careful' are the opposites of 'decorous', but they are not.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsThe diminutive figure bounces over the track with unfathomable lightness
questions.explanation: The word 'unfathomable' means something that is impossible to understand or measure. Its antonym would be 'predictable,' which implies something that can be easily understood or anticipated. The phrase 'unfathomable lightness' describes a quality that is mysterious or hard to grasp, so the opposite would logically be something clear or expected. The other options—'invigorating,' 'irresistible,' and 'impressive'—do not directly oppose the meaning of 'unfathomable.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'unfathomable' with words like 'unfamiliar' and selecting an antonym that does not directly contrast the intended meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsI'm not interested in buying that shirt, I think it's overpriced
questions.explanation: The phrase 'overpriced' means that something is too expensive. To find the opposite in meaning, we need to choose an option that means the opposite of 'too expensive'. The correct answer is 'cheap', which is the opposite of 'overpriced'. The other options, 'too expensive' is a synonym, 'overrated' means having a higher reputation than deserved, and 'priceless' means extremely valuable, do not convey the opposite meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'too expensive' as the answer because it seems similar to 'overpriced', or choosing 'priceless' because it seems like an opposite, but actually means something is very valuable.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsDespite his laxity in other matters, Ojo's father drew the line at truancy
questions.explanation: The word 'laxity' in the sentence means leniency or lack of strictness. The phrase 'drew the line at truancy' indicates that Ojo's father does not tolerate truancy, implying rejection. The opposite of 'laxity' in this context is 'rejected' (option B), as it reflects strict opposition to truancy. Other options like 'ignored' (D) would contradict the father's strict stance, while 'favoured' (A) and 'emphasized' (C) do not align with the context of rejecting truancy.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'ignored' with 'rejected' due to the father's strictness, but 'ignored' implies neglect, not active opposition.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsThe string was taut
questions.explanation: The word 'taut' means stretched tight or firm. The opposite of 'taut' would be 'loose,' which means not tight or slack. 'Tight' (option D) is a synonym, not an antonym. 'Firm' (B) and 'stretched' (C) are related but do not directly oppose 'taut' in this context.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'tight' (a synonym) with the correct antonym 'loose' due to similar meanings.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsHypertension is a debilitating disease that everyone should prevent
questions.explanation: The word 'debilitating' means causing a loss of strength or energy. Its antonym should convey the idea of strengthening or energizing. 'Energizing' (option C) directly opposes this meaning. 'Enervating' (option B) is a trap as it is a synonym of 'debilitating', while 'horrible' (option D) refers to unpleasantness rather than physical effect. 'Mortal' (option A) is unrelated to the context.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'enervating' with 'energizing' due to their similar prefixes, leading to selecting the synonym instead of the antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsThe Permanent Secretary left his job under a cloud
questions.explanation: The phrase 'under a cloud' is an idiom meaning to leave under suspicion, disgrace, or a bad reputation. The opposite of this would be 'with a clear record,' indicating an absence of wrongdoing. Options A and D refer to literal weather conditions, which are irrelevant to the figurative meaning. Option C ('in disgrace') is a synonym, not an antonym, of the original phrase.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the idiom with its literal meaning (e.g., weather-related options) or misidentifying synonyms as antonyms.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In each of questions 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italicsWe intend to make the reception a diurnal event
questions.explanation: The word 'diurnal' means occurring during the day or daily. Its direct antonym is 'nocturnal,' which refers to events happening at night. Among the options, 'a nightly' (Option A) best captures this opposition in meaning, as it implies recurring at night. The other options (weekly, short, annual) relate to frequency or duration but do not directly oppose 'diurnal' in terms of time of day.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'diurnal' with other time-related terms like 'weekly' or 'annual' and selecting them due to partial relevance.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: in each of the question 85 to 100, choose the option opposite in meaning to the words(s) or phrase in italicsIt is surprising that this politician has now turnedrenegade
questions.explanation: The word 'renegade' refers to someone who has abandoned their former principles or allegiances, often implying disloyalty. The opposite of this would be 'loyal,' which means faithful to a person, cause, or duty. The other options do not directly oppose 'renegade': 'militant' relates to aggression, 'corrupt' refers to dishonesty, and 'quiet' pertains to noise level, none of which address the core meaning of disloyalty in 'renegade.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'renegade' with 'corrupt' or 'militant' due to overlapping negative connotations, but the key distinction lies in the aspect of loyalty/dissociation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: comprehension passage IOne of the following statements can be deduced from the passage.
questions.passage: UME USE OF ENGLISH 2001 QUESTION APER TYPE :U COMPREHENSION PASSAGE I By 1910 the motor car was plainly conquering the highway. The private car was now part of every rich man’s establishment, although its price made it as yet an impossible luxury for most of the middle class. But for the adventuresome youth, there was the motor cycle, a fearsome invention producing accidents and ear splitting noises. Already, the dignified carriages and smart pony –traps were beginning to disappear from the roads, and coachmen and grooms, unless mechanically minded, were finding it more difficult to make a living. The roads, which had gone to sleep since the coming of the railway, now awoke to feverish activity. Cars and motor cycle dashed along them at speeds which rivalled those of the express trains, and the lorry began to appear. Therefore, the road system was compelled to adapt itself to a volume and speed of traffic for which it had never been intended. Its complete adaptation was impossible. But the road surface was easily transformed and during the early years of the century, the dustiness and greasiness of the highways were lessened by tar- spraying. To widen and strengthen the roads and get rid of blind corners and every steep gradient were task which had scarcely been tackled before 1914. The situation was worst of all in town where not only was any large scheme of road widening usually out of the question, but also where crowding and danger were all too frequently increased by the short-sighted eagerness of town authorities in laying down tramlines. Yet it was not only the road system that was in need of readjustment; the nervous system of those who used and dwelt by the road suffered. The noises caused by conversion of the roads into speedways called for a corresponding tightening up of the nerves; and especially in the towns, the pedestrian who wished to preserve life and limb was compelling to keep his attention continually on the stretch, to practice himself in estimates of the speed of approaching vehicles and to run or jump for hid life if he ventured off he pavement. Adapted from Rachel Carson :the advent

options.option_a: People no longer used trains with the advent of cars and lorries
options.option_b: Significant improvement occurred in road transport since the advent of motor cars, lorries and motorcycles
options.option_c: Human society was static without the express speed of cars and motorcycles
options.option_d: Society would be better of without the chaotic volume and speed of motor cars, lorries and motorcycles

questions.explanation: The passage states that the road system was compelled to adapt itself to a volume and speed of traffic for which it had never been intended. It also mentions that the road surface was easily transformed by tar-spraying, and that efforts were made to widen and strengthen the roads. Therefore, it can be deduced that significant improvement occurred in road transport since the advent of motor cars, lorries, and motorcycles.
questions.common_mistake: Students may be tempted to choose option_a because the passage mentions that people were using trains less, but it does not say that people no longer used trains. Students may also be tempted to choose option_d because the passage describes the chaotic volume and speed of motor cars, lorries, and motorcycles, but it does not say that society would be better off without them.

questions.passage: The emergence of a standard dialect produces the phenomenon known as “accent” which is quite different from dialect.
