questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He needn't have bought that new table
questions.instruction: in each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceHe needn't have bought that new table

options.option_a: it isnt possible that he bought the table
options.option_b: He bought the table, but it wasn't necessary
options.option_c: He didnt buy the table because it wasnt necessary
options.option_d: He doesn't need to buy the table

questions.explanation: The sentence 'He needn't have bought that new table' uses the modal structure 'needn't have + past participle' to indicate that an action was completed but was unnecessary. This contrasts with 'didn't need to + base verb,' which implies the action wasn't done because it wasn't necessary. Option B correctly states that the action occurred (he bought the table) but was unnecessary. Options A and C incorrectly negate the action, while D misapplies present tense logic.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'needn't have + past participle' with 'didn't need to + base verb,' leading to incorrect negation of the action rather than its necessity.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Thanks to that phone call, i was able to obtain the visa
questions.instruction: in each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceThanks to that phone call, i was able to obtain the visa

options.option_a: inspite of that phone call, I obtained the visa
options.option_b: it was because of that phone call that I obtained the visa
options.option_c: I  am grateful to whoever phoned me, and I obtained the visa
options.option_d: If I had not received that phone call I would not have obtained the visa

questions.explanation: The phrase 'Thanks to' indicates causation, meaning the phone call was the reason the speaker obtained the visa. Option B directly states this causal relationship. Option A incorrectly implies the phone call was an obstacle, while Option C focuses on gratitude without emphasizing causation. Option D uses a hypothetical structure that is less direct than the explicit causation in B.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'Thanks to' with expressions of gratitude (Option C) or misinterpreting it as a hypothetical scenario (Option D).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: it is likely that the governor will exact his pound of flesh
questions.instruction: in each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceit is likely that the governor will exact his pound of flesh

options.option_a: He will probably  demand a hefty bribe
options.option_b: He will probably impose engineer the assassination of his opponents
options.option_c: He will probably impose crushing new taxes
options.option_d: He will probably demand for and get all that is due to him

questions.explanation: The phrase 'exact his pound of flesh' is an idiom derived from Shakespeare's 'The Merchant of Venice,' where it refers to demanding a harsh or vengeful penalty. Option D correctly captures this meaning by emphasizing the idea of demanding and receiving what is perceived as one's due, often in a strict or unforgiving manner. The other options misinterpret the idiom: 'hefty bribe' (A) implies corruption, 'assassination' (B) suggests violence, and 'crushing taxes' (C) relates to financial burden, none of which align with the idiom's core meaning of uncompromising retribution or demand.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the idiom with literal demands like bribes or taxes, which are not its intended meaning.
related_topics: Use of Context Clues in Reading Comprehension

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: It was too cold for him to go out
questions.instruction: In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceIt was too cold for him to go out

options.option_a: He had a bad cold, and did not go out
options.option_b: Although it was very cold, he still went out
options.option_c: As it was very cold, he did not go out
options.option_d: He was afraid to go out that day

questions.explanation: The sentence 'It was too cold for him to go out' uses the structure 'too [adjective] to [verb]', which indicates that the condition (cold weather) made the action (going out) impossible. Option C correctly captures this meaning by stating that the cold weather prevented him from going out. Options A and D misinterpret the word 'cold' as a sickness or fear, while Option B contradicts the 'too...to' structure by implying he went out despite the cold.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the word 'cold' as a sickness (Option A) or misinterpreting the 'too...to' structure as a contrast (Option B).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Ado and Abu are always together these days. They must be up to something.
questions.instruction: in each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceAdo and Abu are always together these days. They must be up to something.

options.option_a: They must have reconciled after their quarrel
options.option_b: they are probably planning something bad
options.option_c: They are capable of a praiseworthy achievement
options.option_d: They bear some responsibility for what has happened

questions.explanation: The phrase 'must be up to something' implies suspicion about secretive or potentially negative intentions. The speaker suggests that Ado and Abu's constant togetherness is unusual and possibly indicative of planning something harmful. Option B aligns with this interpretation, while other options either introduce unsupported details (A, D) or misinterpret the tone as positive (C).
questions.common_mistake: Choosing Option A by assuming a prior quarrel exists, which is not mentioned in the original statement, or selecting Option C by misreading 'up to something' as a positive action.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He wants the meeting to be adjourned
questions.instruction: in each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceHe wants the meeting to be adjourned

options.option_c: He wants the meeting to continue till another day
options.option_d: He  wants the meeting to commence another day without delay

questions.explanation: The sentence 'He wants the meeting to be adjourned' implies that he wants the meeting to be temporarily stopped and resumed on another day. Adjournment does not mean cancellation or closure, but rather a temporary postponement. Therefore, option C 'He wants the meeting to continue till another day' is the correct explanation.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'adjourned' with 'cancelled' or 'closed', leading to incorrect interpretations.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: My father is one of the vociferous few challenging the company's appointment of the manager
questions.instruction: in each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceMy father is one of the vociferous few challenging the company's appointment of the manager

options.option_a: My father is the one who shouts with a loud voice against the appointment of the manager
options.option_b: My father and others speak on behalf of the company against the appointment of the manager
options.option_c: my father is one of those objecting to the appointment of the manager
options.option_d: My father is agitated by the appointment of the manager

questions.explanation: The sentence states that the speaker's father is part of a small group ('few') that is 'vociferous' (loudly and forcefully) in challenging the manager's appointment. Option C correctly captures this by stating he is 'one of those objecting,' aligning with the plural 'few' and the active opposition implied by 'vociferous.' Options A and D incorrectly imply singularity or insufficient action, while B misrepresents the relationship between the group and the company.
questions.common_mistake: Misinterpreting 'vociferous' as solely referring to loudness without considering the collective aspect ('few') or the act of challenging.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The voyagers fetched up in Nigeria
questions.instruction: in each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceThe voyagers fetched up in Nigeria

options.option_a: The foreigners fetched up in Nigeria
options.option_b: The journey by sea ended in Nigeria
options.option_c: The travellers made a stoppover in Nigeria
options.option_d: The discoverers landed in NIgeria after a long journey

questions.explanation: The phrase 'fetched up' means to arrive at a destination after a journey. The sentence 'The voyagers fetched up in Nigeria' implies that the travelers reached Nigeria after a long journey. Option D correctly interprets this by stating that the 'discoverers landed in Nigeria after a long journey,' aligning with the meaning of 'fetched up' and the context of a journey. While 'voyagers' and 'discoverers' are not exact synonyms, the core meaning of arriving after a journey is preserved. Other options either misinterpret the action (e.g., 'stopover' in C) or add unwarranted details (e.g., 'journey by sea' in B).
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'fetched up' with 'stopover' or assuming the journey was specifically by sea.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In those days in this school, everyone who spoke in a language other than English paid a fine of ten naira
questions.instruction: in each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceIn those days in this school, everyone who spoke in a language other than English paid a fine of ten naira

options.option_a: Everyone of us paid a fine of ten naira because we did not always speak in English
options.option_b: Everyone would pay a fine of ten naira for wanting to use a language other than English
options.option_c: Those who spoke a language other than English on the premises paid a fine to ten naira
options.option_d: Those who intended to speak other languages on the school premises were required to pay naira

questions.explanation: The sentence states that in the past, at the school, anyone who spoke a language other than English had to pay a fine of ten naira. The correct option should convey this information accurately. Option C, 'Those who spoke a language other than English on the premises paid a fine to ten naira', accurately reflects the information in the sentence, using 'on the premises' to imply 'in the school'.
questions.common_mistake: A common mistake would be to misinterpret the conditionality of the sentence, assuming it implies everyone paid the fine (option A), or that it was a future/ intended action (option D), or incorrectly phrasing the condition (option B).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The officer has discussed the vexed issue of incessant power failure In
questions.instruction: in each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceThe officer has discussed the vexed issue of incessant power failureIn

options.option_a: In anger, the officer explained the problem of constant power failure
options.option_b: The officer afdded his voice to the much discussed problem of power cut
options.option_c: The officer's explanations angered those who have suffered the effects of frequent power cut
options.option_d: The officer told the people not to be angered by the frequent power cut

questions.explanation: The original sentence refers to the officer discussing a 'vexed issue' (a long-standing, frustrating problem) of 'incessant power failure' (constant power outages). Option B correctly captures this by stating the officer 'added his voice to the much discussed problem,' indicating he contributed to an ongoing conversation about a widely recognized issue. Other options introduce elements like anger (A, C) or advice (D) not present in the original sentence.
questions.common_mistake: Misinterpreting 'vexed' as implying anger in the officer's tone (Option A) or assuming unintended consequences like angering others (Option C).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The weather condition now prevailing in the town is unbearable
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe weather condition now prevailing in the town isunbearable
questions.explanation: The word 'unbearable' means extremely unpleasant or intolerable. The opposite in meaning would be 'bearable' or 'tolerable', which implies something that is not extreme or unpleasant. Among the options provided, 'uncommon' is the one that is closest to being opposite in meaning to 'unbearable', as it suggests something that is not extreme or unusual.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing an option that is similar in meaning to 'unbearable', such as 'uncontrollable' or 'dominant', instead of one that is opposite in meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The lady was completely nonplussed when her suitor rejected her gifts
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe lady was completelynonplussedwhen her suitor rejected her gifts
questions.explanation: The word 'nonplussed' means confused or puzzled. The opposite of this is 'unpuzzled,' which means not confused. While 'surprised' (B) might seem related, it does not directly oppose 'nonplussed.' 'Unconscious' (C) and 'disappointed' (D) are unrelated in this context. The correct antonym is 'unpuzzled' (A).
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'nonplussed' with 'surprised' and selecting B as the opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: As a public officer, he should act with scrupulous honesty at all times
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsAs a public officer, he should act withscrupuloushonesty at all times
questions.explanation: The word 'scrupulous' means showing careful and thorough consideration, especially in moral or ethical matters. The opposite of 'scrupulous honesty' would be acting without care or attention to ethical standards, which is best captured by 'careless.' 'Impeccable' (A) means flawless, which is a synonym. 'Transparent' (C) relates to openness, not the opposite of carefulness. 'Uncompromising' (D) refers to firmness, not the opposite of scrupulous.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'uncompromising' (D) as the opposite due to its negative connotation, or misinterpreting 'impeccable' (A) as a typo for 'impeccable' and assuming it is the opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Men from the agency went into the market in search of  unwholesome  food items
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsMen from the agency went into the market in search ofunwholesomefood items
questions.explanation: The word 'unwholesome' means unhealthy or harmful. Its direct antonym is 'healthy,' which refers to being in good physical condition. The other options do not convey the opposite meaning: 'imported' refers to origin, 'banned' relates to prohibition, and 'uncooked' describes preparation method. The context of the sentence (searching for harmful food items) reinforces that 'healthy' is the correct opposite.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'unwholesome' with 'banned' or 'uncooked' due to partial semantic overlap, rather than focusing on the health aspect.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The condition of the hostels has become deplorable
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe condition of the hostels has become deplorable
questions.explanation: The word 'deplorable' means deserving or causing deep regret or sadness. Its opposite should be a positive term. 'Admirable' (option A) means worthy of admiration, which is the direct antonym. 'Regrettable' (B) is a synonym, 'bearable' (C) is neutral and not a direct opposite, and 'malignant' (D) is more negative but not the opposite.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'bearable' (C) as the opposite, mistaking it for a positive term when it merely implies tolerance rather than positivity.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The plan to merge the two local government areas has met with much apathy
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe plan to merge the two local government areas has met with muchapathy
questions.explanation: The word 'apathy' means a lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern. The opposite of apathy is 'enthusiasm,' which signifies active interest and eagerness. The other options do not fit: 'hospitality' refers to friendliness, 'criticism' implies disapproval, and 'consideration' means careful thought. The sentence context requires a word indicating active engagement, making 'enthusiasm' the correct antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'criticism' (B) as the opposite due to a misunderstanding of 'apathy' as disapproval rather than indifference.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: There is now a dearth of talent in the industry , she said
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThere is nowa dearth of talentin the industry , she said
questions.explanation: The word 'dearth' means a scarcity or lack of something. The opposite of 'dearth' is 'abundance,' which signifies a large quantity or surplus. In the sentence, the speaker is emphasizing the scarcity of talent, so the correct antonym is 'an abundance.' Options A and D ('a lack' and 'a shortage') are synonyms of 'dearth,' not antonyms. 'A rebirth' (C) is unrelated to the context of scarcity.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'dearth' with 'shortage' (option D) because they are synonyms, not antonyms.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The students vandalised their hostel during the riot
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe studentsvandalisedtheir hostel during the riot
questions.explanation: The word 'vandalised' means to damage or destroy property maliciously. The opposite of this action would be 'repaired,' which involves fixing or restoring something that has been damaged. 'Protected' (C) refers to preventing damage, but since the vandalism already occurred, 'repaired' is the more direct antonym. 'Deserted' (A) and 'decorated' (D) do not convey the opposite meaning of damaging property.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'protected' (C) because it relates to preventing damage, but the context requires an action that reverses the damage already done.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: His kind-hearted master bought him a motorcycle
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsHiskind-heartedmaster bought him a motorcycle
questions.explanation: The word 'kind-hearted' describes someone who is compassionate and generous. The opposite of this trait is 'stingy,' which means unwilling to spend or give. While 'generous' (B) is a synonym, 'shrewd' (C) relates to being clever, and 'angry' (D) refers to an emotion, none of which are direct antonyms of 'kind-hearted.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'angry' (D) as the opposite due to misinterpreting emotional traits rather than focusing on generosity.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: mutual love is what Kabi and Musa have in common, and nothing else
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsmutual loveis what Kabi and Musa have in common, and nothing else
questions.explanation: The word 'mutual' refers to a feeling, action, or relationship that is shared or experienced by two or more people equally (reciprocal). In the context of the sentence, it means both Kabi and Musa love each other. The opposite of a shared, two-way feeling is one that is felt by only one person, which is 'one-sided' (unilateral).
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse antonyms with synonyms or choose an option that describes a negative quality (like 'insincere') rather than the logical opposite of the word's directional meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Always strive to get what is legitimate
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsAlways strive to get what islegitimate
questions.explanation: The word 'legitimate' means something that is lawful, valid, or conforming to the law. Since the instruction requires the option opposite in meaning (antonym), 'ilicit' (a variant spelling of 'illicit') is the correct choice because it means illegal or forbidden by law. 'Legal' is a synonym, while 'good' and 'impure' do not capture the legal/formal context of legitimacy.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing Option B (legal) because it has a similar meaning to 'legitimate,' failing to follow the instruction to find the word 'opposite' in meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: some aspects of their culture are out of date
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicssome aspects of their culture areout of date
questions.explanation: The phrase 'out of date' means something is old-fashioned, obsolete, or no longer in style or use. To find the opposite, we look for a word that describes something current, modern, or popular. 'Fashionable' refers to something that is currently in style or contemporary, making it the direct antonym of 'out of date'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'out of date' with 'fake' or 'counterfeit,' leading them to choose 'genuine' or 'fake'. However, 'out of date' refers to time and relevance, not authenticity.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: on the first day of her examination, Amina felt very confident
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicson the first day of her examination, Amina felt veryconfident
questions.explanation: In this context, 'confident' means feeling self-assured, calm, and certain of one's success. The instruction asks for the opposite in meaning. 'Strung up' is an idiomatic expression meaning to be extremely nervous, tense, or anxious. Since being nervous/tense is the direct emotional opposite of being confident and poised during an examination, option D is the correct choice. Option A (excited) is a positive emotion; Option B (dull) refers to a lack of intelligence or interest; Option C (beefed up) means strengthened.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'dull' because they mistakenly associate 'confident' with 'bright' or 'intelligent'. Others might choose 'excited' if they confuse the instruction for synonyms instead of antonyms.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: My father is always very frank about his intentions
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsMy father is always veryfrankabout his intentions
questions.explanation: The word 'frank' means to be honest, direct, and open in expression. In the context of the sentence, the father does not hide what he intends to do. The opposite of being open and direct is being 'secretive', which means inclined to conceal one's feelings, intentions, or actions. While 'deceitful' implies dishonesty, 'secretive' is the more precise antonym for the lack of openness implied by 'frank'.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often mistakenly choose synonyms (like 'open') instead of antonyms because they forget to strictly follow the instruction to find the opposite in meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The speaker was rather bold in his presentation of the case
questions.instruction: in each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe speaker was ratherboldin his presentation of the case
questions.explanation: In this context, 'bold' refers to a speaker who is assertive, confident, and outspoken in their delivery. The instruction asks for the word opposite in meaning. 'Reserved' is the correct choice because it describes someone who is restrained, reticent, or shy in their manner or speech, which is the direct behavioral opposite of being bold.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'ashamed' because they associate being bold with being 'shameless' or 'brazen.' However, 'ashamed' refers to a feeling of guilt, whereas 'bold' and 'reserved' refer to communication styles and personality traits.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The doctor tried to soothe the patient before the operation
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe doctor tried tosoothethe patient before the operation
questions.explanation: The word 'soothe' means to gently calm a person's feelings, reduce their anxiety, or alleviate their pain. In the context of a patient awaiting an operation, they are likely feeling nervous or distressed. Therefore, the doctor would attempt to 'calm' them. Option A (examine) refers to a physical check-up; Option B (treat) refers to the general medical care; and Option D (induce) means to bring about or cause a physical state, such as sleep or labor.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'treat' because it is a general medical term related to doctors, without considering the specific emotional state implied by 'soothe'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The charge brought against my brother was hardly tenable
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe charge brought against my brother washardly tenable
questions.explanation: The word 'tenable' is an adjective used to describe a belief, argument, or position that is able to be maintained or defended against attack or objection. In a legal context, a 'tenable charge' is one that can be supported by evidence and justified in court. Therefore, 'defensible' is the direct synonym. The sentence 'The charge... was hardly tenable' implies that the accusation was weak and difficult to defend or justify.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'flimsy' (Option D) because the sentence as a whole implies the charge was flimsy. However, 'flimsy' is an antonym of 'tenable'. Since the instruction asks for the meaning of the italicized word 'tenable' specifically, 'defensible' is the correct choice.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The man described his son as a wilful character
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe man described his son as awilfulcharacter
questions.explanation: The word 'wilful' (or willful) is used to describe someone who is headstrong, stubborn, and determined to have their own way regardless of the consequences or the advice of others. 'Obstinate' is the nearest in meaning because it refers to a person who is stubbornly refusing to change their opinion or chosen course of action, even when persuaded to do so.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'wilful' with 'wild' because of the similar phonetic start, or with 'wicked' because they assume that being headstrong is inherently evil, but 'wilful' specifically describes the trait of stubbornness.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: our teacher described Agbo's story as a phantom
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsour teacher described Agbo's story as aphantom
questions.explanation: The word 'phantom' refers to something that is illusory, non-existent in physical form, or a product of the imagination. When a story is described as a 'phantom,' it implies that it is not based on reality or lacks substance. 'Fanciful' means existing only in the imagination or characterized by fancy rather than reason or experience, making it the closest synonym in this context. While phantoms (ghosts) can be 'scary' (Option A), the word itself describes the nature of being unreal rather than the emotion of fear.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'scary' because they associate the word 'phantom' with ghosts, failing to realize the word refers to the 'unreal' or 'imaginary' quality of the story.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I find the way she approaches her customers quite repugnant
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsI find the way she approaches her customers quiterepugnant
questions.explanation: The word 'repugnant' is an adjective used to describe something that is extremely distasteful, offensive, or disgusting. In the context of the sentence, it describes a negative reaction to someone's behavior. Among the options provided, 'unpleasant' is the nearest in meaning as it denotes something that is not pleasing or is disagreeable. While 'repugnant' is stronger than 'unpleasant,' it is the only logically negative synonym available; 'attractive' and 'encouraging' are opposites, and 'ungodly' refers more to religious or extreme behavior rather than a general sense of distaste.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse 'nearest in meaning' with 'opposite in meaning' and might mistakenly choose 'attractive' (Option B). Additionally, some might choose 'ungodly' (Option C) because it sounds like a strong negative word, but it does not accurately fit the context of business interaction.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: participation in the programme is optional
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsparparticipation in theprogramme is optional
questions.explanation: The word 'optional' means something that is not compulsory or mandatory; it is left to one's own discretion or preference. In the context of the sentence, if participation is optional, it means it is up to the individual to decide whether to join or not. Therefore, 'a matter of choice' is the phrase nearest in meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates may mistakenly choose 'unnecessary' (Option A) because they assume that if something isn't required, it isn't needed. However, 'optional' focuses on the freedom to decide, not the utility or value of the action.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Scientists have invented ways of preserving fruits much longer
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsScientists haveinventedways of preserving fruits much longer
questions.explanation: In this context, 'invented' refers to the creation of a new method, system, or process through thought and experimentation. 'Devised' is the nearest synonym as it means to plan or invent a complex procedure or mechanism by careful thought. 'Coined' is typically used for the creation of new words or phrases, while 'arranged' and 'organised' refer to the orderly placement of existing things rather than the act of original creation.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse 'coined' with 'invented'; however, 'coined' is specifically used for language (words/phrases), whereas 'devised' is the correct term for scientific methods or schemes.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The attempt to count the population was largely  successful
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe attempt to count the population waslargelysuccessful
questions.explanation: The word 'largely' is an adverb used to mean 'to a great extent' or 'for the most part'. In the context of the sentence, saying an event was 'largely successful' means it was successful in most aspects, but not necessarily in its entirety. Therefore, 'mostly' is the most accurate synonym. 'Completely' and 'totally' imply 100% success, which is more absolute than 'largely', while 'hardly' is an antonym meaning 'barely'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'largely' for absolute terms like 'completely' or 'totally'. It is important to recognize that 'largely' suggests a high degree but allows for minor exceptions.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The governor has approved the award of the contract
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe governor hasapprovedthe award of the contract
questions.explanation: In the context of the sentence, 'approved' means to give official sanction or formal consent to a proposal or act. 'Endorsed' is the nearest in meaning because it means to declare one's public approval or support for something, or to sign a document to make it valid. While 'acknowledged' means to recognize receipt and 'vetoed' is the direct opposite (to reject), 'endorsed' captures the authoritative backing required for a contract award.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse synonyms with antonyms and might mistakenly choose 'vetoed' (Option C), which is the opposite of 'approved'. Some might also choose 'acknowledged' (Option B), which is too passive for a formal contract process.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I cannot stand Simon . I find his attitude offensive
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsI cannot stand Simon . I find his attitude offensive
questions.explanation: In this context, the word 'offensive' describes an attitude that is highly unpleasant, disagreeable, or causing resentment. The word 'obnoxious' is the nearest in meaning as it specifically describes someone or something that is extremely unpleasant, rude, or offensive to others. 'Unapproachable' means difficult to talk to, 'wicked' means evil, and 'unpardonable' means unforgivable; none of these capture the specific nuance of a disagreeable personality as accurately as 'obnoxious' does.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse 'offensive' with 'wicked' (Option C). While offensive behavior can be bad, 'wicked' implies a level of moral evil or depravity that goes beyond a generally unpleasant or annoying attitude.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The man would not withdraw what he had said
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe man would notwithdrawwhat he had said
questions.explanation: In the context of speech or a statement, to 'withdraw' means to retract, recant, or admit that what was said was incorrect or should not have been spoken. The phrasal verb 'take back' is the direct idiomatic equivalent used when someone wants to retract a statement. Options B, C, and D do not carry the specific meaning of retracting words; 'take out' refers to removal or social dates, 'take away' refers to subtraction or physical removal, and 'take from' refers to lessening the value of something.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'take back' with 'take away'. While 'take away' means to remove an object physically, 'take back' is the specific expression used for retracting words or promises.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The disagreement between the two men became obvious during the meeting
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThedisagreementbetween the two men became obvious during the meeting
questions.explanation: The word 'disagreement' refers to a difference of opinion or a lack of consensus. In the context of the sentence, when this disagreement becomes 'obvious' during a meeting, it signifies a visible clash or 'confrontation' between the two parties. Option A (insult) refers to offensive remarks; Option C (passion) refers to strong emotion; and Option D (insinuation) refers to an indirect hint. Among the choices, 'confrontation' is the closest in meaning to a situation where a disagreement manifests openly.
questions.common_mistake: Students may choose 'insult' because they associate disagreements with rude behavior, but a disagreement is primarily a conflict of views, which leads to a confrontation, not necessarily an insult.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The principal detested his recalcitrant attitude
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe principal detested hisrecalcitrantattitude
questions.explanation: The word 'recalcitrant' is an adjective used to describe someone who is stubbornly uncooperative or resistant toward authority or discipline. In the context of a school setting involving a principal, a recalcitrant attitude refers to a student or staff member who refuses to obey rules. Therefore, 'disobedient' is the closest synonym. 'Arrogant' refers to pride, 'voracious' refers to an insatiable appetite, and 'vengeful' refers to seeking revenge.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse 'recalcitrant' with 'arrogant' (Option B) because rebellious behavior is sometimes associated with pride. However, recalcitrance specifically focuses on the act of defiance and disobedience rather than self-importance.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The union officials suddenly became restive
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe union officials suddenly becamerestive
questions.explanation: The word 'restive' describes a state of being unable to remain still, silent, or submissive, especially because of boredom, dissatisfaction, or impatience. In the context of union officials, it implies they were becoming agitated or restless due to a lack of progress or patience. While 'unruly' (Option A) can be a result of being restive, 'impatient' is the primary characteristic of the word in this context. It is a common 'trap' word in JAMB because it sounds like it should mean 'restful,' but it actually means the opposite.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often mistake 'restive' for 'restful' or 'calm' due to its spelling, or they confuse it with 'unruly,' which refers more to disruptive behavior than the internal state of agitation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The popularity of the military dictator waned after the war
questions.instruction: in each of question 51 to 65 , choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe popularity of the military dictatorwanedafter the war
questions.explanation: The word 'waned' means to decrease in vigor, power, or extent; to become weaker or smaller. It is often used to describe the phases of the moon (getting smaller) or the fading of influence and popularity. In the context of the sentence, the dictator's popularity decreased after the war. Therefore, 'declined' is the nearest in meaning. Options A and D are antonyms (opposites), and Option B is too vague.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'wane' with its opposite 'wax' (to grow or increase). Another common mistake is choosing 'changed' because it is technically true, but in synonym questions, you must choose the most specific and accurate meaning provided.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The chairman addressed the .........
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The chairman addressed the .........
questions.explanation: In English, there is a conventional order for cumulative adjectives preceding a noun. The general order is: Quantity/Number > Opinion > Size > Age > Shape > Color > Origin > Material > Purpose > Noun. In this sentence, 'one hundred' is a quantity/number, 'university' functions as an adjective describing the nature/origin of the teachers, and 'French' describes the subject specialization. Option A correctly places the number at the beginning, followed by the descriptors and the noun head.
questions.common_mistake: Students often fail to realize that numbers must always precede descriptive adjectives, leading them to choose options that scatter the number (one hundred) in the middle of the phrase.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Kanuri is a language........
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Kanuri is a language........

options.option_b: that i can't speak it well
options.option_c: of which  I cant speak it well

questions.explanation: The correct answer is D because the relative clause 'I can't speak well' correctly omits the relative pronoun 'that/which' when it functions as the object of the verb 'speak.' Options A, B, and C incorrectly include redundant pronouns ('it') or unnecessary prepositions ('of which'), violating the rules of relative clause construction. In formal grammar, the relative pronoun is omitted when it serves as the object and the clause is non-restrictive.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing options with redundant pronouns (A, B) or incorrect prepositions (C) due to confusion about relative clause structure.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Last Tuesday, Ochunu asked me .........
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Last Tuesday, Ochunu asked me .........

options.option_c: whether I had come the day before

questions.explanation: The correct answer is C because the sentence requires a reported question structure. The main clause 'asked me' indicates reported speech, so the subordinate clause must use 'whether' or 'if' followed by the past perfect tense ('had come') to show an action completed before the past time mentioned ('Last Tuesday'). 'The day before' is the correct temporal adjustment for 'yesterday' in reported speech. Options A and B use direct question structures incorrectly, while D fails to adjust the time reference properly.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing option D due to the use of past perfect without adjusting the time reference from 'yesterday' to 'the day before'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The young man has......to sober...after been drunk
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The young man has......to sober...after been drunk
questions.explanation: The sentence requires the past participle form of the verb 'begin' because it follows the auxiliary verb 'has' (present perfect tense). The past participle of 'begin' is 'begun' (begin - began - begun). Furthermore, the phrasal verb 'sober up' is the correct idiomatic expression used to describe the process of becoming sober after being intoxicated.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the past tense 'began' with the past participle 'begun' after auxiliary verbs. Additionally, some may incorrectly use 'sober down' or 'sober in' due to a misunderstanding of English phrasal verbs.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: my mother had.....the fire wood before it began to rain
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).my mother had.....the fire wood before it began to rain
questions.explanation: The sentence is in the Past Perfect tense, which is formed using 'had' + the past participle of the main verb. The verb 'split' is an irregular verb where the base form, past tense, and past participle are identical (split - split - split). Therefore, 'split' is the correct past participle, while 'splited' and 'splitted' are non-existent words in standard English.
questions.common_mistake: Many students incorrectly assume that all verbs form the past participle by adding '-ed', leading them to choose 'splitted' or 'splited', which are grammatically incorrect.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The police offier warned the ........communities against taking the law ......hand
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The police offier warned the ........communities against taking the law ......hand
questions.explanation: The sentence requires two parts: a descriptive adjective for communities and a specific idiomatic phrase. First, 'feuding' is the correct adjective to describe communities that are in conflict or at war with each other; 'feudal' refers to the medieval social system. Second, the correct idiomatic expression for someone who ignores legal processes to seek personal vengeance is 'to take the law into one's own hands.' Therefore, 'feuding / into their own' is the grammatically and idiomatically correct choice.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the adjective 'feudal' (relating to feudalism) with 'feuding' (engaged in a feud/conflict). Additionally, students sometimes incorrectly use the preposition 'in' instead of the required 'into' for the idiom 'taking the law into one's own hands'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Agbo could not travel as he had come........influenza
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Agbo could not travel as he had come........influenza
questions.explanation: In English, the phrasal verb 'come down with' is specifically used to describe the act of falling ill with a particular disease or ailment. Since influenza is an illness, 'down with' is the idiomatic expression required to complete the sentence.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'come down with' (to fall ill) with 'come over' (to visit someone) or 'come on' (to start), leading them to select incorrect options based on surface-level interpretations of the verbs.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: when he .....from his journey tell him I want to see him
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).when he .....from his journey tell him I want to see him
questions.explanation: In an adverbial clause of time introduced by 'when', we do not use the future tense (e.g., 'will return') to refer to a future event. Instead, we use the simple present tense ('returns') to indicate a future action that is expected to happen. Since the main clause ('tell him I want to see him') is an imperative (a command/request), the subordinate clause must use the simple present tense.
questions.subtopic: Sequence of Tenses / Adverbial Clauses of Time
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistakenly use the future tense 'will return' because they perceive the action as happening in the future, forgetting that time clauses in English grammar require the simple present tense for future meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I knocked at his door, but he.......
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).I knocked at his door, but he.......
questions.explanation: The sentence describes two actions that happened in the past: knocking at the door and the act of leaving. According to the rule of the sequence of tenses, when an action is completed before another action in the past, the 'past perfect' tense (had + past participle) must be used. Since the person had already left before the narrator knocked, 'had already left' is the grammatically correct choice.
questions.common_mistake: Students often wrongly choose 'has already left' (present perfect), which is incorrect because the entire sentence is set in the past tense ('knocked'), making the present perfect tense incompatible.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: .....of the students turned up, so the lecture was cancelled.
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s)......of the students turned up, so the lecture was cancelled.
questions.explanation: The word 'students' is a countable noun, which eliminates 'little' and 'a little' (used for uncountable nouns). The sentence indicates that the lecture was cancelled, implying that an insufficient number of students arrived. 'Few' means 'not many' (a negative connotation indicating scarcity), whereas 'a few' means 'some' (a positive connotation). Since the event was cancelled due to the lack of attendance, 'few' is the correct choice.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'few/little' with 'a few/a little'. 'Few' and 'little' have negative implications (almost none), while 'a few' and 'a little' have positive implications (at least some).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He bought a ....against his neighbour
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).He bought a ....against his neighbour
questions.explanation: The sentence requires a direct object to complete the verb 'bought'. In English grammar, 'complaint' is a noun, which serves as the object of the verb. 'Complains' is a verb (present tense), 'complain' is the base form of the verb, and 'complaining' is a participle/gerund. None of these function as a count noun in this context. Therefore, 'complaint' is the only grammatically correct option.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the verb 'complain' with the noun 'complaint' and may incorrectly choose 'complaining' if they mistakenly assume the sentence structure requires a gerund.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The hotel lacks the ......for accommodating so many guests
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The hotel lacks the ......for accommodating so many guests
questions.explanation: In English usage, 'capacity' refers to the physical volume or the maximum amount that a container, space, or facility can hold or accommodate. Since the sentence refers to the physical limitations of a hotel building regarding the number of guests it can house, 'capacity' is the most appropriate term. 'Ability' and 'capability' refer to skills or power to perform an action, while 'competence' refers to the skill or knowledge to do something successfully.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'capacity' (volume/space limit) with 'capability' (the power or potential to do something), choosing 'capability' because they associate it with the hotel's 'ability' to perform a service.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: if you are not careful, you would ..........your money
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).if you are not careful, you would ..........your money
questions.explanation: The sentence requires the verb form 'lose', which means to be deprived of something or to fail to keep it. The word 'lose' (rhymes with 'ooze') is a verb. 'Loss' is a noun (meaning the state of having lost something), 'loose' (rhymes with 'goose') is an adjective (meaning not tight), and 'lost' is the past tense or past participle of 'lose'. Since the auxiliary verb 'would' requires a base form of the verb, 'lose' is the only grammatically correct option.
questions.common_mistake: Many students confuse 'lose' (verb) with 'loose' (adjective). Remembering that 'loose' has an extra 'o' and sounds like 'goose' helps distinguish it from the verb 'lose'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: You must practise in order to.........perfection
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).You must practise in order to.........perfection
questions.explanation: In English, certain words are conventionally paired together, a linguistic feature known as 'collocation'. While 'obtain', 'have', and 'get' are synonymous in a general sense, they do not collocate with the noun 'perfection'. The phrase 'achieve perfection' is the standard idiomatic expression used to describe reaching a state of flawless performance through effort and practice.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'get' because it is a versatile, informal verb; however, 'get perfection' is grammatically awkward and lacks the formal precision required in standard English usage.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The condition of the room was so .................so I went outside
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The condition of the room was so .................so I went outside
questions.explanation: The word 'intolerable' means 'unable to be endured' or 'unbearable'. In this context, the room's condition was so bad (e.g., too hot, dirty, or noisy) that the speaker could not stay inside, leading them to go outside. 'Intolerant' refers to a person's inability to accept others' views; 'inconstant' refers to something that is not constant or changes frequently; 'invariable' means something that never changes. None of the other options logically fit the context of a room's physical condition.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'intolerant' and 'intolerable'. 'Intolerant' is used for humans or attitudes, while 'intolerable' is used for situations, conditions, or levels of pain.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: You dont like mathematics .................you
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).You dont like mathematics .................you
questions.explanation: The sentence is a statement that uses a negative verb phrase ('do not like'). According to the rules of English grammar, when the main statement is negative, the question tag must be positive. Therefore, the tag should be the auxiliary verb 'do' followed by the subject pronoun 'you'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mirror the negative form of the main clause in the tag (e.g., 'You don't like mathematics, don't you?'), which is grammatically incorrect. The rule is that the tag must be the opposite polarity of the main statement.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: They have had their debt written.........by their creditors
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).They have had their debt written.........by their creditors
questions.explanation: The correct phrasal verb here is 'write off'. In accounting and business English, 'to write off' a debt means to accept that a debt will not be paid and remove it from the financial records as an asset. 'Write down' refers to reducing the book value of an asset, while 'write up' refers to increasing it. Therefore, 'written off' is the appropriate term for debt cancellation.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'write off' with 'write down'. 'Write down' is used for valuation adjustments, whereas 'write off' specifically refers to the total cancellation or abandonment of a debt.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Uncle Ochai now had enough money to complete his........ building
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Uncle Ochai now had enough money to complete his........ building
questions.explanation: In English grammar, when a noun phrase is used as an adjective to describe another noun (in this case, 'building'), it must be hyphenated if it functions as a compound modifier. The term 'two-storey' acts as a compound adjective modifying 'building'. Furthermore, the correct adjectival form is 'storeyed' (British English usage), rather than just 'storey'. Therefore, 'two-storeyed building' is the standard grammatical construction.
questions.common_mistake: Students often assume 'two-storey' is the adjective, forgetting the 'ed' suffix required for the adjectival participle or failing to hyphenate the compound modifier, leading to incorrect choices like 'two storey' or 'two-story'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: By the end of this month...
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).By the end of this month...
questions.explanation: The phrase 'By the end of this month' acts as a future time marker that indicates the completion or duration of an action up to a specific point in the future. The future perfect continuous tense ('will have been' + verb + -ing) is used to describe an action that will still be in progress at a certain time in the future. Option B, 'I will have been studying', correctly reflects this duration leading up to the end of the month.
questions.common_mistake: Many students often choose the simple future ('I will study'), which fails to capture the sense of duration leading up to a future deadline, or they fail to notice the spelling errors provided in the options ('stuyding'/'styding').

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He .........the picture on the table
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).He .........the picture on the table
questions.explanation: The verb 'to lay' is a transitive verb, meaning it requires a direct object (in this case, 'the picture'). The principal parts of 'to lay' are: lay (present), laid (past), and laid (past participle). Since the sentence describes an action already completed in the past, the past tense 'laid' is the correct form. 'Lie' (to recline) is intransitive and does not take an object.
questions.subtopic: Tenses and Verb Usage (Lie vs. Lay)
questions.common_mistake: Many students confuse 'lay' (transitive) with 'lie' (intransitive). Students often incorrectly choose 'lied' (the past tense of 'to tell a falsehood') or 'lain' (the past participle of 'to recline'), neither of which fits the transitive context of placing an object.

questions.subject: english
questions.instruction: In each of questions 86 to 88, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlinedcooled..............
questions.explanation: The underlined letters 'oo' in the word 'cooled' represent the long vowel sound /uː/. Let's analyze the options: (A) 'cold' contains the diphthong /əʊ/, (B) 'could' contains the short vowel sound /ʊ/, (C) 'court' contains the long vowel sound /ɔː/, and (D) 'you' contains the long vowel sound /uː/. Therefore, 'you' shares the same vowel sound as 'cooled'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the short /ʊ/ sound (as in 'could', 'put', 'book') with the long /uː/ sound (as in 'food', 'cooled', 'you').

questions.subject: english
questions.instruction: In each of questions 86 to 88, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlinedshirt........
questions.explanation: The word 'shirt' contains the long central vowel sound /ɜː/. Comparing the options: (A) 'shut' has the short vowel /ʌ/, (B) 'shade' has the diphthong /eɪ/, (C) 'surf' has the long vowel /ɜː/, and (D) 'shed' has the short vowel /e/. Therefore, 'surf' shares the identical vowel sound with 'shirt'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the long vowel /ɜː/ (as in shirt, surf, bird) with the short vowel /ʌ/ (as in shut, cut, bus) because they are both central vowels.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: walet
questions.instruction: In each of questions 86 to 88, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlinedwalet
questions.explanation: The word 'wallet' contains the short vowel sound /e/, as in 'bed'. Looking at the options: (A) 'fete' is pronounced /feɪt/ (long /eɪ/), (B) 'says' is pronounced /sez/ (short /e/, but it is often confused with the /eɪ/ sound in 'say'), (C) 'plait' is pronounced /plæt/ (short /æ/), and (D) 'breakfast' is pronounced /ˈbrekfəst/. The 'ea' in 'breakfast' produces the exact short /e/ sound found in 'wallet'. Therefore, 'breakfast' is the correct option.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mispronounce 'breakfast' or confuse the spelling patterns (like the 'ai' in 'plait') with the actual phonetic sounds produced. Many also struggle with the 'ea' digraph, which frequently changes sound depending on the word.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: thatch
questions.instruction: In each of questions 89 to 91, choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlinedthatch
questions.explanation: The underlined letters in the word 'thatch' represent the voiceless dental fricative sound /θ/. Analyzing the options: (A) 'clothing' contains the voiced dental fricative /ð/; (B) 'mother' contains the voiced dental fricative /ð/; (C) 'then' contains the voiced dental fricative /ð/; (D) 'method' contains the voiceless dental fricative /θ/. Therefore, 'method' is the correct match.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the voiceless dental fricative /θ/ (as in 'thatch' or 'method') with the voiced dental fricative /ð/ (as in 'then' or 'mother'). The difference lies in the vibration of the vocal cords during articulation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: chateau
questions.instruction: In each of questions 89 to 91, choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlinedchateau
questions.explanation: The underlined letters 'ch' in the word 'chateau' are pronounced as the voiceless postalveolar fricative /ʃ/. Looking at the options: (A) 'chart' is /tʃ/ (affricate), (B) 'church' is /tʃ/ (affricate), (C) 'champagne' is /ʃ/ (fricative), and (D) 'chemical' is /k/ (plosive). Therefore, 'champagne' shares the same /ʃ/ consonant sound as 'chateau'.

questions.passage: Nigeria is currently with two major problems which necessitate the use of the broadcast media to satisfy the ever –increasing demand for qualitative education in the country. These are population explosion and debilitating mass poverty. Population explosion in the country has greatly increased the need for more schools so much that demand now far outstrips provision of educational opportunities particularly at the post-secondary level in addition, the Nigerian society is currently handicapped by a crippling economic crisis which has forced many people out of school as a result of growing inability to meet the cost of training, like tuition fees and boarding charges A way out of these problems lies in the provision of educational opportunities through the use of radio and television broadcast. Only when radio and television are fully utilized for teaching and learning can the foundation be laid for mass education in the country. Besides using radio and television to transmit educational to transmit educational programmes can cut the cost of education as boarding and tuition will become unnecessary for most beneficiaries. At the moment, many Nigerians are unable to enroll or stay on in school because of the high cost of education and because government is unable to provide the staggering amount needed to finance mass education via traditional school system. Also of importance is the fact that radio and television will offer good opportunities for the standardization of education in the country. At the moment, the best schools in terms of facilities and qualified teachers are concentrated in the urban centres to the detriment of the rural areas. This has given to imbalance and uneven distribution of qualitative education in the country so much so that experienced and qualified teachers often reject posting to rural schools, while over-concentration leads to under- utilization of capable hands in urban schools. Since educational broadcasting involves the best brains producing and broadcasting educational materials from one central location and reaching out simultaneously to scattered audience in rural and urban areas. The quality of educational provision will be made even throughout the country. The usual argument against the use of radio and television for reaching is the absence immediate feedback which is thought to be essential for learning. But this handicap is more than compensated for by the listeners or watchers ability to record and play back as often as he or she likes, any part of the lesson he or she may find confusing or difficult to understand. Besides, support facilities like telephone and postal services may be used to clarify difficulties or answer student’s questions in addition. Since Nigeria is still largely on orate society, using radio and television for direct teaching will pose a serious communication problem. A beginning must be made to promote aggressive school broadcast in the country.

options.option_a: the absence of educational broadcasts and underutilization of urban teachers
options.option_b: the reluctance of most teachers to work in rural areas and the fact that Nigeria is an orate society
options.option_c: the absence of immediate feedback in the teaching process and lack of teaching facilities
options.option_d: widespread penury and ever-increasing demand for formal education.

questions.explanation: The first paragraph of the passage explicitly identifies the two major problems facing education in Nigeria. It states: 'Nigeria is currently with two major problems... These are population explosion and debilitating mass poverty.' 'Population explosion' corresponds to the 'ever-increasing demand for qualitative education,' and 'debilitating mass poverty' is synonymous with 'widespread penury.' Therefore, Option D accurately captures these two core issues mentioned in the opening of the text.
questions.common_mistake: Students often make the mistake of selecting options that discuss solutions (like radio/TV broadcasting) or minor points (like the 'orate' nature of society or the rural-urban teacher imbalance), which are mentioned later in the passage as secondary concerns rather than the primary 'greatest problems' defined in the introduction.

questions.passage: The standardization processes of Nigeria pidgin seems to have started during the post –colonial period. Naturally Nigerians pidgin appears to be the first choice of most Nigerians in formal situations especially when they are among those from different ethnic and linguistic backgrounds. Thus the selection process has tactically taken place. Among all the languages used in Nigeria today, English inclusive, Nigerian pidgin could be said to be that most widely spoken. Evidence abounds in motor parks, parties, congregations, and most social occasions, there is also ample evidence in the electronic and print media, especially in political propaganda, campaigns and product advertisement. Thus in terms of spread and extensive use of Nigerians pidgin in contemporary Nigeria could rightly be called a national lingua franca. The use of Nigerian pidgin in contemporary Nigeria could be described as most productive, extensive and complex it appears that the standardization processes- selection codification, elaboration of functions and acceptance which stared in post –colonial era, are now being completed in contemporary Nigeria. The reasons for this assumption is simple apart from its complex use as a lingua franca language of media advertisement, social interaction, unofficial military training and limited literacy output, Nigerians pidgin has attained widespread acceptability in the media, political propaganda and campaigns as well as in the soap opera, It is also the language of radio and television jingles. Most electronics media now use in some appreciable percentage of their airtime to cast news and give reports in Nigeria pidgin. Even through its use in some newspaper columns has declined, especially with the demise of the Waka About the column in the Daily Times, it’s however found extensively in some newspaper advertisements. In places like Warri Sapele and port Harcourt, there were reports that teachers at the lower primary level taught their pupils in Nigerian pidgin, this unofficial adoption of Nigerian pidgin as the language of the lower primary education by those teachers is justifiable considering the provision in the national policy on education which states that in addition to English the major languages in the child’s environment could be used at the elementary level of education similarly, Nigerian pidgin has become a language of religious preaching, especially Christianity in most rural and even urban centres where congregations are not all very well educated pastors resorts to the use of Nigerian pidgin. The use of Nigerian pidgin as a literary language tends to have started in the sixties with the works of Achebe Soyinka and others. But it is in the contemporary times that it has become most widespread. The numbers of poems novels and plays written and published in Nigerian pidgin is growing even more rapidly. Many more literary writers now attempt to experiment with the languages therefore the evidences of codification and elaboration of functions and the partial or tactical acceptance of Nigerian pidgin are clearly visible.

options.option_b: pidgin will continue to enjoy acceptance by many Nigerians
options.option_d: Nigerian pidgin is used at all levels.

questions.explanation: The passage states that teachers in certain areas unofficially adopt Nigerian Pidgin as the language of lower primary education, justifying this practice by citing the National Policy on Education. The policy permits the use of major languages in a child’s environment in addition to English at the elementary level. By including Pidgin under this umbrella of 'major languages in the child's environment,' the author implies that the government’s policy framework inadvertently or officially provides a basis for the recognition and usage of Nigerian Pidgin in formal education settings.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose option D ('Nigerian pidgin is used at all levels') because the passage mentions Pidgin's widespread use. However, the National Policy on Education specifically limits the use of such languages to the 'elementary level,' making option D factually incorrect according to the text.

questions.explanation: A 'lingua franca' is a sociolinguistic term referring to a bridge language, common language, or trade language used to make communication possible between people who do not share a native language. In the passage, the author identifies Nigerian Pidgin as a national 'lingua franca' because it is the most widely spoken language across Nigeria's diverse ethnic and linguistic groups, serving as a common medium for communication in social, political, and commercial settings.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often mistake 'lingua franca' for 'mother tongue' (the native language one learns from birth) or 'second language' (the official language learned after the mother tongue). While Nigerian Pidgin functions as a common language, the term itself refers specifically to its role as a shared medium of communication among diverse speakers, not its status as a first or second language.

The use of Nigerian pidgin in contemporary Nigeria could be described as most productive, extensive and complex it appears that the standardization processes- selection codification, elaboration of functions and acceptance which stared in post –colonial era, are now being completed in contemporary Nigeria. The reasons for this assumption is simple apart from its complex use as a lingua franca language of media advertisement, social interaction, unofficial military training and limited literacy output, Nigerians pidgin has attained widespread acceptability in the media, political propaganda and campaigns as well as in the soap opera, It is also the language of radio and television jingles. Most electronics media now use in some appreciable percentage of their airtime to cast news and give reports in Nigeria pidgin. Even through its use in some newspaper columns has declined, especially with the demise of the Waka About the column in the Daily Times, it’s however found extensively in some newspaper advertisements. In places like Warri Sapele and port Harcourt, there were reports that teachers at the lower primary level taught their pupils in Nigerian pidgin, this unofficial adoption of Nigerian pidgin as the language of the lower primary education by those teachers is justifiable considering the provision in the national policy on education which states that in addition to English the major languages in the child’s environment could be used at the elementary level of education similarly, Nigerian pidgin has become a language of religious preaching, especially Christianity in most rural and even urban centres where congregations are not all very well educated pastors resorts to the use of Nigerian pidgin. The use of Nigerian pidgin as a literary language tends to have started in the sixties with the works of Achebe Soyinka and others. But it is in the contemporary times that it has become most widespread. The numbers of poems novels and plays written and published in Nigerian pidgin is growing even more rapidly. Many more literary writers now attempt to experiment with the languages therefore the evidences of codification and elaboration of functions and the partial or tactical acceptance of Nigerian pidgin are clearly visible.
questions.explanation: The passage discusses the status of Nigerian Pidgin as a language that has gained widespread acceptance across various domains, including media, politics, and social interaction. By citing the use of Pidgin in primary education in specific cities (Warri, Sapele, and Port Harcourt), the author provides evidence of its functional role in the environment. This adoption confirms the earlier claim in the passage that Nigerian Pidgin is effectively serving as a 'national lingua franca.' While it is used in education, the context of the passage focuses on its status as a widely used bridge language, making 'lingua franca' the most encompassing and accurate answer.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'a language of instruction' because the text mentions its use by teachers. However, this is a literal interpretation of a specific example given to support the broader argument that Pidgin has reached the status of a lingua franca.

questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'simple' because it is a common adjective, failing to recognize that 'full relationship' describes a professional state of mutual understanding and engagement in a business context.

questions.question_text: Read the comprehension above and select the correct option from the options below
questions.instruction: The passages below has gaps numbered 16 to 25. Immediately following each gap, four options are provided choose the most appropriate option for each gap. PASSAGE IV Each questions carries 2 marksRead the comprehension above and select the correct option from the options below
questions.passage: Business executive selling industrial and high price tag customers gods have come to the ….16….< A realization B conclusion C level D point > that there should be better approach to buyers –sellers …..17…< A relationship
questions.explanation: The context of the sentence discusses business executives seeking a 'better approach' to interactions between buyers and sellers. In professional business English, when executives are evaluating or exploring a new strategy for interaction, the verb 'discuss' is the most appropriate term for the ongoing deliberation or formulation of a strategy. While 'analyze' is a strong distractor, 'discuss' fits the context of identifying a 'better approach' through collaboration or strategic planning between parties.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'analyze' because it sounds more technical; however, in the context of improving a professional interaction or method, 'discuss' implies the active engagement and negotiation required to establish a new approach.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: it was our collective idea but Ado was doing everything to steal the show.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.it was our collective idea but Ado was doing everything to steal the show.

options.option_a: Ado was not part of the Planning but he tried to rub us of the benefits of it
options.option_b: We planned the show together but Ado was trying to abort it.
options.option_c: It was a joint project but Ado is trying to attract the most attention.
options.option_d: We collated the idea for the show but Ado was trying to steal the programme.

questions.explanation: The idiom 'to steal the show' means to attract the most attention or praise, often unexpectedly, thereby overshadowing others who were also involved. In the context of the sentence, although the idea was 'collective' (a joint effort), Ado was acting in a way that would make him the center of attention, effectively taking credit or focus away from the rest of the group. Option C accurately captures this meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Students often interpret 'steal the show' literally as theft or sabotage (like in options A or D), rather than as an idiomatic expression referring to attention-seeking behavior.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: As we watched, he just popped along to the shop for some bread.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.As we watched, he just popped along to the shop for some bread.

options.option_a: He has walked slowly to the shop.
options.option_b: He stole some bread from the shop but we could not stop him.
options.option_c: broke into the bread shop before our very eyes.
options.option_d: He went quickly to the shop for some bread.

questions.explanation: In English, the phrasal verb 'pop along' (or 'pop to') implies going somewhere quickly, casually, or for a short duration. It does not carry any implication of theft or criminal behavior (as suggested in options B and C), nor does it imply a slow, leisurely stroll (as suggested in option A). Option D correctly captures the sense of brevity and the casual nature of the trip to the shop.
