questions.common_mistake: Students often misinterpret 'popped' as 'broke' due to the phonetic similarity to 'popped a lock' or similar criminal slang, or they confuse the informal 'popped' with the physical action of bursting, ignoring the context of the sentence.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In all ramifications, Chief Adeyemi was a successful principal of the school.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.In all ramifications, Chief Adeyemi was a successful principal of the school.

options.option_a: He was partly a failure and partly a success,
options.option_b: Everyone admitted that he was largely successful during his tenure.
options.option_c: He was not totally successful in the school.
options.option_d: His tenure witnessed a huge success.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'in all ramifications' is an idiom that means in every aspect, detail, or respect. It implies a comprehensive or total state of affairs. Therefore, saying Chief Adeyemi was a successful principal 'in all ramifications' indicates that his success was total or covered every area of his tenure. Option D, 'His tenure witnessed a huge success,' best captures this sense of overall and complete achievement compared to the other options, which suggest partial failure or uncertainty.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often mistake 'in all ramifications' to mean 'many' or 'several' areas, leading them to choose options that imply partial success (like B), rather than the total or comprehensive success implied by the idiom.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I couldn't buy the biscuit because of the hold-up in the supermarket.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.I couldn't buy the biscuit because of the hold-up in the supermarket.

options.option_d: There was nobody to attend to me.

questions.explanation: In Nigerian English usage, the term 'hold-up' is often used to describe traffic congestion. However, within the specific context of a building like a 'supermarket,' the term 'hold-up' is widely understood as a synonym for an armed robbery or a situation where people are being detained by force. Therefore, Option C is the most logical explanation for why someone would be unable to make a purchase, as an armed robbery incident would prevent normal commercial activity.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'hold-up' strictly for vehicular traffic congestion (the most common use of the word in Nigerian English). While traffic is a 'hold-up,' it does not typically occur inside a supermarket; context dictates the meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: You could have heard the sound, if you weren't asleep.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.You could have heard the sound, if you weren't asleep.

options.option_a: You were not asleep so you heard the sound.
options.option_b: You were asleep so you did not hear the sound.
options.option_c: You heard the sound though you were asleep.
options.option_d: You did not hear the sound though you were not asleep.

questions.explanation: The sentence 'You could have heard the sound, if you weren't asleep' is a counterfactual (unreal) conditional sentence referring to the past. It implies that the condition (not being asleep) was not met, therefore the result (hearing the sound) did not happen. Since the person was asleep, they missed the sound. Option B correctly identifies that the state of being asleep prevented the action of hearing the sound.
questions.common_mistake: Students often misinterpret the 'if' clause by assuming the person actually heard the sound or assuming that because the sentence mentions being asleep, the person must have been awake. They often fail to realize that the 'if' clause in this context describes an unreal past situation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Musa will not do the job well because he has an itching palm.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.Musa will not do the job well because he has an itching palm.

options.option_a: He has rashes in his palm.
options.option_b: He is always looking for something to touch.
options.option_c: He is always ready.to accept bribe.
options.option_d: He is always tapping people on the back.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'an itching palm' is an idiomatic expression that describes a person who is greedy or habitually seeks money, especially in the form of bribes. In this context, it suggests that Musa cannot be trusted to do a good job because his primary interest is in receiving illicit payments rather than performing his duties professionally.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often interpret idiomatic expressions literally. In this case, choosing option A (rashes) is a common error caused by focusing on the literal word 'itching' rather than the figurative meaning of the phrase.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Emeka was always conspicuous by his absence when it came to attending lectures
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.Emeka was always conspicuous by his absence when it came to attending lectures

options.option_a: That Emeka always attended lectures made him conspicuous at school.
options.option_b: Erneka's absence from lectures was all too glaring.
options.option_c: It was obvious that Emeka was not present at lectures
options.option_d: What made Emeka conspicuous was his occasional absence from school.

questions.explanation: The idiom 'conspicuous by one's absence' is a paradoxical expression used to describe a situation where someone's absence is so noticeable that it attracts as much attention as if they were actually present. In this context, Emeka's repeated failure to attend lectures made his absence 'all too glaring' or very obvious to everyone. Option B captures the essence of the idiom perfectly.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'conspicuous' for 'positive' or 'good' behavior. They might choose option C; however, while C is factually true, Option B is a better semantic match for the idiom 'conspicuous by his absence,' as it emphasizes the 'glaring' nature of the void left by his absence.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He was injured by friendly fire.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.He was injured by friendly fire.

options.option_a: He was wounded in a war by a friend of his who fired a shot mistakenly.
options.option_b: He was injured by a gunshot that was fired by a friend.
options.option_c: He was hit in a war by a weapon fired by his own side.
options.option_d: It was a war and he was hit by a bomb fired by an unknown soldier.

questions.explanation: In military terminology, 'friendly fire' refers specifically to an attack by one's own forces or allies upon one's own side (often due to misidentification or errors). Option C captures this technical meaning precisely, whereas Options A and B imply an act of betrayal or personal animosity between friends, which is not what the idiom implies.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is interpreting the word 'friendly' literally, leading students to choose Options A or B, which suggest the act was committed by an actual personal friend rather than an allied military force.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Kola visits us on occasions, and I don't like that.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.Kola visits us on occasions, and I don't like that.

options.option_a: I do not like Kola because he visits us only when an event is being celebrated.
options.option_b: I hate the fact that Kola only visits us when something is being celebrated.
options.option_c: That Kola does not visit us often is something I object to.
options.option_d: Kola seldom visits us and that is because he is a fair-weather friend.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'on occasions' in this context is an idiomatic expression that implies 'occasionally' or 'infrequently' (from time to time). The speaker expresses a dislike for this infrequent pattern of visitation. Option C correctly captures the essence of the original sentence by identifying that the infrequent nature of Kola's visits is the cause of the speaker's objection. Other options incorrectly introduce extra information not present in the original sentence, such as 'events being celebrated' or the term 'fair-weather friend'.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often misinterpret the phrase 'on occasions' as 'on special occasions' or 'events', whereas in this specific sentence structure, it acts as a synonym for 'infrequently' or 'sometimes'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: At the time I arrived, Olu was lying in third place.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.At the time I arrived, Olu was lying in third place.

options.option_a: Olu's third position coincided with my arrival.
options.option_b: When I arrived Olu was sleeping in the space reserved for him.
options.option_c: It was a competition and Olu was in third position when I arrived.
options.option_d: On my arrival at the competition, Olu went to sleep.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'lying in third place' is an idiomatic expression commonly used in competitive contexts (such as races or tournaments) to indicate a person's current standing or ranking. Therefore, the sentence means that at the moment the speaker arrived, Olu was ranked third in a competition. Option A is incorrect because it implies the position was caused by the arrival, rather than being a state of competition. Option B and D misinterpret 'lying' as the physical act of sleeping, which is contextually incorrect in this structure.
questions.common_mistake: Students often misinterpret 'lying' as the literal act of resting or sleeping. In competitive contexts, 'lying' followed by a positional phrase (e.g., 'lying in first/second/third place') refers to one's current rank or performance status, not physical posture.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: We had difficulty eating the meat because it was leathery.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.We had difficulty eating the meat because it wasleathery.
questions.explanation: The word 'leathery' describes something tough, firm, and not soft. The opposite of 'leathery' in the context of meat texture would be 'tender,' which means soft and easy to chew. 'Bitter' refers to taste, 'stringy' describes fibrous texture, and 'tough' is a synonym of 'leathery,' making 'tender' the correct antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'tough' as the opposite instead of a synonym, or selecting 'stringy' due to a misunderstanding of texture-related terms.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The boy is too indolent to do well at school
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.The boy is tooindolentto do well at school
questions.explanation: The word 'indolent' means lazy or unwilling to work. The opposite of 'indolent' is 'industrious,' which means hardworking. Options C and D ('inactive' and 'slothful') are synonyms of 'indolent,' while 'intelligent' (A) is unrelated to the concept of laziness. Thus, 'industrious' (B) is the correct antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'industrious' with 'indolent' due to their similar prefixes ('ind-'), or selecting 'inactive' (C) as a false antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Salasi's stremendous effort has yielded results.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.Salasi'sstremendouseffort has yielded results.
questions.explanation: The word 'tremendous' means exceptionally large or great. Its antonym is 'insignificant,' which means lacking importance or very small in amount. The other options do not fit: 'absolute' refers to completeness, 'unimaginable' relates to difficulty in imagining, and 'prohibitive' refers to something preventing action (e.g., cost).
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'tremendous' with 'absolute' due to their contrasting connotations, or misinterpreting 'unimaginable' as a direct opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The computerised service of the new banks is heartwarming.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.Thecomputerisedservice of the new banks is heartwarming.
questions.explanation: The word 'computerised' refers to a system that is operated or managed by a computer, implying automation and speed. The opposite of a computerised system, in the context of banking services, is a system that is performed by human hands without the aid of automated digital technology. Therefore, 'manual' (done by hand) is the direct opposite.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'mechanical' with 'manual'. While a computerised system is a form of technology, 'mechanical' refers to machines or gears and is not the direct antonym of the digital/computerised process in this context.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Life has become a misery for many owing to the harsh economic condition in the country.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.Life has become a misery for many owing to theharsheconomic condition in the country.
questions.explanation: The word 'misery' refers to a state of great distress, suffering, or unhappiness. To find the opposite, we look for a word that denotes well-being, ease, or satisfaction. 'Comfort' is the direct antonym as it represents a state of physical or mental ease and freedom from pain or hardship. 'Drudgery' is a synonym for hard, menial work (often associated with misery), 'ridicule' is mockery, and 'ritual' is a ceremonial act; none of these serve as an opposite to misery.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse antonyms with words that are simply related to the topic. For example, some might incorrectly choose 'drudgery' because they associate it with the suffering caused by poor economic conditions, forgetting that the question specifically asks for the 'opposite in meaning'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The company director has a vivacious personality.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.The company director has avivaciouspersonality.
questions.explanation: The word 'vivacious' means attractively lively, animated, energetic, or full of life. To find the opposite, we look for a word that suggests a lack of energy or appeal. 'Unimpressive' serves as the best antonym here because it denotes someone who is dull, lackluster, or fails to catch attention, which is the direct opposite of being lively and vibrant. Option A (positive) is too broad, option B (unmanageable) is unrelated to energy, and option D (gregarious) is a synonym (meaning sociable), not an antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'gregarious' as the opposite because they might not recall its definition (sociable/outgoing), or they confuse 'vivacious' with 'talkative', leading them to look for words related to silence.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Young people have a penchant for fast cars
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.Young people have apenchantfor fast cars
questions.explanation: The word 'penchant' means a strong or habitual liking for something or a tendency to do something. Synonyms for penchant include fondness, passion, preference, or inclination. Since the question asks for the word opposite in meaning, 'dislike' (a feeling of aversion or lack of interest) serves as the correct antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'penchant' for 'passion' (which is a synonym) or 'madness' (which implies a lack of logic, but is not the direct opposite of a preference/liking).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Most of his latest actions are militant in nature
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.Most of his latest actions aremilitantin nature
questions.explanation: The word 'militant' describes someone who is combative, aggressive, or engaged in warfare/conflict to achieve a goal. Its opposite should describe someone who is peaceful, orderly, or non-aggressive. Option B, 'civil', relates to a civilized or peaceful manner of behaving, which is the direct antithesis of 'militant' behavior.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse 'militant' with 'zealous' (passionate/enthusiastic) or 'commanding' (authoritative). While these words describe an intense personality, they do not carry the specific nuance of 'aggression or combativeness' inherent in 'militant', making 'civil' the only logical contrast.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: His ideas sounded quite palatable yet they were jettisoned by the group.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.His ideas sounded quite palatable yet they werejettisonedby the group.
questions.explanation: To solve this, first identify the meaning of the word in italics. To 'jettison' means to discard, reject, or throw something away (often as unnecessary or burdensome). Since the question asks for the word opposite in meaning, we are looking for a term that implies retaining or embracing the ideas. 'Accepted' is the direct opposite of 'jettisoned' (rejected). The other options—'dumped' is a synonym, 'denied' relates to truthfulness, and 'criticized' relates to judgment, not the act of discarding.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often mistake 'criticized' for an opposite because they associate rejection with negative feedback. However, criticism is a process of evaluation, whereas 'jettisoning' is the act of discarding. Always look for the action of 'keeping' or 'adopting' to counter the act of 'discarding'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The compulsory leave made her feel listless
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.The compulsory leave made her feellistless
questions.explanation: The word 'listless' describes a state of lacking energy, enthusiasm, or interest (lethargic). To find the opposite, we look for a word that denotes high energy or vitality. 'Energetic' is the direct antonym as it implies being full of activity and vigor. Option A (restful) relates to relaxation, Option B (great) is too vague/general, and Option C (fat) is physically descriptive and unrelated to the mental or physical state of energy.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'listless' for 'tired' and look for synonyms like 'restful' or 'relaxed', failing to distinguish between the state of 'lack of energy' versus the state of 'recovering energy'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: A novel is an embellished falsehood , said the teacher
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.A novel is anembellished falsehood, said the teacher
questions.explanation: To 'embellish' means to make something more attractive or interesting by adding decorative details or fictitious features. Therefore, 'embellished' suggests an addition, decoration, or enhancement. Option A (enriched), Option B (exaggerated), and Option C (adorned) are synonyms or contextually similar to 'embellished'. Option D (obliterated) means to destroy utterly or wipe out, which stands in direct contrast to the act of adding detail or decoration.
questions.common_mistake: Many students mistake 'exaggerated' for an antonym, but it is actually a synonym in the context of a falsehood, as embellishing often involves exaggeration.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I have had enough of your impudence
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.I have had enough of yourimpudence
questions.explanation: The word 'impudence' means the quality of being rude, disrespectful, or lacking modesty. To find the opposite, we look for a word that denotes respectful behavior. 'Politeness' refers to having good manners and being respectful, which is the direct antonym of impudence. The other options—incivility (rudeness), arrogance (pride), and boldness (daring)—are either synonyms or related negative traits.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often mistake 'impudence' for 'importance' or assume it refers to confidence (boldness), leading them to select option D. It is vital to distinguish between positive confidence and negative rudeness.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: We were collectively responsible for keeping the machine in good shape
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.We werecollectivelyresponsible for keeping the machine in good shape
questions.explanation: The word 'collectively' means done as a group or acting together as a whole. Its direct opposite is 'severally', which implies being separate, individual, or distinct. While 'jointly' is a synonym of 'collectively', the options 'dutifully' and 'socially' are unrelated in this context. Therefore, 'severally' is the only term that represents individual responsibility as opposed to group responsibility.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'severally' for 'severely' (which relates to harshness) or choose 'jointly' because they fail to notice the instruction asks for the word *opposite* in meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: His comment was not printable
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.His comment was notprintable
questions.explanation: In English, the adjective 'printable'—when applied to comments, remarks, or stories—means that the content is decent, proper, or fit for public consumption. Therefore, a comment that is 'not printable' is one that is considered obscene, indecent, or unfit to be published. To find the opposite, we look for a word that implies decency or suitability. Option B ('suitable') is the direct opposite because it suggests the comment is appropriate for publication.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'printable' for 'punishable' (Option A) due to a phonetic similarity or assume 'not printable' refers to something being 'offensive' (Option C), which is actually a synonym for the phrase itself rather than an antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Curiously, he escaped unhurt
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. (Questions 36 to 100 carry 1 mark each.) each of questions 36 to 50, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.Curiously, he escaped unhurt
questions.explanation: The word 'curiously' in this context means 'in a way that is strange, unexpected, or surprising.' To find the opposite, we must look for a word that implies that the event was expected or normal. 'Unsurprisingly' denotes that an event occurred as predicted, which directly opposes the element of surprise or strangeness inherent in 'curiously'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'interestingly' (Option A) for an antonym, but 'interestingly' often functions as a synonym for 'curiously' when used to introduce a surprising fact. Students also frequently confuse the adverbial function of these words.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Agwube's explanation of her poor performance at the examination only begged the question
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsAgwube's explanation of her poor performance at the examinationonly begged the question
questions.explanation: In English, the idiom 'to beg the question' is often misused. Its formal logical definition refers to a fallacy where the premise of an argument assumes the truth of the conclusion (circular reasoning). In a general context—as used in standard aptitude tests like JAMB—it means to evade the point, fail to provide a satisfactory answer, or to ignore the core issue at hand. Therefore, saying the explanation 'begged the question' implies that the explanation failed to address the root cause or the actual problem.
questions.common_mistake: Many students mistake 'beg the question' for 'raise the question' (meaning to bring an issue to one's attention). In examinations, it is almost exclusively tested as 'avoiding the issue' or 'circular reasoning'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: We have every need to preserve some of our national monuments for posterity
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsWe have every need to preserve some of our national monuments forposterity
questions.explanation: The word 'posterity' refers to all future generations of people. In the context of the sentence, preserving national monuments is done so that those who come after us can witness our history. Therefore, 'future' is the option closest in meaning to 'posterity'.
questions.common_mistake: Many candidates confuse 'posterity' with 'prosperity' (Option A) due to their similar spellings, despite the words having completely different meanings ('prosperity' means being successful or wealthy).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He commands the confidence and respect of all his subordinates
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsHecommandsthe confidence and respect of all his subordinates
questions.explanation: In this context, the verb 'commands' does not imply giving an order or forcing someone to do something. Instead, it is used in a figurative sense to mean 'possesses' or 'is naturally entitled to' because of one's character or position. To 'command respect' means to 'enjoy' or 'receive' respect naturally from others. Therefore, 'enjoys' is the nearest in meaning as it reflects the state of being held in high regard by others.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is choosing 'enforces' (Option C). Students often equate 'command' with military or authoritative orders, leading them to believe the subject is forcing respect upon his subordinates, whereas the sentence implies respect earned through merit.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The president has mapped out so many laudable projects to embark upon
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe president has mapped out so manylaudableprojects to embark upon
questions.explanation: The word 'laudable' is derived from the Latin 'laudabilis', which means 'deserving of praise'. In the context of the sentence, projects that are 'laudable' are those that are commendable or worthy of approval. Therefore, 'praiseworthy' is the direct synonym. While 'good' and 'valuable' may describe a project, they do not capture the specific sense of moral approval or merit implied by the word 'laudable'.
questions.common_mistake: Many students often confuse 'laudable' with 'laughable' (Option A) due to the slight phonetic similarity in spelling, despite the two words having completely opposite meanings.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Adamu's father is a stern man
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsAdamu's father is astern man
questions.explanation: The word 'stern' describes a person who is serious, severe, or unrelenting in their manner, discipline, or authority. Among the given options, 'strict' is the closest in meaning as it denotes someone who insists on obedience and maintains rigorous standards of behavior. 'Wicked' implies moral evil, 'playful' implies lightheartedness, and 'conservative' relates to traditional values, none of which perfectly capture the nuance of 'stern' as well as 'strict'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'stern' with 'wicked' (Option A) because they mistakenly associate a serious or cold demeanor with malicious intent, whereas 'stern' refers to the enforcement of discipline rather than moral corruption.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Nobody knew the source of the altercation between the couple
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsNobody knew the source of thealtercationbetween the couple
questions.explanation: The word 'altercation' refers to a noisy argument or disagreement, especially in public. Among the given options, 'quarrel' is the most accurate synonym, as it also describes an angry argument or disagreement between people.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'altercation' for 'alter ego' because they share the same prefix 'alter-'. However, 'alter ego' refers to a person's secondary personality, which does not fit the context of a couple's conflict.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: His poetry is said to be inscrutable
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsHis poetry is said to beinscrutable
questions.explanation: The word 'inscrutable' refers to something that is impossible to understand, interpret, or investigate; it is often used to describe things that are enigmatic or difficult to fathom. Among the options provided, 'mysterious' is the nearest in meaning because both terms imply a quality of being obscure or beyond immediate comprehension. 'Ludicrous' means ridiculous, 'unlearnable' implies something that cannot be taught, and 'inseparable' means unable to be separated; none of these share the core meaning of 'inscrutable'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'inscrutable' with 'unlearnable' because both suggest a difficulty in mental processing, but 'inscrutable' focuses specifically on the nature of being hidden or enigmatic, whereas 'unlearnable' refers to the process of acquisition.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Hers was a specious argument about the government of the day
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsHers was aspeciousargument about the government of the day
questions.explanation: The word 'specious' refers to an argument or claim that appears correct, reasonable, or attractive on the surface but is actually false, deceptive, or lacking in real merit. Option A, 'misleading', captures this essence perfectly as it describes something that gives a wrong impression. Option B ('precious') relates to value, Option C ('spacious') relates to physical size or roominess, and Option D ('true') is an antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse 'specious' with 'spacious' due to the phonetic similarity between the two words. However, 'spacious' refers to having ample space, which is entirely unrelated to the validity of an argument.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The Lagos bus conductor wore his professional livery
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe Lagos bus conductor wore hisprofessional livery
questions.explanation: The word 'livery' refers to a special uniform worn by an official, a servant, or an employee of a specific organization or trade. In the context of the sentence, it describes the distinctive clothing worn by the bus conductor, making 'uniform' the only appropriate synonym among the given choices.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'livery' for 'badge' because both are associated with professional identification. However, 'livery' specifically refers to the garment or set of clothes, whereas a 'badge' is merely an emblem or signifier pinned to the clothing.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: If Joy hadn't been tripped up halfway through the race, she would have come first
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsIf Joy hadn't beentrippedup halfway through the race, she would have come first
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'tripped up' in this context refers to an action that caused Joy to lose her balance or pace, effectively hindering her progress in the race. Among the options provided, 'interrupted' is the nearest in meaning as it denotes an action that breaks the continuity or progress of an event. 'Disqualified' implies an official ruling, 'discouraged' relates to a mental state, and 'exhausted' relates to physical fatigue, none of which necessarily describe the physical act of being tripped.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'tripped up' for 'disqualified' because they associate the result of the action (losing the race) with an official penalty, failing to realize the phrase describes the physical cause of the hindrance rather than the administrative consequence.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: There must be something sinister about her late arrival
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThere must be somethingsinisterabout her late arrival
questions.explanation: The word 'sinister' refers to something giving the impression that something harmful, evil, or threatening is happening. Among the given options, 'ominous' is the closest in meaning because it describes an impression that something bad or unpleasant is going to happen. Options A, B, and C convey positive or neutral meanings that contrast sharply with the negative connotation of 'sinister'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'sinister' with 'serious' or 'mysterious'. While a sinister event might be mysterious, the specific nuance of the word lies in the underlying sense of evil or threatening danger, which makes 'ominous' the precise synonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The unification of the country has brought about great technological advancement
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsTheunificationof the country has brought about great technological advancement
questions.explanation: The word 'unification' refers to the process of being united or made into a whole. In the context of a country, it implies the act of bringing different parts or groups together to function as a single unit. 'Cohesion' is the closest synonym because it refers to the action or fact of forming a united whole and the state of sticking together, which reflects the essence of unification.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'stability' (Option D) because they associate the result of unification with a stable government; however, while unification may lead to stability, 'stability' is an effect, not a synonym for the act of unifying.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: His amnesia has affected his career
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsHisamnesiahas affected his career
questions.explanation: The word 'amnesia' is a medical term derived from the Greek 'amnesia', meaning 'forgetfulness'. It refers to a partial or total loss of memory. Therefore, 'loss of memory' is the precise definition that conveys the same meaning as the italicized word in the sentence.
questions.common_mistake: Some students confuse 'amnesia' with other 'a-' prefix medical conditions like 'anemia' (a deficiency of red blood cells) or 'aphasia' (the loss of ability to understand or express speech).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Idris' forbearance endeared him to us
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsIdris' forbearance endeared him to us
questions.explanation: The word 'forbearance' refers to the quality of being patient, self-controlled, and tolerant, especially when faced with provocation or delay. Option B, 'patience', is the closest synonym because it shares the same core meaning of restraining oneself and enduring a situation calmly. The other options (hard work, wisdom, and good manners) represent different positive traits that do not capture the specific essence of self-restraint inherent in 'forbearance'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'forbearance' with 'good manners' (etiquette), but while a patient person often has good manners, 'forbearance' specifically highlights the ability to endure or wait without reacting negatively.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: They hated the police and, By implication, me
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 51 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThey hated the police and, By implication, me
questions.explanation: The phrase 'by implication' means that something is suggested or inferred indirectly. In the sentence, the hatred towards the speaker is inferred from their hatred towards the police. 'Inference' (option B) directly aligns with this meaning. 'Extension' (A) refers to expansion, 'examination' (C) to analysis, and 'application' (D) to practical use, none of which match the contextual nuance of indirect suggestion.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'implication' with 'extension' due to similar-sounding words, leading to incorrect selection.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He is really very mean. He ------. not lend me the money I wanted,
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).He is really very mean. He ------. not lend me the money I wanted,
questions.explanation: The sentence requires a modal verb to express refusal in the present. 'Won't' (will not) is the correct choice because it indicates a present refusal, aligning with the context of the person being 'mean' and refusing to lend money. 'Would' (option C) is incorrect as it implies a past habitual action or hypothetical scenario, which does not fit the present context. 'Should' and 'could' do not convey refusal.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'would' (past/future hypothetical) with 'won't' (present refusal). Students may also misinterpret the context as requiring a past tense.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: When the cashier told him to join the queue, he considered it ------- his dignity.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).When the cashier told him to join the queue, he considered it ------- his dignity.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'an affront on' because 'affront' means an insult or offense, which aligns with the context of the sentence where the action is perceived as disrespectful to one's dignity. The preposition 'on' is essential here to complete the collocation 'affront on something.' Other options like 'drawback to' or 'strain on' do not convey the intended meaning of an insult.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'affront on' with similar-sounding phrases like 'a strain on' or 'a drawback to,' which have different meanings related to stress or disadvantage rather than insult.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: If anyone greets you, it is only polite to return ----- greeting
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).If anyone greets you, it is only polite to return ----- greeting
questions.explanation: The sentence starts with the indefinite pronoun 'anyone'. In formal English, when an indefinite pronoun like 'anyone' or 'one' serves as the antecedent, the corresponding possessive determiner or pronoun used later in the sentence must be consistent. Therefore, 'one's' is the correct possessive form to refer back to 'anyone' to maintain grammatical agreement in a formal context.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'your' (Option A) because they focus on the second person address ('If anyone greets you...'), forgetting that the subject of the sentence is the indefinite pronoun 'anyone', which requires the reflexive or possessive form 'one's' rather than 'your'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Amma lives ---- campus.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Amma lives ---- campus.
questions.explanation: In English usage, especially within academic or institutional contexts, the preposition 'on' is the standard choice for the noun 'campus'. We say someone lives 'on campus' to indicate they reside within the grounds or property of a university or college. Other prepositions like 'in', 'at', or 'inside' are considered idiomatic deviations from standard academic English in this specific collocation.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistakenly choose 'in' or 'at' because they confuse campus with other types of locations like cities ('in') or specific buildings ('at'). While we say 'at the university', the specific idiomatic convention for 'campus' is 'on'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: An acceptance of the offer would be a departure from the several rejections that -----
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).An acceptance of the offer would be a departure from the several rejections that -----
questions.explanation: The sentence uses a conditional structure ('would be'). The phrase 'a departure from the several rejections' implies that these rejections occurred in the past, relative to the hypothetical 'acceptance' being discussed. Therefore, the 'past perfect' tense ('had taken place') is the most appropriate choice because it denotes an action completed before another point in the past or a state established prior to the current hypothetical situation.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'have taken place' (present perfect), forgetting that the sequence of tenses requires the past perfect when the main clause is set in a hypothetical or past-oriented context ('would be').

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The ---- part of a new book is often written by a more experienced writer than the author.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The ---- part of a new book is often written by a more experienced writer than the author.
questions.explanation: The word 'foreword' refers to an introductory section of a book, usually written by someone other than the author to provide context or endorsement. Options A, C, and D are incorrect: 'foreward' is a misspelling, 'forward' is an adverb or adjective meaning 'onward' or 'ahead', and 'forword' is a non-existent word.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'foreword' (the introductory section of a book) with 'forward' (direction) or create non-existent variants like 'foreward' by mistakenly combining the two prefixes.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The officer acted in ----- the instructions.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The officer acted in ----- the instructions.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'in accordance with' is a standard English idiom used to indicate that something is done in a manner that agrees with or follows a particular rule, regulation, or instruction. No other preposition (by, to, of) is grammatically acceptable in this specific collocation.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse 'in accordance with' with 'according to'. While both convey similar meanings, 'accordance' must always be followed by the preposition 'with'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The bomb was -----
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The bomb was -----
questions.explanation: In the context of explosives, the verb 'detonate' means to cause a bomb or explosive device to explode. Since a bomb is designed to explode, 'detonated' is the most semantically appropriate term for the action of initiating that explosion. While 'dismantled' and 'deactivated' refer to rendering a bomb harmless, 'detonated' is the standard term for the act of triggering a bomb's function.
questions.common_mistake: Many students confuse 'detonated' (to cause to explode) with 'deactivated' (to make safe). While a bomb can be deactivated by experts, in general usage, a bomb is synonymous with detonation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: if you want to succeed in life, don't be envious ---- other people's achievement.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).if you want to succeed in life, don't be envious ---- other people's achievement.
questions.explanation: In English grammar, certain adjectives are followed by specific fixed prepositions. The adjective 'envious' must always be followed by the preposition 'of'. This is a matter of idiomatic collocation; therefore, 'envious of' is the only grammatically correct structure to denote feelings of resentment toward someone else's possession or success.
questions.common_mistake: Students often wrongly assume that because 'envious' relates to someone else, they should use 'to' (as in 'to them') or 'with' (as in 'with their success'), but these violate established English prepositional rules.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: They are taught to value honour ----- their lives.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).They are taught to value honour ----- their lives.
questions.explanation: The sentence requires a preposition that denotes priority or higher importance. The phrase 'to value X above Y' is the standard idiomatic expression used to indicate that X is considered more important or superior to Y. Therefore, 'above' is the only option that correctly establishes the relationship between 'honour' and 'their lives'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistakenly choose 'from' (perhaps confusing it with 'distinguish from') or 'in', which does not capture the intended meaning of prioritizing one entity over another.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Our plan for the trip fell ----- when the rich man did not give us a life ----- ?
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Our plan for the trip fell ----- when the rich man did not give us a life ----- ?
questions.explanation: The sentence requires the use of two specific idioms. First, 'fell through' is a phrasal verb meaning to fail or not be completed (as in a plan). Second, 'a lifeline' is a metaphorical expression referring to a source of help or support that enables someone to escape a difficult situation. Therefore, the phrase 'fell through' and 'lifeline' correctly complete the sentence in this context.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'fell off' (to drop from something) or 'fell down' (to collapse) with the phrasal verb 'fell through' (to fail). Additionally, 'life line' is often incorrectly written as two separate words instead of the compound noun 'lifeline'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I missed the match though it was shown on television on two ------- nights.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).I missed the match though it was shown on television on two ------- nights.
questions.explanation: The word 'consecutive' means following one another in order or without interruption. In the context of the sentence, it describes nights that follow each other immediately (e.g., Tuesday and Wednesday). 'Concurrent' refers to events happening at the same time; 'consistent' means acting or done in the same way over time; and 'concrete' refers to something physical or definite, none of which fit the temporal requirement of describing nights following each other.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'consecutive' with 'concurrent'. 'Concurrent' implies simultaneity (happening at the same time), whereas 'consecutive' implies sequence (happening one after the other).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The company said some money to Abu to ------ him for the losses he suffered during the accident.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The company said some money to Abu to ------ him for the losses he suffered during the accident.
questions.explanation: The sentence requires a verb that means to compensate or pay back for a loss or injury. 'Recompense' means to make amends to someone for loss or harm suffered, which fits the context of an accident perfectly. Option A (indemnity) is a noun; the verb form 'indemnify' would have been grammatically correct, but as a noun, it cannot follow 'to'. Option B (condole with) means to express sympathy, which does not involve money. Option C (settle) is too vague in this context compared to 'recompense'.
questions.common_mistake: Many students choose 'indemnity' because it is a technical term for compensation, but they overlook the fact that it is a noun, while the sentence structure requires an infinitive verb.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: You are just putting the hat on ------- ?
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).You are just putting the hat on ------- ?
questions.explanation: The sentence 'You are just putting the hat on' is in the present continuous tense, with 'are' acting as the auxiliary verb and 'you' as the subject. In English grammar, a question tag must agree with the subject and the auxiliary verb of the main clause. Since the main clause is positive ('You are...'), the question tag must be negative. Therefore, 'are' becomes 'aren't' and the pronoun 'you' is retained, resulting in 'aren't you?'.
questions.common_mistake: Many students wrongly choose 'isn't it' because they confuse the structure with an impersonal statement or incorrectly apply the singular/plural agreement to the subject.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Government has frowned upon politicians who are out to ----- wealth
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Government has frowned upon politicians who are out to ----- wealth
questions.explanation: In English, the verb 'amass' is the most appropriate term used when referring to the accumulation or gathering of wealth, especially in large quantities or over a period of time. While 'gain' and 'steal' denote acquisition, 'amass' specifically collocates with 'wealth' in formal contexts describing the gathering of large fortunes, which often carries a connotation of greed in political discourse.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'gain' because it is a common synonym for getting something; however, 'gain' usually relates to general benefits or profits, whereas 'amass' is the standard idiomatic choice for large-scale wealth collection.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I tried to discourage him, but he persisted ----- revealing the secret to his son
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).I tried to discourage him, but he persisted ----- revealing the secret to his son
questions.explanation: The verb 'persist' is a phrasal verb that is strictly followed by the preposition 'in'. To 'persist in' something means to continue to do something despite opposition or difficulty. The structure is 'persist + in + gerund (verb + ing)'. Therefore, 'persisted in revealing' is the only grammatically correct construction.
questions.common_mistake: Many students incorrectly use 'on' because of the association with the verb 'insist on'. While 'insist on' is correct, 'persist' must be paired with 'in'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He was determined to ------ all opposition into submission.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).He was determined to ------ all opposition into submission.
questions.explanation: The verb 'cow' means to cause someone to surrender, act submissively, or lose their courage through intimidation. In the context of the sentence, 'to cow into submission' is a standard idiomatic collocation, meaning to frighten someone into obeying. The other options (push, box, pound) do not collocate effectively with the phrase 'into submission' in standard English usage to convey the intended meaning of psychological intimidation.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'pound' because it suggests force or aggression, failing to recognize that 'cow' is the specific verb used in formal and literary contexts to denote intimidation or breaking someone's spirit.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I am told that the market is ------ in to the interests of people from all ----- of life.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).I am told that the market is ------ in to the interests of people from all ----- of life.
questions.explanation: The sentence requires the correct idiomatic collocation. The expression 'all walks of life' is a standard English idiom used to describe people from various social, economic, or professional backgrounds. When something is 'tuned into' the interests of others, it means it is sensitized, adapted, or responsive to those specific needs. Therefore, 'tuned/walks' creates a semantically correct and idiomatic sentence.
questions.common_mistake: Many students often choose 'places' because they associate it with geographical locations; however, the idiomatic expression is exclusively 'walks of life,' not 'places of life.'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Uche has been in ------ with his pen pal for years.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Uche has been in ------ with his pen pal for years.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'in correspondence with' is a standard English collocation used to describe the act of communicating with someone regularly by sending and receiving letters or messages. A 'pen pal' is specifically someone with whom one exchanges written correspondence, making 'correspondence' the only contextually appropriate noun.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'exchange' because they associate 'pen pal' with 'exchanging letters,' but 'in exchange with' is grammatically incorrect in this context.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Abba became ------ about his inability to pass the examination.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Abba became ------ about his inability to pass the examination.
questions.explanation: The sentence describes Abba's reaction to failing an examination. Failure typically induces feelings of sadness, loss of hope, or discouragement. 'Despondent' means feeling or showing profound hopelessness, dejection, or discouragement, which perfectly aligns with the emotional state resulting from academic failure. 'Disenchanted' implies losing fondness or belief in something previously admired, 'dogmatic' relates to asserting opinions arrogantly, and 'joyful' is the antonym of the expected emotional response.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'despondent' with 'disenchanted'. While both have negative connotations, 'despondent' is specific to a state of personal hopelessness or low spirits caused by a specific event like failure, whereas 'disenchanted' refers to the loss of illusion or interest in a person, object, or system.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: caught
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 86 to 88, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.caught
questions.explanation: The word 'caught' is transcribed as /kɔːt/. The underlined letters 'au' represent the long open-mid back rounded vowel sound /ɔː/. Comparing the options: 'water' (/ˈwɔːtə/) contains the same /ɔː/ sound. 'Hot' (/hɒt/) contains the short open back rounded vowel /ɒ/. 'Sup' (/sʌp/) contains the short open-mid back unrounded vowel /ʌ/. 'Wrong' (/rɒŋ/) contains the short open back rounded vowel /ɒ/. Therefore, 'water' is the correct match.
questions.common_mistake: Many students confuse the long vowel /ɔː/ with the short vowel /ɒ/. While they both involve lip rounding, the duration and the specific tongue position differ significantly, leading students to incorrectly choose words like 'hot' or 'wrong'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: country
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 86 to 88, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.country
questions.explanation: The underlined letters 'ou' in the word 'country' represent the short, lax vowel sound /ʌ/ (the 'uh' sound). Analyzing the options: (A) 'worry' contains the /ʌ/ sound. (B) 'courteous' contains the /ɜː/ sound. (C) 'bought' contains the /ɔː/ sound. (D) 'poultry' contains the /əʊ/ (diphthong) sound. Therefore, 'worry' is the only word that shares the same vowel sound as 'country'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake the spelling patterns (e.g., the presence of 'ou') for phonetic sounds, leading them to choose words like 'poultry' simply because they share similar letters rather than phonetic equivalence.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: trap
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 86 to 88, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.trap
questions.explanation: The word 'trap' contains the short vowel sound /æ/ (as in 'cat'). Looking at the options: 'wonder' contains the /ʌ/ (schwa or 'uh') sound; 'because' contains the /ɪ/ and /ɒ/ sounds; 'plait' (a braid of hair) is pronounced /plæt/, which contains the /æ/ sound; 'quantity' contains the /ɒ/ sound. Therefore, 'plait' is the only word that shares the same vowel sound /æ/ as 'trap'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mispronounce 'plait' as /pleɪt/ (rhyming with 'plate') due to the influence of spelling patterns, but in standard English, it is pronounced with the /æ/ sound.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: rest
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 89 to 91, choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.rest
questions.explanation: The underlined letter 's' in the word 'rest' represents the voiceless alveolar fricative /s/ sound. Analyzing the options: (A) 'result' contains /z/, (B) 'show' contains the /ʃ/ sound, (C) 'unasked' contains the /s/ sound, and (D) 'wise' contains the /z/ sound. Therefore, 'unasked' is the only option that shares the identical /s/ consonant sound.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the /s/ sound with the /z/ sound, especially when 's' appears between vowels or at the end of words where it might be voiced (like in 'wise' or 'result').

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: joint
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 89 to 91, choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.joint
questions.explanation: The underlined letters 'j' in 'joint' represent the voiced palato-alveolar affricate consonant sound /dʒ/. Examining the options: (A) 'dagger' /dæɡə/ contains the voiced velar plosive /ɡ/. (B) 'advantage' /ədˈvɑːntɪdʒ/ contains the /dʒ/ sound at the end. (C) 'guardian' /ˈɡɑːdiən/ contains the voiced velar plosive /ɡ/. (D) 'mightier' /ˈmaɪtiə/ does not contain the /dʒ/ sound. Therefore, 'advantage' is the only word that shares the same consonant sound as 'joint'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the /dʒ/ sound (as in 'joint') with the /ʒ/ sound (as in 'measure') or the /g/ sound (as in 'guardian').

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: thought
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 89 to 91, choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.thought
questions.explanation: The underlined letters 'th' in the word 'thought' represent the voiceless dental fricative consonant sound /θ/. Analyzing the options: (A) 'taught' contains the /t/ sound. (B) 'weather' contains the voiced dental fricative /ð/. (C) 'theatre' contains the voiceless dental fricative /θ/. (D) 'fate' contains the /f/ sound. Therefore, 'theatre' is the only word that shares the same consonant sound as 'thought'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the voiceless /θ/ (as in 'thought' or 'theatre') with the voiced /ð/ (as in 'weather' or 'the').

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: sheer
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 92 to 94, choose the option that rhymes with the given word.sheer
questions.explanation: Rhyming is determined by the similarity of the ending sound of words. The word 'sheer' is phonetically transcribed as /ʃɪər/. Among the options, 'dear' is transcribed as /dɪər/. Both words share the identical 'ear' /ɪər/ sound. Options B, C, and D do not share this terminal phonetic structure.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake words that start with the same sound for rhymes (e.g., 'shade'), or focus on spelling patterns rather than the actual phonetic sound produced.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: great
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 92 to 94, choose the option that rhymes with the given word.great
questions.explanation: To determine a rhyme, we look at the phonetic sound of the word. The word 'great' is pronounced /ɡreɪt/. Option D, 'treat', ends in /iːt/ but wait—let us re-evaluate the phonetics: 'Great' (/ɡreɪt/) rhymes with 'crate' (/kreɪt/). However, looking at the provided options, 'treat' is often confused due to spelling, but 'crate' is the actual phonetic match. *Correction*: Upon phonetic analysis of the options, 'crate' (/kreɪt/) shares the identical /eɪt/ rhyme scheme with 'great' (/ɡreɪt/). Therefore, Option B is the correct rhyme.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'rhyming' with 'spelling' or 'near-rhymes'. Many students choose 'treat' because it looks similar in structure, but it has a different vowel sound (/iː/ vs /eɪ/).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: own
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 92 to 94, choose the option that rhymes with the given word.own
questions.explanation: To identify a rhyme, we focus on the phonetic sound of the word rather than its spelling. The word 'own' is pronounced /əʊn/. Option D, 'phone', is pronounced /fəʊn/. Both words share the same vowel sound (/əʊ/) and final consonant sound (/n/), making them rhyme. Options A (brown), B (frown), and C (gown) all end in the /aʊn/ sound, which does not match the /əʊn/ sound of the target word.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake visual similarity (spelling patterns) for auditory rhyme. Many candidates choose options A, B, or C because they end in '-own', assuming that words with identical spelling patterns must rhyme, even though their vowel sounds differ significantly.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: ceremoniously
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 95 to 97, choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. Tho syllables are written in capital letters.ceremoniously
questions.explanation: In English phonology, words ending in the suffix '-ious' generally attract the primary stress to the syllable immediately preceding the suffix. The word 'ceremoniously' is derived from 'ceremony' (where the stress is on the first syllable). When the suffix '-ious' and the adverbial suffix '-ly' are added, the stress shifts to the syllable containing the root vowel that precedes the suffix chain. Specifically, in 'ce-re-MO-ni-ous-ly', the primary stress falls on the third syllable ('MO').
questions.common_mistake: Many students incorrectly stress the first syllable because the base word 'ceremony' is stressed on the first syllable (/ˈser.ə.mə.ni/). It is vital to remember that adding suffixes often changes the stress placement in English.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: understandable
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 95 to 97, choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. Tho syllables are written in capital letters.understandable
questions.explanation: In English phonetics, the word 'understandable' is a five-syllable word (un-der-stand-a-ble). According to the rules of word stress, the primary stress falls on the third syllable, which contains the main root of the verb 'stand'. Therefore, it is pronounced /ˌʌndəˈstændəbl/, with the primary stress on the 'STAND' syllable.
questions.common_mistake: Students often misplace the stress on the final syllable '-ble' or the first syllable 'un-', failing to recognize that in complex derivatives, the stress often shifts to the root of the word.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: management
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 95 to 97, choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. Tho syllables are written in capital letters.management
questions.explanation: The word 'management' is a three-syllable word with the primary stress on the first syllable (MAN-age-ment). In English, stress placement often follows patterns where the first syllable is stressed in compound or derived words. The correct stress pattern here is 'MAnagement' (option A), as the primary stress falls on the initial syllable, while the other syllables receive secondary or no stress.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing stress patterns with similar-sounding words like 'management' and 'manipulate,' where stress might shift. Learners might incorrectly assume the second or third syllable is stressed due to mishearing or overgeneralizing stress rules.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: LAM called Uche a pilot.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 98 to 100, the word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.LAM called Uche a pilot.

options.option_b: Did Okoro call Uche a pilot?
options.option_c: Did Lam call Uche a driver?
options.option_d: Did Lam wish Uche to be a pilot?

questions.explanation: In English, emphatic stress is used to highlight the specific information that is being questioned or clarified. When a word is stressed in a sentence, it implies that the speaker is correcting a misconception about that specific word. By stressing 'LAM' in the sentence 'LAM called Uche a pilot', the speaker is emphasizing the identity of the person who performed the action. Therefore, the question being answered must seek to identify the subject (who performed the action). Option B asks 'Did Okoro call Uche a pilot?', to which the emphatic response 'LAM called Uche a pilot' correctly clarifies that it was Lam, not Okoro, who performed the action.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake emphatic stress for a simple declarative sentence. They fail to realize that the stressed word acts as the 'answer' to an implicit question where that specific part of the sentence was in doubt.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The girl DANCED in the village square.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 98 to 100, the word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.The girl DANCED in the village square.

options.option_a: Who danced in the village square?
options.option_b: Is this the village square where the girl danced?
options.option_c: Did the girl dance in the village square?
options.option_d: Did the girl sing in the village square?

questions.explanation: In English, emphatic stress is used to highlight the specific piece of information being corrected or clarified. When a word is stressed in a sentence, the question it answers must challenge that specific part of the statement. Here, the verb 'DANCED' is stressed. Option D asks if the girl 'sang', which implies a contrast between the action of dancing and singing. By stressing 'DANCED', the speaker is correcting the assumption that the girl did something else (like singing). Options A, B, and C focus on the actor (the girl), the location (square), or the entire event, which would require stressing 'girl', 'square', or the whole sentence respectively.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose the option that repeats the exact word stressed, rather than the option that provides a context where that specific word acts as the focus of correction. They often mistake the stress for a question about 'who' or 'where' when those nouns are not the ones being emphasized.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: My father READ the newspaper.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 98 to 100, the word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.My father READ the newspaper.

options.option_a: Did my father steal the newspaper?

questions.explanation: In emphatic stress, the stressed word in the sentence points to the information being corrected or clarified. When the verb 'READ' is stressed in the sentence 'My father READ the newspaper', it serves to correct a misconception regarding the action performed. Option A ('Did my father steal the newspaper?') provides a context where the speaker is clarifying that the father performed the action of 'reading' rather than 'stealing'. The stress on the verb negates the previous assumption about the action.
questions.common_mistake: Students often assume that the emphatic stress simply highlights the most important word in a sentence, rather than realizing it is specifically used to correct a false assumption or provide contrast in a dialogue.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Which Use of English Question Paper Type is given to you
questions.instruction: Read the passages I II and III carefully and answer the questions that follows Each question carries 3 marks PASSAGE IWhich Use of English Question Paper Type is given to you
questions.passage: One of the interesting things to do about our spaceship is that it is a mechanical vehicle, just as is an automobile if you own a car, you realize that as you must put water in the radiator and take care of the car as a whole. You begin to develop quite a little thermodynamics sense. You know that you are either going to have to keep the machine in a good order or it is going to be in trouble and fail to function. We have not been seeing our spaceship earth as an integrally designed machine which to be persistently successful must be comprehended and serviced totalNow there is one outstanding important fact regarding spaceship earth and that is that no instruction book came with it. I think it is very significant that there is no instruction book for successfully operating our ships in view of the infinite attention to all other details displayed by our ship it must be taken as a deliberate and purposeful that an instruction book was omitted, lack of instructions has forced us to find out that there are two kinds of mangoes, unriped mangoes that will kill us and ripen mangoes which will nourish us. And we had to find out ways of telling which was which mangoes before we ate it or otherwise we would die, so we were forced because of this devise scientific experimental procedures and to interpret effectively the significance of the experimental findings thus because the instruction manual was missing we are learning how we can safely survive on the planet. Quite clearly, all living beings are utterly helpless at the moment of birth, the human child stays helplessly longer than the young of any species, apparently it is part of the invention that man is meant to be utterly helpless through certain anthropological phases when he begins to be able to get on a little better he is meant to discover some of the physical principle inherent to in the universe as well as the many resources around him which will further multiply his knowledge designed into this spaceship. Earths total wealth was a big safety factor. This allowed man to be very ignorant for a long time until he had amassed enough experiences from the instruction book forced man to discover retrospectively just what his most important capabilities are he learned to generalize fundamental principles of universe. Adapted from olulkpe B,O et el (2005) intensive English for secondary school 2 Onitsha AFP
questions.explanation: This question is a 'procedural' or 'administrative' question common in JAMB UTME. It does not test reading comprehension of the provided passage, but rather the candidate's ability to identify the specific code printed on their individual examination paper. Because the paper type (A, B, C, or D) varies from student to student to prevent malpractice, there is no single 'correct' answer that applies to all candidates. A candidate must look at their specific question booklet to provide the correct answer.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is ignoring the instruction to look at the front of the physical question paper and instead trying to 'find' the answer within the comprehension passage or guessing based on external knowledge.
