options.option_b: Evil thoughts will continue to stings us likes vipers as long as there are enemies who cause offence
options.option_c: like the pendulum, evil thoughts will always come to our minds no matter what we do
options.option_d: like most birds evil thought fly swiftly in our minds without perching

questions.explanation: The passage uses metaphors to convey a consistent moral lesson: while we cannot always prevent 'bad thoughts' from entering our minds (like birds flying overhead or thieves looking in windows), the writer emphasizes that we must not allow them to 'reign' or take root. The writer’s core view is that we have the power and the moral obligation to reject these thoughts ('we must not open to them') and instead welcome good thoughts. Option A accurately summarizes this stance: it acknowledges the occurrence of evil thoughts but highlights the virtue (wisdom) of keeping them out.
questions.common_mistake: A common mistake is selecting Option C or D. While these options use metaphors found in the text (pendulums, birds), they misinterpret the writer's argument. The writer does not argue that we are helpless against thoughts; rather, the passage is a call to discipline the mind.

questions.passage: PASSAGE IIIIn 1962, a team of scientists produced a special radio station that had a range of fifteen moles. Even though communication was being accomplished in space at a range of more than a million times this distance, the new radio station caused must excitement among scientists. The reason: its power supply was battery made of bacteria. For the first time practical amounts of electricity were being produced by a form of life and put to use.‘Biocell’ the new power supply had a liquid fuel containing tiny forms of life that changed the fuel directly into electric energy. This was far more than an interesting experiment. The biocell is being developed as producer of electricity for radios for signals to guide ships, for lightening and for other uses. Thought the working biocell is only a few years old, some scientists feel that it will one day produce power cheaply as is now being done by other methods, and that the biocell will use materials that would otherwise be considered a waste. Early biocells were powered with sugar, but a wide range of fuels can be used. Work is being done using seawater to feed the bacteria.Electricity from living cells is no new idea. Man experience the strange ‘shock’ produced by some fish even before electricity was really discovered. Then in time, there were other discoveries. Benjamin Franklin found that lightening in the sky was electricity. Lulgi Galvani found some electricity in the muscles and nerves of animals. Bust the African catfish produces far more electricity than most other living creatures. And another fish, the electric eel, well named for it has an even greater electric charge. Research works also discovered that even human produce small amounts of electricity in their bodies. Our hearts produce a very small amount that can be measured, so do our brains. The boicell is completely new in the field of power production and as yet, no mass –produced models have begun to replace the older types of batteries. It might bewondered, then what the excitement is all about.
questions.explanation: The passage primarily focuses on the development and potential of the 'biocell'—a device that utilizes living bacteria to generate electricity. While the author mentions historical context regarding electric fish and human body electricity, these are supporting details used to contextualize the core subject: harnessing energy from biological organisms. Option A, 'Energy from living things', encapsulates the invention of the biocell and the broader scope of biological electricity mentioned in the text. Other options are either too narrow (D) or too vague/misleading (B and C).
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose titles based on minor supporting details (like the electric eel or human electricity) instead of the main focus, which is the revolutionary development of the biocell as a power source.

questions.instruction: comprehension passage IIIThe attitude of the writer of the passage can be described as
questions.passage: It is said that experience is the best teacher, but to learn consciously through wisdom may even be a better and more convenient way, to learn by experience is to learn from mistakes. It means you have burnt your fingers and now your eyes are open this is tough, costly and inconvenient way to learn. Rather than leaving our learning experience, why do we not learn consciously through wisdom? We can learn by conscious going out of our way to acquire knowledge and wisdom rather than leave our learning to chance surely we can learn from mistakes but why wait till when we make mistakes before we learn? We should give more premium to learning by wisdom than by experience. This is will involve one making up one one’s mind to be decisive in learning. We must decide to learn consciously and not necessarily from negative experiences. The first step is to realize that life is simply the outcome and outplay of decisions our life now is the sum total of our decision and our future will be determined by our decisions today if we decide to learn today we are likely to make mistakes and we when we do not make mistakes experience need not be our best teacher To avoid making experience our best teacher we will take more than a decision, we must couple our decision with a complete and wholehearted devotion. We must be resolved resolute and resilient in our bid to learn by wisdom and not necessarily by experience this is crucial because situations and circumstances will want us to make detour and leave our learning and life to chance we must therefore be disciplined to remain with our resolve to make clean break with experience as our best teacher. Discipline in this regard means learning something new every day by wisdom rather experience it means consciously getting better by the day in your chosen field, discipline will demand taking advantage of every learning opportunity that comes our way it will mean we must pay the price for learning by wisdom invest in books, magazine, seminars and other means by which may become wiser. It is much easier and cheaper to learn consciously by wisdom than to learn by experience. When we learn by experience the deed is done and we are just picking up the pieces- learning in regret how to avoid such predicament next time. Consider the child who grasp a burning coal, he has learned the hard way through the painful experience but his fingers will remain burnt, thus the saying that experience is the best teacher may not be justifiable after all Adapted from Sunday tribune July 2007
questions.explanation: The writer is 'critical' because they are challenging a long-held conventional wisdom (the adage that 'experience is the best teacher'). Throughout the passage, the author systematically critiques this proverb, labeling it as a 'tough, costly and inconvenient way to learn' and urging the reader to abandon this approach in favor of 'learning by wisdom.' A critical attitude involves evaluating an existing idea and proposing an alternative perspective, which is exactly what the author does here.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'critical' for 'negative' or 'angry.' In literary analysis, a 'critical' tone simply means the author is analyzing, questioning, or passing judgment on the validity of an idea or situation, which the author does effectively here.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Hardworking students must not have a finger in every pie at school
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentences. Each question carries 2 marksHardworking students must not have a finger in every pie at school

options.option_a: hardworking students must have a role to play in most activities in the school
options.option_b: only hardworking students must participate in all activities in the school
options.option_c: hardworking students do not participate in all activities in the school
options.option_d: hardworking students must ask others to participate in school activities

questions.explanation: The idiom 'have a finger in every pie' means being involved in too many activities. The sentence advises hardworking students to avoid overcommitment. Option C correctly states that hardworking students do not participate in all activities, aligning with the idiom's meaning. Other options misinterpret the idiom or contradict the sentence's intent.
questions.common_mistake: Misinterpreting the idiom as a positive statement about participation rather than a caution against overextension.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The Vice Chancellor is riding the crest of the last quarter of his administration
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentences. Each question carries 2 marksThe Vice Chancellor is riding the crest of the last quarter of his administration

options.option_a: The Vice Chancellor enjoys the acknowledgement of the success of his administration
options.option_b: The Vice Chancellor does not enjoy the people's criticism of his administration
options.option_c: The Vice Chancellor hopes to overcome soon, the poor comments on his administration
options.option_d: The Vice Chancellor does not talk of his success in office

questions.explanation: The phrase 'riding the crest' metaphorically refers to being at the peak or enjoying the high point of a situation. In the context of the 'last quarter of his administration,' it implies the Vice Chancellor is in the final phase of his tenure and is experiencing recognition or success. Option A correctly captures this by stating he 'enjoys the acknowledgement of the success of his administration.' Other options misinterpret the idiom as negative or critical contexts.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'riding the crest' with overcoming challenges (Option C) or misinterpreting it as criticism (Option B), ignoring the positive connotation of the idiom.
