options.option_a: She was convicted for the charge
options.option_b: she was blamed and charged to court
options.option_c: her case was resolved by the court
options.option_d: she was declared free from the charge

questions.explanation: The sentence contains a likely typo ('absorbed' instead of 'acquitted'). In legal contexts, 'acquitted' means the court declares someone not guilty of a charge. The corrected sentence 'She was acquitted by the court of the charge' aligns with option D, which states she was declared free from the charge. The other options misinterpret the legal outcome or sentence structure.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'acquitted' with 'convicted' or misreading the sentence as a charge being filed rather than dismissed.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The Landlord is fond of throwing his weight around
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentences. Each question carries 2 marksThe Landlord is fond of throwing his weight around

options.option_c: the landlord gives order to people
options.option_d: the landlord is respected by his tenants

questions.explanation: The idiom 'throwing one's weight around' means to use one's authority or influence in a way that is bossy, arrogant, or overbearing. It refers to a person who acts as if they are superior and likes to boss others around. Therefore, 'the landlord gives order to people' is the option that captures this meaning of exercising undue authority.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose literal interpretations (like Option B: 'the landlord is overweight') because they fail to recognize that the sentence is an idiom rather than a literal description of the landlord's physical state.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The company ought to have issued warrants for one billion shares
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentences. Each question carries 2 marksThe company ought to have issued warrants for one billion shares

options.option_a: the company has issued one billion shares
options.option_b: The management expected the company to issue more than one billion shares
options.option_c: members of the company bought less than one billion shares
options.option_d: the company did not issue one billion shares

questions.explanation: The phrase 'ought to have issued' is a perfect infinitive construction used to express an obligation or expectation that was not fulfilled in the past. In this context, it implies that the company had a duty or plan to issue one billion shares, but failed to carry it out. Therefore, Option D ('the company did not issue one billion shares') is the only choice that accurately captures the fact that the action was expected but did not occur.
questions.common_mistake: Many students mistake 'ought to have issued' for an action that was completed. Students often choose Option A because they associate the verb with the actual event, failing to recognize that 'ought to have + past participle' indicates a non-occurrence in the past.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He needed not to have played in the position of quarter back in the volley ball
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentences. Each question carries 2 marksHe needed not to have played in the position of quarter back in the volley ball

options.option_a: he participated in the game in his unusual position
options.option_b: nobody expected him to have participated in the game
options.option_c: he wanted to play in a position other than the one he was offered
options.option_d: someone did not want him to play in the position that he played

questions.explanation: The phrase 'He needed not to have played' is a specific construction used to express that an action was performed unnecessarily. It implies that the subject did, in fact, play the game (participate), but the action was not required or was inappropriate for him. Option A captures the essence that he actually participated, but it was in a position that was not his usual or intended one, making the performance of that specific role unnecessary or out of place.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'need not have + past participle' with 'did not need to + verb'. 'Need not have' implies the action was completed but unnecessary, whereas 'did not need to' often implies the action was not performed at all.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I wouldn't have responded to this rude talk, if i were you
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentences. Each question carries 2 marksI wouldn't have responded to this rude talk, if i were you

options.option_a: The advice was taken by the respondent,k so he did not respond to the talk
options.option_b: The adviser put himself in the respondent's position, so he did not respond to the talk
options.option_c: The respondent replied to the speakers talk, although he oughtnot to have done so
options.option_d: What was advisable was that the respondent gave it back to the speaker

questions.explanation: The sentence 'I wouldn't have responded to this rude talk, if I were you' is a hypothetical conditional structure expressing regret or disapproval of an action that has already occurred. By saying 'if I were you', the speaker is placing themselves in the listener's shoes to judge their past behavior. The use of 'wouldn't have responded' implies that the respondent actually did respond, and the speaker is critiquing that action. Option C accurately captures this implication: the respondent replied, and the adviser is stating that, in their view, it was the wrong thing to do.
questions.common_mistake: Many students mistake this for a future possibility (Type 2 conditional) and fail to realize that the structure 'would not have [past participle]' serves as a retrospective critique of an action already taken in the past.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He could not speak out because he had a feet of clay
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentences. Each question carries 2 marksHe could not speak out because he had a feet of clay
questions.explanation: The idiom 'feet of clay' refers to a hidden fault, weakness, or character flaw in someone who is otherwise perceived as strong, powerful, or admirable. In the context of the sentence, the person could not speak out because their underlying weakness or lack of moral courage (cowardice) prevented them from taking a stand. Option B is the best fit as it captures the sense of being vulnerable or lacking the necessary strength to act.
questions.common_mistake: Students often interpret idioms literally (as seen in option A) by focusing on the words 'feet' and 'clay' rather than understanding the metaphorical meaning of the phrase.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The player wasted a golden opportunity during the penalty shoot-out
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentences. Each question carries 2 marksThe player wasted a golden opportunity during the penalty shoot-out

options.option_a: The player first hit the bar
options.option_b: The player did not score the shot
options.option_c: The player scored the shoot that made them win the golden cup
options.option_d: Instead a silver cup, they received the golden one

questions.explanation: The phrase 'golden opportunity' in this context refers to a highly favorable chance to achieve a goal. In the context of a penalty shoot-out, 'wasting' this opportunity means failing to convert the penalty kick into a goal. Option B is the only statement that logically describes the failure to score during that specific sporting event.
questions.common_mistake: Students often get distracted by the word 'golden' and mistakenly associate it with the actual trophy or cup (as seen in Options C and D), ignoring the fact that the sentence is describing an action (missing a shot) rather than a reward.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: As far as Abu is concerned, Mero should be given fifty naira at the most
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS.In each of questions 26 to 35, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentences. Each question carries 2 marksAs far as Abu is concerned, Mero should be given fifty naira at the most

options.option_a: All Abu is saying is that Mero probably deserves more that fifty naira and not less
options.option_b: All Abu is concerned with is that Mero should be given nothing more than fifty naira
options.option_c: In Abus estimation, Mero merits not more that fifty naira
options.option_d: In Abu's opinion, Mero deserves fifty naira or probably more

questions.explanation: The phrase 'at the most' serves as an upper limit or a maximum ceiling. When Abu says Mero should be given fifty naira 'at the most', he is expressing that fifty naira is the highest amount Mero should receive; anything above that would be excessive in his opinion. Option C ('In Abu's estimation, Mero merits not more than fifty naira') captures this meaning perfectly, as 'not more than' is a direct synonym for 'at the most'.
questions.common_mistake: Many students often confuse 'at the most' with 'at least'. If the sentence had used 'at least', the meaning would imply a minimum threshold (Option D). Option B is incorrect because it focuses on the act of giving rather than the merit/valuation of the amount.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The minister considered the ministry's budget to be a drop in the ocean in view of the number of projects in the pipeline.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS In each of questions 36 to 45, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.The minister considered the ministry's budget to be a drop in the ocean in view of the number of projects in the pipeline.

options.option_a: The amount available may be inadequate for projected expenditure.
options.option_b: The minister may be dropped for failing to complete a number of projects.
options.option_c: The money approved cannot complete the pipeline project across the ocean.
options.option_d: The pipeline project across the ocean will be abandoned unless budgetary allocation improves.

questions.explanation: The idiom 'a drop in the ocean' refers to a very small amount that is insufficient compared to what is actually required. In the context of the sentence, the minister believes the budget is too small to cover the numerous projects 'in the pipeline' (a term meaning projects currently being planned or under development). Therefore, option A is the only choice that accurately captures this disparity between the available funds and the required expenditure.
questions.common_mistake: Students often fall for literal interpretations of idioms, as seen in options C and D, which mistakenly introduce the concept of an actual 'pipeline' or 'ocean'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The police are looking for the woman who farmed her children out to her neighbours.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS In each of questions 36 to 45, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.The police are looking for the woman who farmed her children out to her neighbours.

options.option_a: The woman and her children are in the habit of working in neighbours' farms and the police are not well disposed to this.
options.option_b: The police may arrest the woman for allowing her neighbours to take care of her children.
options.option_c: The woman may be arrested for allowing her children to be a nuisance to her neighbours.
options.option_d: The police wanted the woman for allowing her children to destroy her neighbours' crops.

questions.explanation: The idiomatic expression 'farm out' means to send work or responsibility to others, often to get rid of it or to delegate it to another party. In this context, 'farming out her children' means the woman has transferred the responsibility of caring for her children to her neighbors. The sentence implies that the police are seeking the woman because this act of delegation may be legally questionable or linked to an offense, making 'B' the only option that captures the meaning of delegating child-rearing duties.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often misinterpret the word 'farm' literally, assuming it involves agricultural activities, as seen in options A and D. It is important to recognize that 'farm out' is a phrasal verb distinct from working on a farm.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Jummai's father remarked that pigs would fly before she passed.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS In each of questions 36 to 45, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.Jummai's father remarked that pigs would fly before she passed.

options.option_a: It would-be possible to pass only if she worked harder.
options.option_b: It would never be possible for her to pass.
options.option_c: He would have to bribe her teachers to enable her to pass.
options.option_d: She would have to cheat in order to pass.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'pigs might fly' (or 'pigs would fly') is a well-known English idiom used to describe an event that is impossible or highly unlikely to occur. By saying this, Jummai's father is expressing strong skepticism or conviction that Jummai will never pass, as he believes the occurrence is as impossible as a pig flying.
questions.common_mistake: Students often make the mistake of interpreting the idiom literally or assuming it implies a condition (like working harder or cheating), rather than recognizing it as a hyperbolic expression of impossibility.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The president said that he found himself between a rock and a hard place when the press said that he had resigned.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS In each of questions 36 to 45, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.The president said that he found himself between a rock and a hard place when the press said that he had resigned.

options.option_a: He dreamt that he was abandoned.
options.option_b: He thought that hard places were unsafe.
options.option_c: He had a hard decision to make.
options.option_d: Hard places are dangerous for the president.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'between a rock and a hard place' is a common idiom meaning to be in a very difficult situation where one has to choose between two equally unpleasant or unfavorable alternatives. In the context of the sentence, the president is faced with the dilemma of how to handle the false report of his resignation, which presents a difficult decision-making scenario.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is interpreting the idiom literally (as seen in options B and D). Students often confuse idiomatic expressions with physical descriptions of the environment or literal safety concerns.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Kunana is like a bear with a sore head
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS In each of questions 36 to 45, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.Kunana is like a bear with a sore head
questions.explanation: The idiom 'like a bear with a sore head' is used to describe someone who is extremely irritable, grumpy, or in a very bad mood. Because a bear in pain would naturally be aggressive and unpleasant to be around, the phrase figuratively characterizes a person who is acting short-tempered or disgruntled.
questions.common_mistake: Students often make the mistake of interpreting the idiom literally by associating it with physical appearance (e.g., 'ugly' or 'a bully'), rather than understanding it as a state of emotional temperament.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Olu gave his brother a bumpy ride.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS In each of questions 36 to 45, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.Olu gave his brother a bumpy ride.

options.option_a: Olu's brother rode on Olu's back to success.
options.option_b: Olu took his brother on a bumpy road.
options.option_c: Olu gave his brother a difficult time.
options.option_d: Olu gave his brother a ride in his car.

questions.explanation: In English, the expression 'to give someone a bumpy ride' is an idiom that means to make things difficult, unpleasant, or troublesome for someone. It implies creating obstacles or causing distress in a situation. Option C is the only choice that captures this figurative meaning, whereas the other options interpret the phrase literally, which is incorrect in the context of advanced idiomatic usage.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is interpreting the sentence literally (Option B or D). Students often fail to recognize that 'bumpy ride' is a metaphorical expression for 'trouble' or 'difficulty' rather than a description of a physical journey on a poorly maintained road.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Adeola doesn't have to go to the farm today.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS In each of questions 36 to 45, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.Adeola doesn't have to go to the farm today.

options.option_a: Adeola may go to the farm today if he so wishes.
options.option_b: Adeola ought not to have gone to the farm today.
options.option_c: Adeola must not go to the farm today.
options.option_d: Adeola should not go to the inn today.

questions.explanation: In English grammar, the phrase 'doesn't have to' expresses a lack of necessity or obligation. It means the person is not required to perform the action, but they are free to do so if they choose. Option A correctly captures this sense of 'optionality.' Option C ('must not') is incorrect because it expresses a prohibition, which is a different modal meaning entirely.
questions.subtopic: Modal Verbs of Obligation and Necessity
questions.common_mistake: Many students confuse 'doesn't have to' (lack of necessity) with 'must not' (prohibition). They assume that if someone doesn't have to do something, they are forbidden from doing it.
related_topics: Modal Verbs (Can, Should, Must, Ought to)

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: My boss asked me to take my eyes off the ball.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS In each of questions 36 to 45, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.My boss asked me to take my eyes off the ball.

options.option_a: should stop paying attention to what is most important.
options.option_b: I should be focused when I am about to stay off football
options.option_c: i should stay off fcotbali after sustaining an injury.
options.option_d: I should be focused when playing football.

questions.explanation: The idiom 'to take one's eye off the ball' means to stop paying attention to the most important things or to lose focus on a task or goal. In a business context, it implies a lapse in concentration or negligence regarding one's core responsibilities. Therefore, the statement means the boss is advising the speaker to stop paying attention to what is most important, likely as a form of instruction to take a break or due to a misunderstanding of the idiom's typical negative connotation in some contexts, but A remains the only option that correctly defines the idiomatic meaning.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is interpreting the sentence literally, assuming it has something to do with the sport of football, as seen in options B, C, and D.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The robber was hedged in by the people.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS In each of questions 36 to 45, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.The robber was hedged in by the people.

options.option_a: The robber was surrounded by the people.
options.option_b: The robber was killed by the people.
options.option_c: The robber was exposed by the people.
options.option_d: The robber was caught by the people.

questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'to hedge in' means to surround someone or something in a way that prevents escape or limits movement. In the context of the sentence, the people formed a perimeter around the robber, effectively trapping them. Option A ('surrounded') is the most accurate synonym for this idiomatic expression.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse 'hedged in' with 'hanged' or 'hunted,' leading them to select options related to violence (B) or apprehension (D). While the result of being hedged in might lead to being caught, the phrase itself specifically refers to the act of encircling.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Many workers are not happy because they live a hand-to-mouth life.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS In each of questions 36 to 45, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence. Each question carries 2 marks.Many workers are not happy because they live a hand-to-mouth life.

options.option_a: They work hard with their hands
options.option_d: They have rejected the use of spoons

questions.explanation: The idiom 'hand-to-mouth' describes a situation where someone spends money as soon as they earn it because they earn very little. It implies a state of poverty or financial instability where one's income is just enough to cover basic daily needs, such as food, with nothing left for savings. Therefore, 'barely surviving' is the option that most accurately captures this state of financial struggle.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often make the mistake of interpreting the idiom literally (focusing on 'hand' and 'mouth'), leading them to choose options like 'A' (working hard with their hands) or 'D' (eating habits), which do not reflect the figurative meaning of the phrase.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Prolonged strike action debilitated the industry
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 46 to 55, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrasse in italicsProlonged strike actiondebilitatedthe industry
questions.explanation: To solve this question, you must understand the meaning of the word 'debilitated'. To debilitate means to make someone or something weak, infirm, or to sap its energy. In the context of the sentence, the strike made the industry weak. Therefore, the opposite must be a word that means to strengthen or energize. 'Invigorated' means to give strength or energy to someone or something, making it the perfect antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'destroyed' (Option D) as the opposite. While 'destroyed' represents a negative outcome, it is not an antonym for 'weakened'; it is a more extreme form of damage. Antonyms must represent the logical reverse of the original action.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: One of the students bought a plagiarized copy of the book.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 46 to 55, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrasse in italicsOne of the students bought aplagiarizedcopy of the book.
questions.explanation: The word 'plagiarized' refers to work that has been copied from another source and presented as one's own, effectively making it a fake, unauthorized, or counterfeit version. The opposite of a counterfeit or copied work is an 'original' work, which is produced directly by the author and is authentic.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'plagiarized' with 'outdated' or 'second-hand'. While a plagiarized book might be old or used, the antonym must specifically address the property of authenticity rather than the condition or age of the item.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The young girl was taken aback by her father's gift of a car.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 46 to 55, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrasse in italicsThe young girl was takenabackby her father's gift of a car.
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'taken aback' means to be suddenly surprised, shocked, or bewildered by something unexpected. To find the option opposite in meaning, we must look for a term that signifies a lack of reaction or emotional neutrality. Option B, 'unmoved', means to be unaffected or not emotionally touched by an event, which is the direct opposite of the surprise associated with being 'taken aback'. Options A (shocked), C (surprised), and D (nonplussed) are all synonyms of 'taken aback'.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'nonplussed' (Option D) because they mistake it for a state of being calm or unaffected, whereas 'nonplussed' actually means to be so surprised and confused that one is unsure how to react.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Musa is a gifted but erratic player.
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 46 to 55, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrasse in italicsMusa is a gifted buterraticplayer.
questions.explanation: The word 'erratic' refers to something or someone that is inconsistent, unpredictable, or lacking a regular course. To find the opposite, we must look for a word that implies consistency or regularity. Option B, 'regular', is the direct opposite because it denotes acting or happening at uniform intervals or being consistent in performance.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'erratic' for 'unstable' (Option D) or 'unpredictable' (Option C), which are actually synonyms of 'erratic', not antonyms. Always ensure you are selecting the word that conveys the opposite meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The lamp shades were translucent
questions.instruction: LEXIS, STRUCTURE AND ORAL FORMS. In each of questions 46 to 55, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrasse in italicsThe lamp shades weretranslucent
questions.explanation: The word 'translucent' refers to a substance that allows light to pass through, but not in a way that allows clear images to be seen (semi-transparent). Its direct opposite is 'opaque,' which describes a material that does not allow any light to pass through at all. Option D (transparent) is a near-synonym, not an antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Many students mistakenly choose 'transparent' because they confuse the degrees of light transmission. While both involve light passing through, 'transparent' is the opposite of 'opaque,' not 'translucent.'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: My niece has an unquenchable thirst for adventure stories.
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.My niece has anunquenchable thirstfor adventure stories.
questions.explanation: The word 'unquenchable' is derived from the verb 'quench,' meaning to satisfy or put out (usually thirst or fire). Therefore, 'unquenchable' means impossible to satisfy or extinguish. Option D, 'inextinguishable,' is a direct synonym as it carries the same meaning of something that cannot be put out or suppressed.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'unquenchable' with 'spurious' (false/fake) because they may be guessing based on the complexity of the word, rather than breaking down the root word 'quench'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Some of my neighbours have an antipathy to dogs.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 46 to 55, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrasse in italicsSome of my neighbours have anantipathy todogs.
questions.explanation: The word 'antipathy' refers to a deep-seated feeling of dislike, aversion, or hostility towards someone or something. To find the antonym (opposite), we must look for a word that signifies fondness or attraction. 'Affection for' describes a feeling of liking or love, which is the direct opposite of 'antipathy'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'antipathy' for 'apathy' (lack of interest). While they sound similar, 'antipathy' specifically implies an active negative feeling, making 'affection' the most appropriate opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The dressmaker unpicked the seam of the shirt.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 46 to 55, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrasse in italicsThe dressmakerunpickedthe seam of the shirt.
questions.explanation: The word 'unpicked' means to undo the stitches or seams of a garment that has been sewn. Therefore, the opposite action is to fasten or join the fabric back together. 'Sewed up' is the direct antonym as it describes the process of creating or repairing a seam by passing a needle and thread through fabric.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'threaded' (Option A). While 'threading' is related to sewing, it refers to passing a thread through the eye of a needle, not the act of joining fabric pieces together.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The testimony of the witness was vague.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 46 to 55, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrasse in italicsThe testimony of the witness wasvague.
questions.explanation: The word 'vague' means uncertain, indefinite, or unclear in character or meaning. To find the opposite, we look for a word that signifies precision or lack of ambiguity. Option D, 'clear', is the most accurate antonym because it denotes something that is easy to perceive, understand, or interpret, which is the direct opposite of being vague.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'ambiguous' (Option B). However, 'ambiguous' is a synonym of 'vague', not an antonym. Always ensure you identify the direction of the question (opposite vs. similar) before selecting an answer.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: As a student, Isa tried communal living for a few years.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 46 to 55, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrasse in italicsAs a student, Isa triedcommunal livingfor a few years.
questions.explanation: The term 'communal' refers to something shared by all members of a community or group; it implies living in a setting where resources, space, or facilities are held in common. The direct opposite of 'shared' or 'communal' is 'private', which refers to something kept or used by a single individual, exclusive of others.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'collective' or 'general' because they are synonyms of communal. In 'opposite in meaning' questions, it is crucial to avoid selecting words that mean the same thing as the italicized word.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The chairman admires incessant meetings.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.The chairman admiresincessantmeetings.
questions.explanation: The word 'incessant' describes something that continues without interruption; it is synonymous with 'ceaseless,' 'perpetual,' or 'constant.' In the context of the sentence, the chairman enjoys meetings that happen frequently and without pause. Therefore, 'constant' is the option nearest in meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'incessant' for 'irregular' because they confuse the prefix 'in-' (which often implies negation) with a lack of pattern, whereas 'incessant' specifically implies a non-stop, continuous flow.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Todays weather is favourable for a game of tennis.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.Todays weather isfavourablefor a game of tennis.
questions.explanation: The word 'favourable' means expressing approval or providing conditions that are helpful and likely to lead to success. In the context of weather conditions for a sport, 'favourable' means the weather is good, suitable, or 'encouraging' for the game to take place. Option C is the closest in meaning as it implies the conditions support the activity.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'favourable' with 'impartial' (which relates to fairness/neutrality) or misinterpret the word as 'favourite'. Context is key here; weather cannot be 'impartial', it is either suitable or unsuitable.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: All the candidates looked aghast at the first reading of the questions.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.All the candidates lookedaghastat the first reading of the questions.
questions.explanation: The word 'aghast' refers to a state of being filled with horror, shock, or amazement. In the context of a candidate reading an examination paper, it suggests they were surprised or alarmed by the difficulty of the questions. Among the options, 'dismayed' is the only word that captures the sense of shock or distress, making it the closest synonym.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'aghast' for 'ghostly' or 'afraid' in a physical sense. While it implies a negative reaction, it specifically denotes a sudden emotional reaction to an event or stimulus rather than simple physical fear.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Joke gave Muhammed a jaunty smile.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.Joke gave Muhammeda jauntysmile.
questions.explanation: The word 'jaunty' describes something bold, confident, and cheerful. In the context of a smile, it conveys a lighthearted, carefree, and positive expression. Among the options, 'a cheerful' (D) best captures this meaning. The other options—'discouraging' (A), 'inviting' (B), and 'frightful' (C)—do not align with the positive and confident tone of 'jaunty.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'jaunty' with 'inviting' (B) due to the smile's social context, but 'jaunty' emphasizes cheerfulness rather than invitation.
related_topics: Adjectives and Their Shades of Meaning

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The first round of the tournament was a dodle
questions.instruction: In each of questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.The first round of the tournament was adodle
questions.explanation: The word 'dodle' in the sentence is a misspelling of 'doddle,' which is an informal British English term meaning something very easy. The phrase 'a doddle' is equivalent to 'a piece of cake' in American English. The context of the sentence (a tournament round being described as a 'dodle') implies that the round was effortless to win or complete, aligning with 'easy' (option A).
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'dodle' with 'dodgy' (option C), which means risky or unreliable, or misinterpreting the informal phrasing as a literal word.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The lazy man cast a lustful glance at his neighbour's wife.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.The lazy man cast alustfulglance at his neighbour's wife.
questions.explanation: The word 'lustful' in the sentence refers to a strong, often sexual, desire. 'Covetous' (option C) best matches this meaning as it denotes an intense desire for something belonging to someone else. 'Envious' (D) relates to resentment over another's possessions, while 'hateful' (A) and 'quick' (B) are unrelated to the context of desire. The sentence implies the man desires the neighbor's wife, aligning with 'covetous'.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'covetous' with 'envious' due to their similar connotations of desire for others' possessions.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: They accused him of fomenting political unrest
questions.instruction: In each of questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.They accused him offomentingpolitical unrest
questions.explanation: To 'foment' means to instigate, stir up, or incite undesirable or violent behavior, particularly in a political or social context. Looking at the options, 'inciting' shares this exact definition, as it means to encourage or stir up (violent or unlawful behavior). The other options (discouraging, preventing, and guiding) are antonyms or unrelated to the negative, provocative nature of fomenting.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'foment' for 'formulate' or 'promote' due to a slight phonetic resemblance. While 'promote' can be positive, 'foment' is almost exclusively used in the context of negative or subversive activities.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: You can learn a great deal just from watching the players.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.You canlearna great deal just from watching the players.
questions.explanation: In this context, the phrase 'learn a great deal' refers to the process of gaining knowledge or insight through observation. Among the options, 'discover' is the closest in meaning as it denotes the act of finding out or gaining new information or understanding. While 'accumulate' means to gather or collect, it is typically used for items or data, whereas 'discover' better captures the intellectual process of learning something new from an experience.
questions.common_mistake: Students often select 'accumulate' because they associate 'a great deal' with the act of gathering or collecting, but 'learning' is an act of discovery and intellectual acquisition rather than simple physical accumulation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: All the researchers were asked to gamer information on the new viral infection.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.All the researchers were asked togamerinformation on the new viral infection.
questions.explanation: The word 'garner' (often misspelled as 'gamer' in this context) means to gather, collect, or store up. In the context of research, researchers collect data or information to study. Therefore, 'collect' is the nearest in meaning. 'Distort' means to twist, 'disseminate' means to spread or broadcast, and 'give' is the opposite of the gathering process required here.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often mistake 'garner' for 'gather' or confuse it with 'disseminate' (to spread), failing to realize that researchers must first acquire information before they can share it.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The dispute between the two countries has resulted in the severing of diplomatic relations
questions.instruction: In each of questions 56 to 65, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics.The dispute between the two countries has resulted in theseveringof diplomatic relations
questions.explanation: The word 'severing' is derived from the verb 'sever,' which means to cut off, terminate, or break a connection. In the context of international politics, 'severing of diplomatic relations' means the formal termination or 'breaking' of ties between two nations. Therefore, 'breaking' is the closest in meaning. 'Securing' means making safe, 'swapping' means exchanging, and 'strengthening' means making stronger; none of these fit the context of a dispute.
questions.common_mistake: Students sometimes confuse 'severing' with 'serving' due to phonetic similarity, which leads to choosing incorrect options based on an misinterpretation of the word's root meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He was both a writer and a politician, but he was better ----- a singer
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).He was both a writer and a politician, but he was better ----- a singer
questions.explanation: The structure 'better as' is used here to indicate a comparison of roles or capacities. When describing someone's professional aptitude or performance in a specific role, we use 'as' to introduce the capacity. 'Better than' would imply comparing the person to a singer, but the sentence structure 'better ____ a singer' specifically requires 'as' to complete the comparative predicate correctly (i.e., 'he was better [in the capacity of] a singer').
questions.common_mistake: Many students mistakenly choose 'like' (Option B) because they confuse it with descriptive similes. However, 'like' implies similarity (resemblance), whereas 'as' is required here to denote actual function or role.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Vacancies in the company will be notified by ----
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Vacancies in the company will be notified by ----
questions.explanation: In professional and corporate contexts, the act of informing the public about job openings is formally referred to as an 'advertisement'. While 'bulletin' and 'publication' are nouns related to written materials, they do not accurately describe the process of announcing vacancies in a job context. 'Advertisement' is the standard terminology for a notice placed in newspapers, websites, or boards to attract candidates for employment.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'publication' because it sounds formal, but 'publication' refers to the act of making information generally available (like a book or article), whereas 'advertisement' specifically denotes the promotion of a vacancy to solicit applications.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The driver was short of petrol, so he ... down the hills with the engine switched off
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The driver was short of petrol, so he ... down the hills with the engine switched off
questions.explanation: The word 'coasted' is the most accurate term here. In the context of driving, to 'coast' means to allow a vehicle to move under its own momentum, usually downhill, without the use of the engine or with the engine switched off. 'Glided' generally refers to smooth movement through the air or on water; 'wheeled' usually describes moving something on wheels or turning; and 'taxied' refers specifically to an aircraft moving on the ground under its own power before takeoff or after landing.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'glided' because it implies smooth motion, but 'coasted' is the specific technical term used in automotive contexts for driving without engine power.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He started his career as an ... teacher.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).He started his career as an ... teacher.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling of the word meaning a helper or a person providing supplementary support is 'auxiliary'. It is derived from the Latin word 'auxiliarius'. Options B, C, and D contain incorrect spellings (e.g., misspelling the 'ia' sequence or omitting letters). Note: Option A and Option D are identical in the provided list; in such JAMB scenarios, selecting the first correct instance is standard, though both are technically correct representations of the word.
questions.common_mistake: Students often misspell the word by omitting the second 'i' or confusing the placement of the 'l' and 'a'. Common incorrect variations include 'auxillary' or 'auxilary'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: His many years of success in legal practice, ----- didn't come without challenges
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).His many years of success in legal practice, ----- didn't come without challenges
questions.explanation: The sentence requires a non-restrictive relative clause that refers back to the 'success' mentioned in the main clause. 'Indeed' functions here as an adverbial intensifier that can introduce a parenthetical clause (often set off by commas). When we say '..., indeed, it didn't come without challenges,' we are emphasizing the reality of the statement. Options B and D (but/however) are conjunctions that would create a run-on sentence or a grammatical mismatch because there is already a comma present, and a relative pronoun or specific adverbial structure is required to bridge the clause.
questions.common_mistake: Students often pick 'however' because it implies contrast, but 'however' cannot function as a relative pronoun and would require a semicolon or a full stop to separate two independent clauses, which the current punctuation (comma) does not support.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: One should be careful how ---- behaves in public, shouldn---
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).One should be careful how ---- behaves in public, shouldn---
questions.explanation: The sentence employs the indefinite pronoun 'one' as the subject. In formal English, if a sentence begins with 'one', all subsequent references to that subject must also use 'one' to maintain grammatical consistency. In the question tag, the same principle applies: the pronoun used in the subject position must be reflected in the tag. Therefore, 'one' matches 'one' in the first gap, and 'one' is used in the tag, resulting in 'shouldn't one?'.
questions.common_mistake: Many students mistakenly switch to 'he' or 'they' because they find 'one' to be formal or repetitive. For example, writing 'One should be careful... shouldn't he?' is a common error in English usage.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: -------, a good leader must have two characteristics.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).-------, a good leader must have two characteristics.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'first and foremost' is a standard English idiom used to emphasize that something is the most important or primary point. The spelling of 'foremost' consists of 'fore-' (meaning 'before') and '-most'. Option D is the only option with the correct orthography.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often misspell 'foremost' as 'formost' or 'formust' due to phonetic confusion or lack of attention to the prefix 'fore-'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: We visited his house ----- three times.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).We visited his house ----- three times.
questions.explanation: In this context, the speaker needs an adverbial modifier to express an approximation of the number of visits. The word 'about' serves as an adverb meaning 'approximately' or 'nearly'. 'We visited his house about three times' is grammatically sound. The use of 'for' (as seen in options B and D) is redundant and grammatically incorrect because 'visited' is a transitive verb that directly takes the object 'his house' and does not require a prepositional phrase for duration here; furthermore, 'for about' would imply a duration of time rather than a frequency of occurrence.
questions.common_mistake: Students often use 'for' before expressions of frequency (like 'three times') due to confusion with expressions of duration (e.g., 'for three hours'). Using 'for' with a frequency count is grammatically incorrect in this context.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: She was ... the verge of tears
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).She was ... the verge of tears
questions.explanation: The phrase 'on the verge of' is a fixed idiomatic expression in English. It means to be at the point or edge of something happening (usually an emotional state or an event). Therefore, 'on' is the only preposition that correctly collocates with 'the verge of'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistakenly choose 'at' because it is commonly associated with locations or points in time, but it is grammatically incorrect in this specific idiomatic context.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Everyone makes mistakes occasionally, nobody is -----
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Everyone makes mistakes occasionally, nobody is -----
questions.explanation: The word 'infallible' means incapable of making mistakes or being wrong. The sentence structure implies a contrast: because humans make mistakes (as stated in the first clause), nobody is 'infallible'. While 'imperfect' might seem logically sound, 'infallible' is the precise antonym for the ability to make mistakes. 'Incorrigible' refers to someone who cannot be reformed, and 'indestructible' refers to something that cannot be destroyed.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'imperfect' because it is a synonym for 'having mistakes.' However, in the context of the sentence structure—which emphasizes the act of making mistakes—'infallible' is the more specific and appropriate term that directly negates the possibility of erring.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The woman would not part with her ----- pot.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The woman would not part with her ----- pot.
questions.explanation: In English, multiple adjectives preceding a noun must follow a specific standard order: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Color, Origin, Material, Purpose. In this question, 'discarded' functions as an adjective related to age/condition, 'black' is a color, and 'earthen' is the material. Following the rule (Age/Condition -> Color -> Material), the correct sequence is 'discarded' (condition), 'black' (color), and 'earthen' (material).
questions.common_mistake: Students often arrange adjectives based on what 'sounds right' or by placing the material adjective (earthen) first, forgetting that material adjectives must always come immediately before the noun they describe.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: We stood up when the principal came in, ------- ?
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).We stood up when the principal came in, ------- ?
questions.explanation: The sentence 'We stood up when the principal came in' is a statement in the simple past tense. According to the rules of question tags, if the main clause is positive, the tag must be negative. Since the verb 'stood' is in the simple past, the auxiliary verb 'did' must be used for the tag. Therefore, the negative tag is 'didn't' followed by the subject pronoun 'we'.
questions.common_mistake: Many students wrongly choose 'isn't it' because they fail to identify the tense of the sentence (simple past) and incorrectly try to form a tag based on the present tense.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: This professor of... medicine has ... the mystery of bird flu.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).This professor of... medicine has ... the mystery of bird flu.
questions.explanation: The word 'veterinary' is the correct spelling for the branch of medicine concerned with animals. Regarding the word 'unravelled', in British English (which is the standard for JAMB), the consonant 'l' is doubled when adding the suffix '-ed' to a word ending in a single vowel followed by 'l'. Therefore, 'unravelled' with double 'l' is the standard spelling.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'veterinary' for 'vetinary' due to mispronunciation, and they may be confused by the American English spelling 'unraveled' (single 'l'), which is generally considered incorrect in the context of standard Nigerian/British English examination curriculum.
related_topics: British vs. American English Spelling conventions

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Her mother brought her some...
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Her mother brought her some...
questions.explanation: In English grammar, 'cloth' refers to the material or fabric used for making garments. When a parent brings someone material to sew, they bring 'some cloth'. 'Clothes' is a plural noun referring to finished garments (shirts, trousers, etc.); while 'some clothes' is grammatically possible, 'some cloth' is the standard idiomatic expression for raw fabric. 'Clothing' is an uncountable collective noun referring to garments in general, but it is rarely used with the quantifier 'some' in this specific context unless referring to a collection of items. 'Yards' is a unit of measurement and requires a number (e.g., 'three yards of cloth'), not just the quantifier 'some'. Therefore, 'cloth' is the most precise and natural fit for the material.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is confusing 'cloth' (the fabric material) with 'clothes' (the finished garments). While 'some clothes' is technically grammatically correct, 'some cloth' is the intended answer in contexts where someone brings material to be tailored.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Many workers were... as a result of the textile closure.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).Many workers were... as a result of the textile closure.
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'laid off' means to discharge a worker or workers from a job, often temporarily or permanently due to a lack of work, downsizing, or company closure. The context of a 'textile closure' clearly indicates that the workers lost their jobs, making 'laid off' the only semantically appropriate choice. Other options have different meanings: 'laid down' (to sacrifice or establish a rule), 'laid out' (to arrange or spend money), and 'laid up' (to be confined to bed due to illness).
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'laid off' with 'laid down' because both involve the verb 'lay'. However, 'laid down' is typically used for weapons or rules, not employment termination.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The driver died in the... road accident.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The driver died in the... road accident.
questions.explanation: In English, certain words are conventionally paired together, a concept known as collocation. The adjective 'fatal' specifically describes an incident that results in death. While the other options describe unpleasant events, 'fatal' is the precise lexical item used to describe an accident that causes loss of life, making it the most appropriate choice to complete the sentence.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'serious' because it describes the severity of the accident, but 'serious' does not inherently imply that a death occurred. 'Fatal' is more specific and semantically accurate in this context.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: ...your parents frown ... our friendship, we shouldn see each other anymore.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s)....your parents frown ... our friendship, we shouldn see each other anymore.
questions.explanation: The sentence requires a subordinating conjunction to introduce a reason and a preposition that collocates correctly with the verb 'frown'. 'As' serves as a causal conjunction meaning 'since' or 'because'. The verb 'frown' in the context of disapproval is idiomatically used with the preposition 'upon' (or 'on'), as in 'frown upon'. Therefore, 'As/upon' creates the most grammatically accurate and idiomatic expression.
questions.common_mistake: Many students wrongly assume 'frown at' is the standard idiomatic expression for disapproval. While 'frown at' can mean a literal facial expression, 'frown upon' is the accepted phrasal verb meaning to disapprove of something.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: For more productivity, the company is focusing attention on the possible ... of available resources.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).For more productivity, the company is focusing attention on the possible ... of available resources.
questions.explanation: In business English, the phrase 'tapping into resources' is a common idiom meaning to make use of available assets, skills, or energy to achieve a specific goal. While 'synergy,' 'alignment,' and 'arrangement' are valid English words, they do not collocate naturally with the word 'resources' in the context of increasing productivity. One 'taps' resources to extract value, making 'tapping' the most semantically appropriate choice.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'synergy' because it sounds more sophisticated or 'business-like,' failing to recognize that 'synergy' refers to the combined effect of elements working together, not the act of accessing or utilizing existing resources.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: ------she didn trust him, she married him.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).------she didn trust him, she married him.
questions.explanation: The sentence expresses a contrast between two clauses: 'she didn't trust him' and 'she married him'. A concession is required to show this contrast. 'Though' is a subordinating conjunction used to introduce a clause that contrasts with the main clause. While 'Much as' can also express concession, 'Though' is the most direct and grammatically standard choice for this construction in JAMB examinations.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the usage of 'Since' (which denotes reason or time) or 'After' (which denotes time) with 'Though' (which denotes contrast). Selecting 'Since' makes the sentence logically incoherent, as marrying someone because you don't trust them contradicts the cause-and-effect relationship.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I wanted to know his political beliefs, so I asked him what ...
questions.instruction: In each of questions 66 to 85, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).I wanted to know his political beliefs, so I asked him what ...
questions.explanation: This question tests the principle of 'sequence of tenses' in reported speech. The main verb of the sentence, 'asked,' is in the past tense. Consequently, the subordinate clause must also follow the past tense sequence. Furthermore, since 'political beliefs' is plural, the corresponding demonstrative pronoun must be plural ('these') rather than singular ('this'). Therefore, 'these were' is the only option that maintains both grammatical number agreement and tense consistency.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistakenly select 'these are' because they overlook the fact that the reporting verb ('asked') is in the past tense, requiring the reported information to shift to the past as well.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: book
questions.instruction: In each of questions 86 to 88, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.book
questions.explanation: The word 'book' contains the short lax vowel sound /ʊ/. When comparing the options: 'cook' also features the same short /ʊ/ sound. Conversely, 'cool', 'fool', and 'tool' all contain the long tense vowel sound /uː/.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the short vowel /ʊ/ (as in 'book') with the long vowel /uː/ (as in 'pool'). They may incorrectly assume all words spelled with double 'o' have the same sound, ignoring the length and tenseness of the vowel.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: village
questions.instruction: In each of questions 86 to 88, choose the optionthat has the same vowel sound as me one represented by the letter(s) underlined.village
questions.explanation: The underlined letter in 'village' is 'i'. In this word, the 'i' represents the short vowel sound /ɪ/ (as in 'sit' or 'bit'). Among the options provided, 'pig' also contains the short /ɪ/ vowel sound. The other options ('page', 'made', and 'came') contain the long diphthong /eɪ/.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake the letter 'i' for its 'long' sound (as in 'kite' /aɪ/) or confuse it with the /iː/ sound (as in 'see'). In 'village', the 'i' is clearly a short vowel /ɪ/.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: patch
questions.instruction: In each of questions 86 to 88, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as me one represented by the letter(s) underlined.patch
questions.explanation: The word 'patch' contains the short vowel sound /æ/. In the provided options, 'starch' contains the long vowel sound /ɑː/. However, in many Nigerian English phonetic contexts, 'patch' and 'starch' share the open vowel quality that distinguishes them from the other options provided. Upon closer phonetic analysis, 'patch' uses /æ/, 'fare' uses /eə/, 'mad' uses /æ/, and 'brave' uses /eɪ/. Given that both 'patch' and 'mad' contain the /æ/ sound, 'mad' (Option C) is technically the most accurate phonetic match. However, in standard JAMB past question sets for this specific year, 'starch' is often mistakenly keyed as the answer due to the vowel quality /ɑː/ being confused with /æ/. Based on standard RP (Received Pronunciation), 'mad' is the correct match.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the short /æ/ sound in 'patch' and 'mad' with the long /ɑː/ sound found in words like 'starch' or 'path', particularly because of regional pronunciations.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: tangerine
questions.instruction: In each of questions 86 to 88, choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.tangerine
questions.explanation: In the word 'tangerine', the underlined letter 'i' (in the third syllable '-rine') represents the schwa sound /ə/ (or sometimes a reduced /ɪ/ depending on the regional pronunciation, but in standard JAMB phonetics context, the focus is on the unstressed neutral vowel). Let us analyze the options: (A) 'gear' contains the /ɪə/ diphthong. (B) 'danger' contains the /eɪ/ diphthong in the first syllable. (C) 'girl' contains the /ɜː/ sound. (D) 'ignore' features the /ə/ sound in the first syllable ('i-gnore'), which matches the sound of the 'i' in 'tangerine'.
questions.common_mistake: Many students confuse the schwa sound /ə/ with the short /i/ sound, or incorrectly assume that because 'tangerine' and 'danger' share the letter 'a' or 'i', they must share the same vowel sound regardless of stress patterns.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: hair
questions.instruction: In each of questions 89 to 91, choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.hair
questions.explanation: The underlined letter in 'hair' is 'h', which represents the voiceless glottal fricative consonant sound /h/. In the options provided, 'heir', 'hour', and 'honest' all begin with a silent 'h' (they are vowel-initial words). Only in 'house' is the letter 'h' pronounced as the /h/ sound. Therefore, 'house' is the correct option.
questions.common_mistake: Many students wrongly assume that all words starting with the letter 'h' contain the /h/ sound. Students often confuse silent 'h' words (like heir, hour, honest) with those where the sound is articulated.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: edition
questions.instruction: In each of questions 89 to 91, choose the option that has the same consonent sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.edition
questions.explanation: The underlined letters in 'edition' represent the consonant sound /ʃ/ (or 'sh' sound). To find the correct answer, we need to identify which option has the same consonant sound. 'Bastion' contains the 'st' and 'sh' or /ʃ/ sound, similar to 'edition'. 'Bash' also has the /ʃ/ sound. However, 'catch' and 'rating' do not have this sound. Between 'bash' and 'bastion', 'bastion' is a better example because it has a similar sound and spelling pattern to 'edition'.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing /ʃ/ with /t͡ʃ/ or /s/ sounds

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: demarcation
questions.instruction: In each of questions 92 to 94, choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The syllables are written in capital letters.demarcation
questions.explanation: The word 'demarcation' is derived from the verb 'demarcate,' which has its primary stress on the second syllable (de-MAR-cate). When forming the noun 'demarcation,' the stress pattern remains consistent with the root verb, placing the primary stress on the second syllable (de-MAR-ca-tion). This aligns with English stress rules for words ending in '-ation' derived from verbs with stress on the second syllable.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'demarcation' with words like 'information,' where the stress shifts to the third syllable. Students might incorrectly apply this pattern here, leading to errors in identifying the correct stress placement.
related_topics: Suffixes and Their Impact on Stress Patterns

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: impossible
questions.instruction: In each of questions 92 to 94, choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The syllables are written in capital letters.impossible
questions.explanation: In English phonetics, the word 'impossible' (/ɪmˈpɒsɪbəl/) consists of four syllables. The primary stress falls on the second syllable, 'POS'. Therefore, the correct pattern is im-POS-si-ble. Looking at the options provided, option A represents the stress on the second syllable (imPOSsible).
questions.common_mistake: Students often misplace the stress on the first syllable (IM-possible) due to the influence of the prefix 'im-', or on the last syllable because it sounds emphatic, both of which are incorrect in standard British English pronunciation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: imperialism
questions.instruction: In each of questions 92 to 94, choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The syllables are written in capital letters.imperialism
questions.explanation: In English phonology, words ending in the suffix '-ism' often exert a strong influence on stress placement. For the word 'imperialism' (/ɪmˈpɪə.ri.ə.lɪ.zəm/), the primary stress falls on the second syllable, which is the 'pe' (phonetically /pɪə/). Therefore, the correct stress pattern is im-PE-ri-al-ism.
questions.common_mistake: Students often misplace the stress on the first syllable ('IM-') or the syllable containing 'al', mistakenly applying the stress rule of the root word 'imperial' to the longer derivative noun without adjusting for the shift caused by the suffix.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: choose the option that has the stress on the first syllable.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 95 to 97, choose the option that has the stress on the first syllable.choose the option that has the stress on the first syllable.
questions.explanation: In English phonology, stress refers to the emphasis placed on a specific syllable within a word. For the word 'madam' (/ˈmad.əm/), the primary stress falls on the first syllable ('mad'). In contrast, 'eighteen' (/ˌeɪˈtiːn/), 'invent' (/ɪnˈvent/), and 'command' (/kəˈmɑːnd/) all carry the primary stress on their second syllables.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the stress pattern of numbers ending in '-teen' (which are stressed on the second syllable) with numbers ending in '-ty' (which are stressed on the first syllable).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: choose the option that has the stress on the first syllable.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 95 to 97, choose the option that has the stress on the first syllable.choose the option that has the stress on the first syllable.
questions.explanation: In English phonology, stress refers to the emphasis placed on a particular syllable. We analyze the options as follows: (A) 'nineteen' is stressed on the second syllable (/ˌnɪnˈtiːn/); (B) 'mother' is a two-syllable word stressed on the first syllable (/ˈmʌðə/); (C) 'estate' is stressed on the second syllable (/ɪˈsteɪt/); (D) 'announce' is stressed on the second syllable (/əˈnaʊns/). Therefore, 'mother' is the only option with primary stress on the first syllable.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mispronounce words by applying an equal rhythm to all syllables, failing to identify the natural stress pattern of disyllabic words, or guessing based on spelling rather than phonetic representation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: choose the option that has the stress on the first syllable.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 95 to 97, choose the option that has the stress on the first syllable.choose the option that has the stress on the first syllable.
questions.explanation: In English, many two-syllable words that function as both nouns and verbs follow a specific stress rule: the noun form is stressed on the first syllable, while the verb form is stressed on the second syllable. 'Export' as a noun is pronounced /ˈeks.pɔːt/ (stress on the first syllable). Conversely, 'commute' (/kəˈmjuːt/), 'import' (as a verb: /ɪmˈpɔːt/), and 'intend' (/ɪnˈtend/) all place the primary stress on the second syllable.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the word 'import' with 'export' or fail to distinguish between the noun and verb forms of the same word (e.g., im-PORT vs. IM-port).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The traditional chief NARRATED the story to the Children.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 98 to 100, the word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relatesThe traditional chief NARRATED the story to the Children.

options.option_a: The children heard the story from the traditional chief.
options.option_b: Who narrated the story to the children?
options.option_c: The children could not listen to the story by the traditional chief.
options.option_d: Did the chief hide the story from the children?

questions.explanation: In English, emphatic stress is used to highlight the specific piece of information that is being asserted, corrected, or clarified. When the word 'NARRATED' is stressed, it implies that the speaker is correcting a misconception about the action performed by the subject. Option D asks if the chief 'hid' the story, which sets up a context where the speaker must clarify: 'The traditional chief NARRATED (did not hide) the story.' The stress on the verb contrasts the action of telling with the action of withholding.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the placement of stress with the subject or the object. If the stress were on 'CHIEF', the answer would relate to who did the action. If it were on 'CHILDREN', the answer would relate to the recipients. Focusing on the verb 'NARRATED' necessitates an answer that centers on the action itself.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The ACCOUNTANT paid the workers July salary in September.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 98 to 100, the word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relatesThe ACCOUNTANT paid the workers July salary in September.

options.option_b: Did the cashier pay the workers' salary in September?
options.option_c: Workers received their July salary in September?
options.option_d: The September salary was paid in July?

questions.explanation: In English, emphatic stress is used to highlight the specific piece of information being corrected or clarified. When a word is stressed in a sentence, it implies that the speaker is correcting a misconception regarding that specific word. Here, the word 'ACCOUNTANT' is stressed. This indicates that the speaker is correcting an assumption about *who* performed the action. Option B ('Did the cashier pay the workers' salary in September?') presents a scenario where the listener might mistakenly believe it was the 'cashier', and the speaker replies using emphatic stress to point out that it was, in fact, the 'ACCOUNTANT'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the stressed word with the focus of the sentence. They may select an option that focuses on the object (salary) or the time (September) instead of the person performing the action.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The cat DEVOURED the rat.
questions.instruction: In each of questions 98 to 100, the word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relatesThe cat DEVOURED the rat.

options.option_a: Did the rat devour the cat?
options.option_c: Did the cat pet the rat?
options.option_d: Is this the rat that the cat devoured?

questions.explanation: In English, emphatic stress is placed on a word to emphasize a particular piece of information, usually to correct a misconception or clarify an action. When the verb 'DEVOURED' is stressed in the sentence 'The cat DEVOURED the rat', it implies a correction regarding the nature of the action performed by the cat. Option C ('Did the cat pet the rat?') suggests an alternative action (petting vs. devouring); by stressing 'DEVOURED', the speaker is clarifying that the cat did not merely pet the rat, but actively devoured it.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistakenly assume that emphasizing a verb is meant to highlight the 'doer' of the action (the subject) or the 'receiver' (the object), which would instead require stressing the subject or object respectively.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Which of these correctly summaries the arguments adduced by the advocates of deregulation?
questions.instruction: Read the passage below carefully and answer the questions that follow.Which of these correctly summaries the arguments adduced by the advocates of deregulation?
questions.passage: Read the passages I,II and III carefully and answer the questions that follows. Each question carries 3 mark PASSAGE I Music plays a vital role in human society. Good music provides entertainment and emotional release, and it accompanies activities ranging from dances to religious ceremonies. Music is heard everywhere in auditoriums, homes , elevators, schools, sports arenas ad streets. Recorded performance is a sensational innovation of the twentieth century. Thanks to modern technology like compact disc ( CD)digital video disc (DVD)and the MP3 player, music can now be heard in diverse places such places include living rooms and cars, jogging paths can also function as a new kinds of concert halls where we can hear what we want as often as we want Live performance provide a special excitement in a live performance, artistes put themselves on the line to avoid embarrassment the artiste must train beforehand and end=sure that technical difficulties are avoided and that the listeners are actively involved. What is performed, how it sounds and how the artistes feel that evening exist for a fleeting moment and can never be repeated. An audience responds to the excitement of such a moment and feelings exchanged between stage and hall Our response to a musical performance or an artiste is subjective and rooted in deep feelings. Even professional critics can differ strongly in their evaluation of a performance there is no one truth about what we hear and feel. Does the performer project a concept overall idea or an emotion? Do some sections of a piece, but not others ,communicate something to you ?can you figure out why ? it is up to us as listeners to evaluate performances of music alert and repeated listening will enhance our ability to compare performances and judge music so that we can fully enjoy it .people listen to music in many different ways. For instance music can be a barely perceived background as in a film or a totally absorbing experience as in a concert . Adapted from Roger K (1990)an Appreciation Music :Fourth Brief Edition ,Mc Grow –Hill Higher Education

options.option_a: Deregulating the economy will make the NNPC more efficient and less wasteful
options.option_b: The government should deregulate every aspect of the Nigerian economy
options.option_c: Competition in the oil industry will be beneficial to several Nigerians
options.option_d: Competition should be allowed in the production and distribution of petroleum products

questions.explanation: This question is fundamentally flawed due to a mismatch between the provided text and the question asked. The comprehension passage is about the role and appreciation of music, while the question asks for a summary of arguments regarding 'deregulation' (a topic related to economics/the oil industry).
