questions.question_text: Jimi was very prominent in Forcados High School because he was
questions.instruction: These questions are based on A. H. Mohammeds The Last Days at Forcados High School.Jimi was very prominent in Forcados High School because he was

options.option_a: the son of a great scholar
options.option_b: the only child of his parents

questions.explanation: In 'The Last Days at Forcados High School,' Jimi's prominence is primarily attributed to his role as a school prefect. Prefects in the novel are depicted as leaders and role models, which naturally elevates their status within the school community. The other options—being the son of a scholar, an only child, or noted for paintings—are not central to his prominence in the narrative. The story emphasizes his responsibilities and influence as a prefect, making option C the most accurate choice.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing Jimi's personal traits (e.g., family background or hobbies) with his official role as a prefect, which is the primary reason for his prominence.
related_topics: Themes in 'The Last Days at Forcados High School'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Mr. Rufus bore the brunt in the last promotion examination.
questions.instruction: For this question, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the question.Mr. Rufus bore the brunt in the last promotion examination.

options.option_a: Mr. Rufus failed the examination woefully.
options.option_b: Mr. Rufus excelled in the examinations
options.option_c: Mr. Rufus was excited about the examination.
options.option_d: Mr. Rufus toyed with the examination.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'bore the brunt' means to suffer the worst effects of a situation or to bear the main burden. In the context of an examination, it implies that Mr. Rufus experienced significant negative consequences, such as failing. Option A correctly interprets this as 'failed the examination woefully,' aligning with the idiomatic meaning. Options B, C, and D misinterpret the phrase as positive or neutral outcomes, which contradicts the intended meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'bore the brunt' with a positive outcome (e.g., excelling) due to unfamiliarity with idiomatic expressions.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: My friend is well off nowadays
questions.instruction: For this question, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the question.My friend is well off nowadays

options.option_b: My friend is well known to people.

questions.explanation: In English, the idiomatic expression 'well off' means to be wealthy or financially secure. Therefore, saying someone is 'well off' implies that they have enough money to live comfortably. Option A, 'My friend is financially sound,' correctly captures this meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'well off' for being in good health (Option C), confusing it with the phrase 'getting well' or simply 'being well.' However, 'well off' specifically refers to economic status, not physical health.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The retired army officer did a yeoman's service to the nation.
questions.instruction: For this question, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the question.The retired army officer did a yeoman's service to the nation.

options.option_a: His activity brought disrepute to the nation
options.option_b: His service to the nation was not exemplary.
options.option_c: He was showered with the responsibility of the yeoman.
options.option_d: He was very loyal to the nation.

questions.explanation: The idiom 'a yeoman's service' refers to work that is performed in a commendable, efficient, loyal, or substantial manner. It implies that the person has done a great deal of useful or helpful work. Among the given options, 'He was very loyal to the nation' is the closest in meaning, as it captures the positive, dedicated nature of the service implied by the idiom. Options A and B suggest a negative meaning, while option C is a literal misinterpretation of the word 'yeoman'.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is interpreting 'yeoman' literally as a peasant or a farmer, rather than recognizing it as part of an idiom that denotes dedicated and loyal service.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He suddenly found himself in the thick of the situation.
questions.instruction: For this question, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the question.He suddenly found himself in the thick of the situation.

options.option_a: He did not agree with the situation.
options.option_b: He used his experience to settle the situation.
options.option_c: He saved himself out of the situation.
options.option_d: He found himself deeply involved in the situation.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'in the thick of the situation' is an idiom meaning to be deeply involved or in the heart of an event. Option D correctly captures this meaning by stating 'He found himself deeply involved in the situation.' The other options misinterpret the idiom: A refers to disagreement, B implies problem-solving, and C suggests escaping, none of which align with the phrase's intended meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the idiom with similar phrases like 'getting out of a situation' (Option C) or misinterpreting it as a disagreement (Option A).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Olu and Ado are about to come to blows.
questions.instruction: For this question, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the question.Olu and Ado are about to come to blows.

options.option_a: They are about to agree with each other.
options.option_b: They are about to accept other people's opinion.
options.option_c: They are about to hit each other.
options.option_d: They are about to disagree with other people's opinion.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'come to blows' is an idiom meaning to engage in a physical fight. The context indicates an imminent physical confrontation between Olu and Ado, making option C the correct choice. Other options misinterpret the idiom as agreement (A), acceptance of opinions (B), or disagreement with opinions (D), which are unrelated to the intended meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the idiom with verbal disagreement (option D) instead of recognizing its literal physical connotation.
related_topics: Synonyms and Antonyms for Conflict-Related Terms

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: By refusing the offer, he has just cut down his own throat
questions.instruction: For this question, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the question.By refusing the offer, he has just cut down his own throat

options.option_a: He has made a big mistake.
options.option_b: He has made the right decision.
options.option_c: He has given up on his idea.
options.option_d: He has used the knife on his throat.

questions.explanation: The idiom 'cut down his own throat' metaphorically means self-sabotage or making a decision that harms oneself. Refusing the offer led to self-harm, implying a poor choice. Option A ('He has made a big mistake') aligns with this interpretation. Options B and C contradict the negative implication of the idiom, while D misinterprets it literally.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing D due to a literal interpretation of the phrase.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: These job cuts are just the end of the wedge.
questions.instruction: For this question, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the question.These job cuts are just the end of the wedge.

options.option_c: Job cuts are the beginning, of unpleasant situations.
options.option_d: Job cuts are the beginning of healthy rivalries.

questions.explanation: The idiom 'the end of the wedge' signifies that the current situation (job cuts) is merely the initial stage of a larger, more significant issue. It implies that further unpleasant developments are likely to follow. Option C correctly captures this meaning by stating that job cuts are the beginning of unpleasant situations.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the idiom with 'tip of the iceberg,' which also refers to a small part of a larger issue, but 'end of the wedge' specifically emphasizes the starting point rather than just a visible part.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Jumai will do well if she was given a fair crack of the whip.
questions.instruction: For this question, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the question.Jumai will do well if she was given a fair crack of the whip.

options.option_a: She would do well if she was given a fair whip.
options.option_b: She would excel if she used the whip well.
options.option_c: She would do well if she was given equal opportunity.
options.option_d: She would do well if she was made to cry.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'fair crack of the whip' is an idiom meaning 'a fair chance or opportunity.' The sentence implies that Jumai will succeed if given equal opportunity. Option C correctly interprets the idiom, while other options take it literally (A, B) or misinterpret it entirely (D).
questions.common_mistake: Misinterpreting idioms literally (e.g., thinking 'whip' refers to a physical object rather than a metaphor for opportunity).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Her death was a bolt from the blue to us.
questions.instruction: For this question, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the question.Her death was a bolt from the blue to us.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'a bolt from the blue' is an idiom meaning an unexpected event. The sentence implies that her death occurred suddenly and without prior warning. Option D directly captures this meaning. Other options misinterpret the idiom: 'bolted us together' (A) is a literal misreading, 'caused confusion' (B) shifts focus to emotional reaction rather than the event's unexpectedness, and 'sealed our hopes' (C) contradicts the context of a death.
questions.common_mistake: Selecting option B due to associating unexpected events with confusion, rather than focusing on the idiom's literal meaning of suddenness.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The students were nosing around.
questions.instruction: For this question, select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the question.The students were nosing around.
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'nose around' means to investigate or snoop in a curious or intrusive manner. While 'roaming about' (A) suggests aimless movement, the phrase implies a purposeful search for information. 'Playing around' (C) and 'disseminating information' (D) are unrelated to the intended meaning. The correct interpretation is 'searching for information' (B), as it aligns with the investigative connotation of the phrasal verb.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'nose around' with 'roam about' due to the physical movement implied, overlooking the investigative intent.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: It is important not to let mistakes blight your life
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsIt is important not to let mistakesblightyour life
questions.explanation: The word 'blight' means to damage or ruin something. Its opposite would be a word that signifies improvement or enhancement. Among the options, 'improve' directly contrasts with 'blight' by indicating positive change. 'Damage' and 'ruin' are synonyms of 'blight,' while 'impart' means to give or communicate, which is unrelated to the antonym requirement.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'impart' with 'improve' due to their similar prefixes, or selecting 'ruin' as a synonym instead of an antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The film was shot in decrepit police station.
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe film was shot indecrepitpolice station.
questions.explanation: The word 'decrepit' means in a state of disrepair or falling into ruin. The opposite of this would be something in good condition or well-maintained. Among the options, 'improved' (A) best conveys the opposite meaning, as it implies enhancement or betterment. 'Damaged' (B) and 'dilapidated' (D) are synonyms of 'decrepit,' while 'impoverished' (C) refers to financial hardship, not physical condition.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'dilapidated' (D) with the opposite of 'decrepit' due to their similar meanings.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Jumoke is fond of carping her sister.
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsJumoke is fond ofcarpingher sister.
questions.explanation: The word 'carping' means to complain or find fault. The sentence states that Jumoke is fond of criticizing her sister. The opposite of 'carping' would be 'praising,' as it involves expressing approval rather than criticism. Options C and D ('complaining about' and 'faulting') are synonyms of 'carping,' while 'joking with' (B) is unrelated to the context of criticism.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'carping' with 'faulting' (option D) due to their similar meanings, or misinterpreting the question as asking for a synonym instead of an antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: A cup of coffee invigorated him.
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsA cup of coffeeinvigoratedhim.
questions.explanation: The word 'invigorated' means to give energy or strength. Its opposite would be a word that signifies weakening or causing exhaustion. 'Debilitated' (option D) means to weaken or make someone very weak, making it the correct antonym. 'Energized' (option B) is a synonym, not an antonym, which is a common confusion. 'Destroyed' (option A) refers to causing damage, while 'angered' (option C) relates to emotions, neither of which directly oppose 'invigorated'.
questions.common_mistake: Selecting 'energized' (option B) due to its similar connotation with energy, despite being a synonym rather than an antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: It is ludicrous to suggest that she was a government agent.
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsIt isludicrousto suggest that she was a government agent.
questions.explanation: The word 'ludicrous' means absurd or ridiculous. The opposite of this would be 'sensible,' which means reasonable or logical. Options A ('odd') and C ('farcical') are closer in meaning to 'ludicrous,' while B ('exciting') is unrelated. Thus, 'sensible' (D) is the correct antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'farcical' with an antonym when it actually reinforces the meaning of 'ludicrous.'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The idea makes me cringe
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe idea makes mecringe
questions.explanation: The word 'cringe' refers to a feeling of discomfort or embarrassment, often accompanied by a physical reaction. The opposite of this would be a state of confidence or determination. Among the options, 'resolute' (C) means firmly determined, which contrasts with the hesitant or uncomfortable feeling of cringing. Options A (quiver), B (tremble), and D (writhe) all describe physical reactions similar to cringe, making them incorrect.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing physical reactions with emotional states; selecting 'quiver' or 'tremble' due to their physical similarity to 'cringe' rather than their semantic opposition.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: His book was one of those books that galvanized democracy.
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsHis book was one of those books that galvanized democracy.
questions.explanation: The word 'galvanized' means to stimulate or energize action. Its opposite would be a word that signifies discouraging or preventing action. 'Dissuaded' (option C) means to advise against doing something, which is the antonym of 'galvanized.' The other options (stimulated, encouraged, promoted) are synonyms of 'galvanized,' making them incorrect choices.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'dissuaded' with 'discouraged' without fully understanding their contextual differences.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He walks in a gawky way.
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsHe walks in a gawky way.
questions.explanation: The word 'gawky' describes someone who moves in an awkward or clumsy manner. The opposite of 'gawky' would be 'graceful,' which implies smooth and elegant movement. Options B and C ('clumsy' and 'lumbering') are synonyms of 'gawky,' while 'suitable' (A) is unrelated to the context of movement. Thus, 'graceful' (D) is the correct antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'clumsy' or 'lumbering' as antonyms instead of recognizing they are synonyms.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The nation is in a period of economic flux
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe nation is in a period of economicflux
questions.explanation: The word 'flux' refers to a state of constant change or instability. The opposite of this would be 'stability,' which denotes a condition of being steady and unchanging. Options A (modification), B (change), and C (fluidity) all align with the concept of flux, making D the correct antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'flux' with synonyms like 'change' or 'modification' instead of recognizing its antonym as 'stability.'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Our son was highly active and exuberant.
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsOur son was highly active and exuberant.
questions.explanation: The word 'exuberant' means full of energy, enthusiasm, or cheerfulness. The opposite of this is 'subdued,' which means less active or excited. 'Lively' (C) is a synonym, while 'fulsome' (B) and 'bright' (D) do not directly oppose 'exuberant' in this context.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'lively' (C) as it is a synonym rather than an antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Mr. Ojo has a fickle character.
questions.instruction: From these questions, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsMr. Ojo has a fickle character.
questions.explanation: The word 'fickle' describes someone who is inconsistent, changeable, or unreliable. Among the options, 'unpredictable' (D) is the closest synonym, as it conveys the idea of being difficult to predict due to frequent changes in behavior or opinion. 'Genuine' (A) refers to authenticity, 'stable' (B) implies consistency, and 'imperfect' (C) suggests flaws rather than inconsistency.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'fickle' with 'imperfect' (C) because both relate to flaws, but 'fickle' specifically emphasizes inconsistency rather than general imperfection.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He picked up the phone expecting to hear the chairman's gruff voice.
questions.instruction: From these questions, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsHe picked up the phone expecting to hear the chairman's gruff voice.
questions.explanation: The word 'gruff' describes a voice that is rough, harsh, or not smooth. Among the options, 'husky' is the closest synonym, as it can also describe a deep, rough, or hoarse voice. 'Gracious' and 'polite' are antonyms, while 'musical' refers to something pleasant and melodic, making them incorrect choices.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'husky' with 'musical' due to the association of 'husky' with the dog breed rather than its vocal connotation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: It has been a fraught day
questions.instruction: From these questions, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsIt has been a fraught day
questions.explanation: The word 'fraught' means filled with or characterized by tension, anxiety, or difficulty. In the context of the sentence, 'fraught day' refers to a day marked by stress or challenges. Among the options, 'difficult' is the closest in meaning. 'Pleasant' and 'wonderful' are positive and contradictory, while 'solemn' refers to seriousness or formality, which does not align with the connotation of 'fraught'.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'fraught' with 'solemn' due to their association with serious contexts, or misinterpreting 'fraught' as a positive term.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: She scowled furiously at his back as he walked away.
questions.instruction: From these questions, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsShe scowled furiously at his back as he walked away.
questions.explanation: The word 'scowled' refers to a facial expression of anger or displeasure. Among the options, 'grimaced' (option B) is the closest synonym as it also describes a facial expression, typically conveying displeasure or distaste. 'Screeched' and 'screamed' (options C and D) are vocal expressions, while 'whispered' (option A) is unrelated to anger. The context emphasizes a facial reaction, making 'grimaced' the most appropriate choice.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing vocal expressions (e.g., 'screamed') with facial expressions due to the emotional context of 'furiously'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The use of this equipment should obviate the problem
questions.instruction: From these questions, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe use of this equipment should obviate the problem
questions.explanation: The word 'obviate' means to make something unnecessary or to eliminate a problem. In the context of the sentence, the equipment is intended to remove the need for the problem to exist, which aligns with 'prevent' (option A). 'Improve' (B) suggests enhancement rather than elimination, 'promote' (C) implies encouragement, and 'worsen' (D) is the opposite of the intended meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'improve' (B) because test-takers might confuse 'eliminating a problem' with 'making it better.'

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Oisa hoodwinked the men into buying and selling.
questions.instruction: From these questions, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsOisa hoodwinked the men into buying and selling.
questions.explanation: The word 'hoodwinked' means to deceive or trick someone into doing something, often through clever or subtle means. Among the options, 'lured' (B) is the closest synonym because it implies enticing someone into an action, often with a false promise or temptation. 'Deluded' (C) refers to making someone believe a falsehood, which is slightly different. 'Grouped' (A) and 'drove' (D) do not align with the deceptive intent of 'hoodwinked'.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'deluded' with 'hoodwinked' due to their overlap in deception, but 'deluded' focuses on false beliefs rather than active trickery.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: There was an infectious gaiety in the children's character.
questions.instruction: From these questions, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThere was an infectious gaiety in the children's character.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'infectious gaiety' refers to a cheerful and lively mood that spreads to others. 'Exhilaration' (option A) best captures this meaning as it denotes a feeling of excitement and happiness. The other options—depression (B), moodiness (C), and desperation (D)—are negative emotions and do not align with the positive connotation of 'gaiety.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'gaiety' with 'moodiness' due to the word 'character,' which might mislead some to think of emotional instability rather than cheerfulness.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The room was filled with the pungent smell of tobacco.
questions.instruction: From these questions, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe room was filled with the pungent smell of tobacco.
questions.explanation: The word 'pungent' describes a strong, sharp, and often irritating smell or taste. In the context of tobacco, it refers to a harsh, acrid odor. Among the options, 'acrid' (option D) is the closest synonym, as it also conveys a sharp, bitter, and unpleasant smell. 'Placid' (A) means calm, 'mild' (B) is the opposite of pungent, and 'illegal' (C) is unrelated to the sensory description.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'pungent' with 'mild' due to a misunderstanding of intensity or associating 'illegal' with tobacco without contextual relevance.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He lifted his hand in a languid manner.
questions.instruction: From these questions, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsHe lifted his hand in a languid manner.
questions.explanation: The word 'languid' describes a lack of energy or enthusiasm, often characterized by slow or weak movement. Among the options, 'sluggish' (B) is the closest synonym, as it also conveys a state of torpor or inactivity. 'Sheepish' (A) relates to shyness, 'friendly' (C) is unrelated, and 'energetic' (D) is the direct antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'languid' with 'sheepish' due to similar connotations of low confidence, or misinterpreting 'languid' as 'energetic' by overlooking the negative connotation of the former.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The lawmaker heckled the chairman of the panel during their last meeting.
questions.instruction: From these questions, choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe lawmaker heckled the chairman of the panel during their last meeting.
questions.explanation: The word 'heckled' refers to interrupting someone with critical or hostile remarks, often in a public setting. Among the options, 'shouted down' best captures this meaning, as it involves disrupting or opposing someone through loud, vocal resistance. 'Cheered up' and 'applauded' are positive actions that contradict the hostile connotation of 'heckled,' while 'restrained' implies physical or emotional suppression, which is not the intended meaning here.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'restrained' with 'heckled' due to their shared implication of limiting action, or misinterpreting 'shouted down' as a literal physical act rather than a verbal one.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The book will sell in
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the options that best complete the gap(s).The book will sell in
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'hundreds of thousands' because it follows the standard English structure for expressing large, unspecified quantities. When using 'hundreds of thousands,' the plural 'hundreds' and 'thousands' indicate a vast, non-specific number. Option B ('a hundred thousand') is a specific count (100,000), which contradicts the generalization implied by 'sell in.' Option C ('hundreds of thousand') incorrectly uses the singular 'thousand,' and Option D ('hundred thousands') misplaces the plural form.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing singular and plural forms in quantifier expressions (e.g., 'hundred thousand' vs. 'hundreds of thousands').
related_topics: Use of Specific vs. General Quantifiers

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: We must be ready to cater for
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the options that best complete the gap(s).We must be ready to cater for
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'the poor and needy.' 'Poor' and 'needy' are collective nouns referring to groups of people in need. When used in this context, they require the definite article 'the' and should not be pluralized (e.g., 'poors' is incorrect). 'Needy' is the correct adjective form for 'those in need,' while 'needs' refers to requirements, not people. Option C correctly combines these elements without redundancy.
questions.common_mistake: Incorrectly pluralizing 'poor' (e.g., 'poors') or using 'needs' instead of 'needy' to describe people.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: After a three-day meeting, two presidents issued a.... calling for peace.
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the options that best complete the gap(s).After a three-day meeting, two presidents issued a.... calling for peace.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'communique' because it refers to a formal public statement issued by officials, especially after a meeting. The context implies a joint public declaration by two presidents, which aligns with the definition of a 'communique.' A 'bulletin' is a general announcement, a 'memorandum' is an internal document, and a 'directive' is an order, none of which fit the public, collaborative nature of the statement described.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'memorandum' with 'communique' due to their formal connotations, but 'memorandum' is typically internal and not public-facing.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Timi has gone to Lagos and he will be back in ......... time.
questions.instruction: For these questions, choose the options that best complete the gap(s).Timi has gone to Lagos and he will be back in ......... time.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'C' (two weeks). The phrase 'in two weeks' is an idiomatic expression indicating a future time. It means 'after two weeks' or 'in a fortnight'. The possessive form (option B: 'two week's') and the incorrect use of 'two's' (option A) are not suitable in this context. Option D is a repetition of option C, likely a typographical error.

'Someone' and 'somebody' are used in affirmative sentences, while 'anyone' is appropriate here to indicate the absence of a person found in the house.

Rising incomes were identified to have triggered more drinking in Africa and Asia whilebinge drinkingis a problem in many developed countries .The organization derived the failure of most government to institute strong alcohol control policies in spite of its heavy toll on society from road accidents ,violence, disease, child neglect and absenteeism at work .The WHO alert on alcohol abuse is timely. questions.common_mistake: Selecting 'proactive' (C) due to misinterpreting the WHO's 'timely alert' as evidence of active policy-making by developed countries, rather than recognizing it as a call to address existing inaction.

questions.passage: CONSOLIDATED JAMB QUESTIONS ENGLISH 2018 COMPREHENSION Read each passage carefully and answer the questions that follow it PASSAGE II   in order to approach the problem of anxiety in playing, let us consider the activity of building a tower. Many mother thinks that her little son is in destructive stage or even has a “destructive personality “because after building a big , big tower, the boy cannot follow her advice to leave the tower for Daddy to see, but instead must kick it and make it collapse. The almost manic pleasure with which children watch the collapse in a second of the product of long play –labor puzzled many especially since the child does not appreciate it at all if his tower falls by accident or by a helpful uncle hands. He the builder must destroy it himself. This game I should think arises from the not so distant experience of sudden falls at the very time when standing upright on wobbly legs afforded a new and fascinating perspective on existence. The child who consequently earns to make a tower ‘stand up enjoys causing the same tower to waver and collapse, in addition to the active mastery over a previously passive event, it makes one feel stranger to know that there is somebody weaker and towers, unlike little sisters can’t and call Mummy !

options.option_a: for daddy to see the tower he has built
options.option_d: to be helped to destroy the tower

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that children take 'manic pleasure' in watching their tower collapse, but only if they destroy it themselves. The phrase 'He the builder must destroy it himself' directly supports option B. Other options contradict the text: the child refuses to leave the tower for Daddy (A), dislikes accidental destruction (C), and rejects help (D).
questions.common_mistake: Misinterpreting the child's refusal to let the tower stand for Daddy as evidence of wanting parental approval (option A), ignoring the emphasis on self-destruction.

questions.passage: PASSAGE II A wolf, seeing a lamb drinking from a river, wanted to find a pretext for devouring him, he stood higher up the stream and accused the lamb of muddying the water so that he could not drink. The lamb said that he drank only with the tip of his tongue and that in any case he was standing lower the river and could not possibly disturb the water the higher up, when this excuse failed him the wolf said well year u insulted my father, I wasn’t even born then replied the lamb You are good at finding answers said the wolf but what do u mean by taking up so much of the path where I am walking? The lamb frightened at the wolf’s angry tone and terrible aspect told him with all due submission that he could not conceive how his walking on such a wide path could occasion him any inconvenience. What exclaimed the wolf, seemingly in great anger and indignation, you are as impudent as your father who seized me by the throat last year, and caused me to be kept in a cage for three months. If you will believe me said the lamb, my parents are poor simple creatures who live entirely by green stuff we are none of us hunters of your species. Ah! I see it’s no use talking to you said the wolf drawing up close to him. It runs in the blood of your family to hate us wolves, and therefore as we have come so conveniently together, I’ll just pay off a few of your forefather’s score before we part; so saying he leapt at the lamb from behind and garroted him.

options.option_a: lamb did not survive the encounter
options.option_c: wolf had encountered the lamb's parent

questions.explanation: The passage concludes with the wolf attacking and killing the lamb ('garroted him'). This directly supports option A, as the lamb's death is explicitly stated. Options B and C are contradicted by the text, while option D misinterprets the wolf's anger as stemming from a direct offense by the lamb, when it is actually a fabricated excuse. The wolf's claim about the lamb's father is a pretext, not a genuine grievance.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the wolf's fabricated excuses (e.g., the lamb's father) with factual events in the story, leading to the incorrect selection of option D.
related_topics: Identifying Main Ideas in a Passage

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I shall find my time for my ....... when i get .....with this difficult assignment
questions.instruction: In each of the question 11 to 20 choose the option that best completes the gap (s)I shall find my time for my ....... when i get .....with this difficult assignment
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D: 'pastime / through'. 'Pastime' refers to a leisure activity or hobby, fitting the context of something to do after completing a task. 'Get through' is the correct phrasal verb meaning to finish or complete something, as in 'get through with the assignment'. Other options either use incorrect spellings (e.g., 'passtime') or inappropriate phrasal verbs (e.g., 'get over', which implies overcoming an emotion or illness).
questions.subtopic: Vocabulary in Context and Phrasal Verbs
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'pastime' with 'past-time' or 'pass-time', and misusing phrasal verbs like 'get over' instead of 'get through'.

options.option_b: He could not care less if the game was lost
options.option_c: He was almost certain that the game would be lost
options.option_d: He was afraid the game would be lost

questions.explanation: The phrase 'for all he cared' indicates complete indifference or lack of concern. The sentence implies that the speaker's apathy rendered the game's outcome inevitable (as good as lost). Option B ('He could not care less if the game was lost') best captures this indifference. Option C incorrectly shifts focus to certainty about the game's loss, while D introduces fear not present in the original statement.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'as good as lost' (idiom for certain failure) with 'for all he cared' (idiom for indifference), leading to misinterpretation of the sentence's core meaning.

questions.subject: english

questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'called off' with similar-sounding phrasal verbs like 'called on' or 'called in', which have different meanings.

questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'ardent' with 'optimistic' (D) due to both being positive adjectives, but 'optimistic' does not capture the intensity of passion implied by 'ardent'.

questions.subject: english

While 'examination' (B) involves inspection, it lacks the connotation of surprising revelation. 'Style' (A) and 'dispatch' (C) are unrelated to the meaning of 'eyeopener'.

questions.common_mistake: Confusing the idiom with unrelated terms like 'cynical statement' (option D) due to a lack of familiarity with figurative language.

questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'verge' with 'shore' due to both relating to edges, but 'shore' is specific to water bodies, while 'verge' here refers to a metaphorical edge of action.

The context of 'dealings with people' emphasizes giving or kindness, aligning with 'generous'.

The question requires identifying the opposite meaning, making 'selfishness' (D) the correct choice.

'Had plucked' (past perfect) correctly matches this structure, showing an action completed before another past action. Other options use incorrect tenses: 'plucked' (simple past), 'have plucked' (present perfect), and 'did pluck' (simple past) do not align with the conditional perfect in the main clause.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing past perfect with simple past tense in conditional sentences, leading to incorrect selection of 'plucked' or 'did pluck'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: By the time the plane reaches Harare, it ..... in the air for twelve hours
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 46 to 55 choose the word(s) or phrase(s)which best fills s the gapsBy the time the plane reaches Harare, it ..... in the air for twelve hours
questions.explanation: The sentence describes an action that will be completed at a specific point in the future (by the time the plane reaches Harare). The correct answer requires the use of the future perfect tense, which is formed with 'will have' + past participle. However, in this case, 'by the time' is used, which often takes the future perfect or simple future. Among the options, 'would have been' is the correct choice because it correctly represents the future perfect in the past, which is suitable for the context of the sentence, indicating that one action (being in the air for twelve hours) will be completed before another action (the plane reaching Harare) in the future.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'has been' (option A), which is incorrect because it is used for actions that started in the past and continue up to the present moment, not for actions that will be completed at a specific point in the future.

questions.subject: english

Other options like 'between' (implies multiple parties), 'for' (implies purpose), and 'to' (implies direction) do not fit the passive voice context.

questions.subject: english

questions.subject: english

Because they do not rely on energy from food to generate body heat snakes can survive on an extremely meagre diet. Some wait for months between successive meals and few biting of small pieces. ,many snakes have specialized jaws that enable them to swallow animals that are far larger their own heads. Although uncommon some snakes such as African the African rock python have been observed eating animals as large as an antelope or small cow With over two thousand five hundred species belonging to more than ten families snakes are a large and successful group. They owe much of this success to their versatility snakes occupy habitat ranging from underground borrows to the top of the tree, to ocean depth as great as one hundred and fifty meters they are found on every continent except Antarctica and although they most abundant I tropical areas. Many survive in the regions marked by the extreme cold the only places without snakes are part of the polar regions and isolated islands such as the republic of Ireland and new Zealand as opposed to places in Nigeria like plateau and Gombe states in the Northern par where there is a large population of snakes Adapted from Microsoft Encarta premium (2009)

options.option_a: snakes are  seldom seen at the Antarctica
options.option_b: snakes are not in the polar regions
options.option_c: snakes are endemic on every continent
options.option_d: there are countless of snakes in the republic of ireland

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that 'the only places without snakes are part of the polar regions and isolated islands such as the Republic of Ireland and New Zealand.' This directly supports option B ('snakes are not in the polar regions'). questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'seldom seen' (option A) with 'not present at all' (the actual text states Antarctica has no snakes). Misinterpreting 'endemic on every continent' (option C) by overlooking the explicit exclusion of Antarctica.

questions.instruction: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follows.The writers arguement that it is foolhardy to offer one's services where such are apparently not required implies that Nigeria
questions.passage: PASSAGE II Whenever I have to ask myself the question why I have not left this country for good, many answers rush to my mind, each striving to be recognized as being the most cogent. I am reminded of the popular slogan that this country belongs to us all; for which reason every Nigerian must join hands in trying to salvage it. I try to demise the argument by reasoning that it is foolhardy attempting to lend a helping hand where one’s services are apparently not required. Then I am reminded that if I left the country in hurry just because of our political instability and economic hardships my commitment to my family and extended family at home would suffer. I reply by saying that soon as long I got settled abroad I would arrange for my family to join me. Other financial problems at home would be taken care of by my regular remittance would I then never think of going to back home in future? Not until the situation in the country improved considerably, I would answer. And who did I expect to carry on with the task of national rehabilitation when the likes of me are all out of the country? Those who messed up In the first place, I would argue and so on. This dialogue of self has been going on for the last ten years or so meanwhile I am yet to leave the country When I wonder how many people share my kind of mental experience, I realize that we must be very few for not many have the slightest opportunity of absconding from the country; they do not have the place to run to, nor do they have the means of escape. Even among the elite who this possibility, the uncertainty of future outside their fatherland intimidates

options.option_a: the authorities do not solicit for  the services of the citizens
options.option_b: mediocrity is the other of  the day
options.option_c: the authorities are indifferent to offers of help from the citizen
options.option_d: to offer to serve the country is dangerous

questions.explanation: The writer argues that offering services where they are 'apparently not required' is foolhardy. This implies that the Nigerian authorities or society are not actively seeking or soliciting the services of its citizens, making option A the correct inference. The passage does not suggest indifference (C) or danger (D), nor does it directly link the argument to mediocrity (B). The focus is on the lack of demand for citizens' contributions.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'indifference' (C) with 'not requiring services.' The passage emphasizes the absence of demand, not a dismissive attitude.

questions.instruction: In each of the questions 11 to 13 choose the appropriate question tag to the sentence providedMy neighbour BRUISED his leg while playing football

options.option_b: Did your neighbor fracture his thigh  while playing football
options.option_c: was your neighbour involved in an accident?
options.option_d: Did your neighbour play football yesterday

questions.explanation: The sentence provided is 'My neighbour BRUISED his leg while playing football'. To form a question tag, we need to change it into a question and add a tag that matches the verb and subject. The correct question tag should have the same verb tense and subject-verb agreement. Option D 'Did your neighbour play football yesterday' is not a perfect question tag, however, the rest of the options do not form a correct question tag either. A correct question tag for the sentence could be 'didn't he?' but that is not among the options. Among the provided options, D seems to be trying to form a related question but does not perfectly fit as a question tag. However based on elimination and understanding of question formation, D can be seen as trying to confirm an action related to the initial statement.
questions.common_mistake: A common mistake would be to confuse the main verb or change the subject in forming the question tag.

This is because the suffix '-ite' usually attracts stress in English words. Therefore, the correct stress pattern is surburbaNITE, which corresponds to option D.
questions.common_mistake: A common mistake is to place the stress on the first or second syllable, which would result in incorrect stress patterns such as SUburbanate (option A) or suBURbanate (option B).

questions.question_text: departmentalize
questions.instruction: In each of the question 14 to 15 choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options the syllables are written in capital lettersdepartmentalize
questions.explanation: The word 'departmentalize' is derived from 'departmental' with the suffix '-ize'. In English, when a suffix like '-ize' is added to a word, the primary stress often shifts to the penultimate (second-to-last) syllable. Here, the base word 'departmental' has stress on the third syllable (de-PART-ment-al), but adding '-ize' shifts the stress to the second syllable, making it de-PART-men-talize. Option B correctly reflects this stress pattern.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing option A (departMENtalize) by retaining the stress from the base word 'departmental' without accounting for the suffix's effect.

'Discovered him' (C) directly aligns with the core meaning of the idiom, making it the most accurate choice.

'Credible' (options A and B) refers to being believable or trustworthy, which is not the same as being overly trusting. 'Fallible' (option D) means prone to error, which is unrelated to the concept of trust.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'credulous' with 'credible' due to their similar roots, but they have distinct meanings.

questions.explanation: The word 'forlon' is likely a misspelling of 'forlorn,' which means lonely, sad, or abandoned. In the context of the sentence, 'forlon little figures' suggests a sense of sadness or unhappiness. Option B ('lovely and unhappy') best captures the emotional state implied by 'forlorn,' even though 'lovely' contrasts slightly with the negative connotation. The key focus is on the 'unhappy' component, aligning with the intended meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'forlorn' with physical descriptions (e.g., 'short and ugly' in option D) rather than emotional states.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The accident victim received superficial wound from the crash
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 16 to 25 choose the option nearest in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsThe accident victim receivedsuperficialwound from the crash
questions.explanation: The word 'superficial' in this context refers to something that is on the surface or not deep. In medical terms, a superficial wound is one that affects only the outer layer of skin (external) rather than penetrating deeper tissues (internal). 'External' (option D) is the most accurate synonym here. 'Serious' (A) relates to severity, not depth. 'Painless' (B) and 'internal' (C) are unrelated to the definition of superficial.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'superficial' with 'internal' due to a misunderstanding of depth-related terminology.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: ........all probability, the train will arrive today.
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 16 to 25 choose the option nearest in meaning to the words or phrases in italics........all probability, the train will arrive today.
questions.explanation: The correct preposition to complete the phrase 'in all probability' is 'in.' This is a fixed expression meaning 'very likely' or 'probably.' The phrase 'in all probability' is commonly used to indicate a high likelihood of an event occurring. The other options ('under,' 'for,' 'by') do not form standard or meaningful expressions in this context.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'in all probability' with similar-sounding phrases like 'by all means' or 'under all circumstances,' which are unrelated in meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Accountability is certainly a desirable quality in a politician
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 16 to 25 choose the option nearest in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsAccountabilityis certainly a desirable quality in a politician
questions.explanation: The word 'accountability' refers to the quality of being answerable for one's actions. In the context of a politician, it implies taking responsibility for decisions and actions. 'Responsibility' (Option A) is the most accurate synonym here. 'Respectively' (B) is an adverb unrelated to the concept. 'Courage' (C) and 'diligence' (D) are positive traits but do not align with the specific meaning of accountability.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'accountability' with 'diligence' due to both being positive traits associated with work ethic.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The men were not pawns in someones else's political game

options.option_c: they were used by someone's political game

questions.explanation: The sentence 'The men were not pawns in someone else's political game' uses the metaphor of a 'pawn' to describe individuals manipulated by others. A 'pawn' in this context refers to someone used without their knowledge for another's benefit. The negation ('not pawns') implies the men acted independently, making their actions their own idea (Option A). Options B and C contradict the sentence by suggesting reliance on others' plans or being used, while D is irrelevant.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'not pawns' with being actively used by others (Option C), misinterpreting the negation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The class was tired of the new boy jawing away all the time
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 26 to 30 select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceThe class was tired of the new boy jawing away all the time

options.option_b: he was always chewing in the class
options.option_d: He was always making trouble for the class

questions.explanation: The phrase 'jawing away' is an idiomatic expression meaning to talk continuously or at length. The sentence indicates that the class was annoyed by the new boy's constant talking. Option C correctly captures this meaning. Options B and A misinterpret 'jawing' as literal chewing or biting, while D incorrectly shifts focus to causing trouble.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'jawing' with literal actions like chewing (Option B) due to the word 'jaw' in the phrase.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The governor parried all the questions put to him by the journalist
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 26 to 30 select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceThe governor parried all the questions put to him by the journalist

options.option_a: The governor answered all the questions brilliantly
options.option_b: The goveernor failed all the question
options.option_c: The governor evaded all the questions

questions.explanation: The verb 'parry' means to avoid or evade something, often by quick or clever action. In this context, it implies the governor avoided answering the journalist's questions. Option C correctly captures this meaning. Options A and B are incorrect because 'parry' does not imply answering brilliantly or failing questions. Option D is invalid as it is empty.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'parry' with 'answer' or 'respond' due to unfamiliarity with its figurative use.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Bassey is as hard as nails
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 26 to 30 select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceBassey is as hard as nails
questions.explanation: The phrase 'as hard as nails' is an idiom used to describe someone who is resolute, determined, or unyielding in their actions or decisions. While 'strong' (A) and 'brave' (B) relate to physical or moral courage, and 'unsympathetic' (D) refers to emotional detachment, the correct interpretation here is 'determined' (C), as the idiom emphasizes steadfastness rather than physical traits or emotional coldness.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the idiom with literal interpretations (e.g., physical strength) or misinterpreting it as emotional unsympathetic behavior.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The conference is biennial
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 26 to 30 select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentenceThe conference is biennial

options.option_a: The conference is held twice every year
options.option_b: The conference is held every two years
options.option_c: The conference is held every other year
options.option_d: The conference last for two years

questions.explanation: The term 'biennial' refers to an event that occurs every two years. The prefix 'bi-' means 'twice' or 'every two,' and 'annual' relates to a year. Therefore, 'biennial' correctly describes an event held every two years. Option B is the most accurate explanation. Options A and C are incorrect because 'biennial' does not mean twice a year (which would be 'biannual') or 'every other year' (which is redundant phrasing for the same meaning as B). Option D is incorrect as it misinterprets the term as a duration rather than frequency.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'biennial' with 'biannual' (twice a year) or misinterpreting 'every other year' as a distinct meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: He gave a painstaking account of his encounter with the ghost of his father
questions.instruction: in each of the question 31 to 40 choose most appropriate option opposite in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsHe gave apainstakingaccount of his encounter with the ghost of his father
questions.explanation: The word 'painstaking' means showing great care, effort, or meticulousness. Its antonym would be a term indicating lack of effort or care. 'Half-hearted' (option C) directly opposes this by implying minimal effort or enthusiasm. 'Sordid' (A) refers to moral corruption, 'fearful' (B) relates to fear, and 'tender-hearted' (D) describes compassion, none of which contrast 'painstaking' in the context of effort.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'tender-hearted' (D) as an antonym due to its emotional connotation rather than its relevance to effort or care.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: If you are really keen on immediate results you just have to adopt this pragmatic approach
questions.instruction: In each of the question 31 to 40 choose most appropriate option opposite in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsIf you are really keen on immediate results you just have to adopt thispragmaticapproach
questions.explanation: The word 'pragmatic' refers to a practical and realistic approach to problem-solving. Its antonym would be a term that signifies the opposite—something not grounded in practicality or realism. Among the options, 'unrealistic' (B) directly opposes 'pragmatic' by implying a lack of practicality. 'Practical' (A) and 'sensible' (D) are synonyms of 'pragmatic,' while 'opportunistic' (C) refers to taking advantage of circumstances, which is unrelated to the core meaning of 'pragmatic.'
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'pragmatic' with 'sensible' or 'practical' and selecting a synonym instead of an antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Measures were taken to authenticate the number of the booklets received
questions.instruction: In each of the question 31 to 40 choose most appropriate option opposite in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsMeasures were taken toauthenticatethe number of the booklets received
questions.explanation: The word 'authenticate' means to verify or confirm the truth or authenticity of something. The opposite of this would be to discredit or question its authenticity. Option B ('discredict') is likely a typo for 'discredit,' which fits as the antonym. Options A ('affirm') is a synonym, C ('discountenance') refers to disapproval rather than authenticity, and D ('count') relates to quantity, not verification.
questions.common_mistake: Misinterpreting the typo in option B or confusing 'discredit' with 'discountenance,' which means to disapprove rather than question authenticity.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The girl idiosyncrasy was a passion for bread and butter
questions.instruction: In each of the question 31 to 40 choose most appropriate option opposite in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsThe girl idiosyncrasywas a passion for bread and butter
questions.explanation: The word 'idiosyncrasy' refers to a unique or peculiar trait that distinguishes an individual. The opposite of this would be a 'general tendency,' which implies a common or widespread behavior rather than a singular, distinctive one. Option B correctly captures this antonymic relationship. Options A and D are unrelated in meaning, while Option C is a synonym, not an antonym.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'idiosyncrasy' with 'singular characteristic' (Option C), which is a synonym rather than an antonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: she is immune to the flatery of young men
questions.instruction: In each of the question 31 to 40 choose most appropriate option opposite in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsshe isimmuneto the flatery of young men
questions.explanation: The phrase 'immune to' means resistant or not susceptible to something. In this context, 'immune to the flattery of young men' means she is not affected or influenced by their flattery. The opposite in meaning would be a word that indicates she is affected or susceptible to it. 'Decline' is the closest in meaning to being affected or susceptible, as it implies a yielding or surrender to something, in this case, the flattery.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing a word that is similar in meaning to 'immune to', rather than opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The chairman's redressed the injustice meted out by the secretary
questions.instruction: In each of the question 31 to 40 choose most appropriate option opposite in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsThe chairman'sredressedthe injustice meted out by the secretary
questions.explanation: The word 'redressed' in the context means to correct or put right a wrong. The opposite of this action would be to worsen or intensify the injustice. 'Aggravated' (option C) means to make a problem worse, which directly opposes the meaning of 'redressed'. 'Corrected' (A) and 'restored' (B) are synonyms of 'redressed', while 'addressed' (D) is a neutral term that does not inherently oppose the action.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'addressed' (D) because it is a general term for dealing with an issue, but it does not convey the opposite meaning of worsening the injustice.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The lions of Cameroun is really an indomitable team
questions.instruction: In each of the question 31 to 40 choose most appropriate option opposite in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsThe lions of Cameroun is really anindomitableteam
questions.explanation: The word 'indomitable' means unyielding, strong, or impossible to defeat. The question asks for the opposite meaning. Among the options, 'a weak' (option C) directly contrasts with 'indomitable' by describing something lacking strength or resilience. 'Cowardly' (option D) refers to a lack of courage, which is not the direct antonym of 'indomitable.' 'A powerful' (option A) and 'a prominent' (option B) are unrelated to the required opposite meaning.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'cowardly' with 'weak,' as both are negative traits but differ in context. 'Cowardly' relates to fear, while 'weak' relates to lack of strength.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The plan to merge the two local government areas has met with much apathy
questions.instruction: In each of the question 31 to 40 choose most appropriate option opposite in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsThe plan to merge the two local government areas has met with muchapathy
questions.explanation: The word 'apathy' means a lack of interest, emotion, or concern. The opposite of apathy would be a strong interest or enthusiasm. Among the options, 'enthusiasm' (option D) directly opposes apathy by signifying active interest and eagerness. 'Criticism' (B) is a negative reaction but not the direct antonym of apathy. 'Hospitality' (A) and 'consideration' (C) are unrelated to the context of emotional engagement.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'criticism' (B) as the opposite, mistaking it for a reaction to apathy rather than recognizing that apathy refers to indifference, not negativity.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Mutual love is what kabi and musa have in common and nothing else
questions.instruction: In each of the question 31 to 40 choose most appropriate option opposite in meaning to the words or phrases in italicsMutuallove is what kabi and musa have in common and nothing else
questions.explanation: The word 'mutual' implies a shared or reciprocal relationship. In the context of 'mutual love,' it means both Kabi and Musa love each other equally. The opposite of this would be a one-sided relationship where only one person loves the other. 'One-sided' (option B) directly contrasts the reciprocal nature of 'mutual.' Other options like 'insincere' (A) or 'disrespectful' (D) do not address the reciprocity aspect but rather focus on sincerity or respect, which are not the primary focus of the question.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'insincere' (A) because it relates to authenticity rather than reciprocity, or 'disrespectful' (D) due to a misunderstanding of the emotional context.

questions.subject: english

questions.explanation: The word 'legitimate' refers to something that is legally recognized or justified. The opposite of 'legitimate' would be 'illicit,' which means illegal or not permitted by law. 'Legal' (option B) is a synonym, not an antonym. 'Good' (option C) relates to morality rather than legality, and 'improve' (option D) is a verb unrelated to the context of legality.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'legal' (synonym) with the correct antonym 'illicit' due to similar thematic context.

questions.subject: english

'Understand' (simple present) is appropriate because it states a general truth or current state of comprehension. The present continuous ('am understanding') implies an ongoing process, which is unnecessary here. 'May be understanding' introduces uncertainty, and 'was understanding' is past continuous, both of which misalign with the present context.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'am understanding' (A) due to confusion between continuous and simple tenses, or 'was understanding' (D) by misinterpreting the time frame.

questions.subject: english

'So shocking for words' implies the languages were extremely shocking, aligning with the grammatical pattern 'so [adjective] that [result].' Options A ('very') and D ('far') lack the necessary grammatical structure to link the clauses, while B ('too') incorrectly implies an excess that prevents an action (e.g., 'too shocking to describe'), which does not fit the context.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'so...that' with 'too...to' structures, leading to incorrect selection of 'too' as the adverb.
related_topics: Use of 'so' and 'such' in adverbial phrases

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: If you .... me that you had run out of petrol, I would have given you some
questions.instruction: In each of the questions 41 to 50 fill the blank spaces with appropriate of options A-DIf you .... me that you had run out of petrol, I would have given you some
questions.explanation: The sentence uses the third conditional structure, which is used to discuss hypothetical past situations. The correct form for the 'if' clause in the third conditional is the past perfect tense ('had + past participle'). Here, 'had told' (option D) correctly matches the structure 'If + subject + had + past participle, ... would have + past participle.' The main clause 'I would have given' already confirms the third conditional, so the 'if' clause must use the past perfect tense to indicate an unreal past action.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing option C ('have told') because it resembles the present perfect tense, which is incorrect for a hypothetical past scenario. Alternatively, selecting option A ('were to tell') might confuse the first conditional (future possibility) with the third conditional (unreal past).

'May' is used to ask for permission in formal or polite contexts. 'Will' and 'shall' are used for future intentions or suggestions, while 'would' is hypothetical and less direct. The structure 'May I...' is standard for such requests.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'may' with 'shall' or 'will' due to their similar functions in future tense or suggestions.

questions.subject: english

'Placated' (meaning calmed or pacified) fits as Tosin resists being soothed, indicating determination. 'Said' (A) is grammatically incorrect in this context. 'Frustrated' (C) implies emotional state but doesn't align with 'refused to be.' 'Different' (D) is semantically irrelevant here.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'frustrated' (C) due to its emotional connotation, but 'placated' better matches the passive voice and intended meaning.

questions.subject: english

The phrase 'in a much deeper sense' is grammatically correct because 'much' is a valid modifier for comparative adjectives like 'deeper.' Options A and D incorrectly use 'more' with 'deeper,' which is redundant since 'deeper' is already a comparative form. Option B incorrectly combines 'most' (a superlative marker) with 'deeper' (a comparative), creating a grammatical inconsistency.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the use of 'more' with already comparative adjectives (e.g., 'more deeper') or misapplying superlative markers like 'most' to comparatives.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: People who live by ........ what loneliness is like

questions.explanation: The correct answer is D ('themselves know'). The phrase 'live by themselves' means to live alone, which logically connects to the concept of loneliness. The subject 'people' is plural, requiring the plural reflexive pronoun 'themselves' and the plural verb 'know' for subject-verb agreement. Options A and B use 'each other' and 'one another,' which imply mutual dependence, contradicting the context of loneliness. Option C incorrectly uses 'oneself' (singular) with the plural verb 'knows,' violating subject-verb agreement.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing reflexive pronouns ('themselves' vs. 'oneself') and misapplying subject-verb agreement rules.

questions.subject: english

questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'surroundings' (A). The sentence requires a plural noun to match the possessive pronoun 'his' and the verb 'keeps.' 'Surroundings' refers to the area around someone or something, making it contextually appropriate. 'Surrounding' (B) is singular and less commonly used in this context. 'Premise' (C) refers to a building or property, which is less likely to be paired with 'his' in this general statement. 'Environment' (D) is grammatically possible but less precise than 'surroundings' for describing immediate physical conditions.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'surroundings' with 'environment' due to their similar meanings, or misinterpreting 'premise' as a suitable option.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Ali has been cured of his amnesia, he no longer suffers from ......

Option B ('loss on memory') is grammatically incorrect (should be 'loss of memory'), but it is the only option addressing memory loss. Other options (anxiety, arm pain, malaria) are unrelated to amnesia. Despite the phrasing error, B is the most contextually appropriate choice.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing option A ('rounds of anxiety') due to confusion between anxiety and memory-related symptoms.

'Prowess' (option C) means skill or strength in action, which aligns with the context of a team showcasing their capabilities in a competitive setting. 'Worth' (A) is too generic, 'position' (B) refers to ranking or location, and 'mettle' (D) implies resilience under pressure but is less specific to skill demonstration.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'prowess' with 'mettle' due to their similar connotations of strength.

questions.subject: english

The gerund form 'failing' is required here to denote the action of not attending. Option A ('failure') uses a noun form incorrectly, while options B and D use incorrect prepositions or verb forms.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing option A ('for failure') due to confusion between noun and gerund forms.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The old politicians were discredited because they tried to .... the people's ignorance

questions.explanation: The correct phrasal verb is 'cash in on,' which means to take advantage of a situation for profit. The sentence implies the politicians exploited the people's ignorance for personal gain. Other options are grammatically incorrect or semantically inappropriate in this context.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'cash in on' with 'cash in with' due to similar structure but incorrect meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The plane overshot the .... in a minor accident
questions.instruction: In each of the question 51 to 60 choose the word or phrases which best fills the gap in each sentencesThe plane overshot the .... in a minor accident
questions.explanation: The sentence refers to a plane overshooting a designated area during landing. 'Runway' is the correct term as it is the strip of land where aircraft take off and land. 'Overshooting the runway' is a standard aviation phrase describing a plane failing to stop before the runway's end. 'Tarmac' (option C) refers to the apron area near the terminal, not the landing strip itself. 'Hanger' (option B) is a storage facility for aircraft, and 'railway' (option A) is unrelated to aviation.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'tarmac' with 'runway' due to overlapping but distinct meanings in aviation contexts.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Journalist always collects and publish.......
questions.instruction: In each of the question 51 to 60 choose the word or phrases which best fills the gap in each sentencesJournalist always collects and publish.......
questions.explanation: The word 'information' is an uncountable noun, meaning it does not take a plural form or articles like 'a'/'an'. Options A ('informations') and B ('an information') incorrectly treat it as countable. Option C ('some information') is grammatically acceptable but redundant in this context, as the verb 'publish' directly requires the base noun 'information' without quantifiers. The correct answer is D, as uncountable nouns are used without articles in such constructions.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing option A due to a misunderstanding of countable/uncountable noun rules, or option C by overusing quantifiers unnecessarily.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: after the team had conceded two goals their enthusiasm ...
questions.instruction: In each of the question 51 to 60 choose the word or phrases which best fills the gap in each sentencesafter the team had conceded two goals their enthusiasm ...
questions.explanation: The sentence uses the past perfect tense in the first clause ('had conceded'), indicating an action completed before another past action. The second clause requires a verb form that logically follows this sequence. 'Was waning' (past continuous) correctly describes the ongoing state of the team's enthusiasm after the goals were conceded. Options A and D use past perfect or past perfect continuous, which would imply the waning began before the goals were conceded, contradicting the 'after' clause. Option C is in the base form, which does not match the past tense context.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing past continuous with past perfect continuous, leading to incorrect sequence of events.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Many goes to school ....bus
questions.instruction: In each of the question 51 to 60 choose the word or phrases which best fills the gap in each sentencesMany goes to school ....bus
questions.explanation: The preposition 'by' is used to indicate the means of transportation in general terms. 'By bus' refers to using the bus as a mode of transport. 'On the bus' would refer to a specific vehicle, but since the sentence does not specify a particular bus, 'by' is correct. 'In' and 'with' are not appropriate here as they do not align with standard prepositional usage for transportation modes.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'on' with 'by' due to the physical act of riding on a bus, or using 'in' for enclosed spaces like cars.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The thief ran .... luck when the policeman running after him caught up with him and knocked him down
questions.instruction: In each of the question 51 to 60 choose the word or phrases which best fills the gap in each sentencesThe thief ran .... luck when the policeman running after him caught up with him and knocked him down
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'out of' because the phrase 'run out of luck' is an idiomatic expression meaning to lose all one's good fortune. In the context, the thief's capture by the policeman signifies the end of his luck. Other options like 'into' or 'with' do not fit the idiomatic structure required here.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'run into' (to encounter unexpectedly) with 'run out of' (to exhaust a resource). Test-takers might incorrectly choose 'into' due to familiarity with the phrasal verb 'run into' without considering the idiomatic nuance.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: We should take care ...the robbers come back
questions.instruction: In each of the question 51 to 60 choose the word or phrases which best fills the gap in each sentencesWe should take care ...the robbers come back
questions.explanation: The phrase 'in case' is used to introduce a precautionary condition, making it the correct choice for expressing preparedness against a possible event. 'Should in case' (B) is grammatically redundant, as 'should' is unnecessary with 'in case.' 'May be' (C) and 'probably' (D) do not fit the sentence structure, which requires a subordinating conjunction to link the main clause with the conditional clause.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'in case' with 'may be' due to their similar meanings of possibility, but 'may be' cannot function as a conjunction here.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The managing Director did not pay his staff last month .....
questions.instruction: In each of the question 51 to 60 choose the word or phrases which best fills the gap in each sentencesThe managing Director did not pay his staff last month .....

questions.passage: Passage III present trends continue, the world would face a major crises by the end of this century, insufficient cheap, convenient energy. For without such energy, industrial production will fall, agricultural output will drop, transport will be restricted, and standard of living in developed countries will plummet. At present, almost all our energy comes from fossil fuels. The earth’s reserves of fossil fuels have been formed from organic matter subjected to enormous heat and pressure for millions of years. But such reserves are finite. Because power demand is increasing very rapidly, fossil fuels will be exhausted within a relatively short time. We can estimate the amount of recoverable fuel under the surface of the earth and we know the rate at which it is being extracted. Fairly simple calculations can therefore determine its remaining life. If present trends continue, gas and oil reserves will be exhausted by the middle of the 21st century --------about 70 years from now. Similar estimates for coal and wood reserves suggest a projected supply of 250 – 300 years. Of course, long before fossil fuels are exhausted, demand will greatly exceed supply. For too many years the world has consumed fossil fuels with little thought for the future. In fact, world energy consumption increased almost 600% between 1900 and 1965 and it is projected to increase by another 450% between 1965 and the year 2000. Crude oil has been pumped out of the ground for about 100years, but over a half of it has been extracted in the past 37 years. In sum, most of the world’s consumption of energy from fossil fuels throughout history, has taken place within living memory.
