We must, however, ask of what real value are political and legal equality to a man who has no bread to eat. No clothes to wear, no roof to shelter him, no chance to earn a livelihood? What we understand as a democratic society must provide for its citizen’s minimum status as member of that society, that keeps him from becoming a beggar, outcast or outlaw and that offers him some protection in his deprivation, losses and fears.In our time, the nations the democratic world have installed elaborate systems of social security and welfare. Ranging from compensation for industrial accidents to subsidizing housing, unemployment insurance, old age pensions, psychiatric care and national health services. It is encouraging that the democratic nations are making a serious effort to provide against the characteristic losses and disasters of human life.The evolving status of the Negro in America is America is attracting the attention of the champions of equality. Much has been written on the wrongs, injustices and inequalities of the colored citizen of the USA and much remains to be said, because the history of this struggle for human rights is still unfolding.

questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose Option A because they assume the American Declaration of Independence immediately guaranteed equal treatment for all, whereas the passage mentions that the struggle for rights is 'still unfolding' and emphasizes the necessity of social welfare to make those rights meaningful.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: University of Lagos has a large intake of student each year.
questions.instruction: In this question, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsUniversity of Lagos has a large intake of student each year.
questions.explanation: In this context, 'intake' refers to the number of students admitted or brought into the university system (the input). The direct opposite of 'intake' in terms of institutional flow is 'output', which refers to the number of students who have completed their studies and are produced by the university (graduates). While 'rejection' is the opposite of 'acceptance', it does not serve as the structural opposite to the noun 'intake' in this context.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'rejection' because they associate 'intake' solely with 'admission'. However, 'intake' describes a flow into a system, making 'output' the most precise antonym for the flow out of that system.

questions.question_text: Mallam salihu teaches ------ at Bint’s school.
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERMallam salihu teaches ------ at Bint’s school.

The scene involves Bint asking him the meaning of 'Au revoir', a French term, which Mallam Salihu could not answer, leading him to call on the French teacher, Miss Magret, for assistance.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Tade’s car is badly damaged; he has to look for an expert mechanic to fix it.
questions.instruction: In this question, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsTade’s car is badly damaged; he has to look for an expert mechanic to fix it.
questions.explanation: The word 'expert' refers to a person who has extensive skill, knowledge, or experience in a specific field. In the context of the sentence, it describes a mechanic with high professional proficiency. To find the opposite, we look for a word that describes a lack of skill or professional standard. 'Amateurish' means lacking professional skill or being characteristic of an amateur rather than a professional, making it the direct antonym of 'expert'.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'uneducated' because they wrongly assume that all experts must be formally educated, or 'awkward' because it describes clumsiness, but neither specifically addresses the lack of professional skill as 'amateurish' does.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The whole community has often described John as belligerent
questions.instruction: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe whole community has often described John as belligerent
questions.explanation: The word 'belligerent' is derived from the Latin word 'bellum' (war) and 'gerere' (to wage). It is used to describe someone who is hostile, aggressive, or eager to engage in a fight or argument. Among the options provided, 'combative' is the most accurate synonym as it also describes a person ready or inclined to fight. In contrast, 'patient' is an antonym, while 'innocent' and 'attractive' are contextually irrelevant.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse 'belligerent' with 'benevolent' (kind) because they both start with 'b', or they mistakenly choose the antonym (patient) instead of the synonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The school library has stopped …… books to student
questions.instruction: In this question, choose the option that best completes the gap(s).The school library has stopped …… books to student
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'lending' because it refers to the act of giving something to someone for a period of time with the expectation that it will be returned. In this sentence, the library is the provider (the giver). Conversely, 'borrowing' refers to the act of receiving something from someone. Since the subject is the library, it 'lends' to students, while the students 'borrow' from the library. 'Renting' usually implies a commercial transaction involving payment, and 'lending' is the standard term used in library contexts.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'lend' and 'borrow'. A common error is saying 'Borrow me your pen' when they should say 'Lend me your pen' or 'Can I borrow your pen?'. Remember: You borrow FROM and you lend TO.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Ade’s father returned home LAST WEEK
questions.instruction: In each of the question, the word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.Ade’s father returned home LAST WEEK

options.option_a: Did Ade’s mother return home last week?
options.option_b: Did Kofi’s father return home last week?
options.option_c: Did Ade’s father leave home last yesterday?
options.option_d: Did Ade’s father leave home last last week?

questions.explanation: Emphatic stress is a principle in Oral English where a specific word in a sentence is emphasized to show its importance or to correct a specific piece of information. The rule for solving these questions is: the correct option (the question) must contradict only the word(s) written in capital letters. In the statement 'Ade’s father returned home LAST WEEK', the stressed words are 'LAST WEEK', which refers to the time. Therefore, the corresponding question must ask about a different time while keeping the subject (Ade's father) and the action (returned) the same. Option C is the only one that introduces a different time frame ('yesterday') to be corrected by 'LAST WEEK', whereas Option A focuses on the subject ('mother') and Option B focuses on the possessive ('Kofi’s').
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose an option that changes a word that is not capitalized. For example, picking Option A because it changes 'father' to 'mother', even though 'father' is not the word being stressed in the statement.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The DRIVER has taken John away.
questions.instruction: In each of the question, the word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.The DRIVER has taken John away.

options.option_c: Where did the driver take John?
options.option_d: Whom did the driver take away?

questions.explanation: In English phonology, emphatic stress (or contrastive stress) is used to highlight a specific word in a sentence to provide new information or correct a misconception. The standard rule for answering these questions in exams like JAMB is that the correct option is the question that targets the capitalized word. In the sentence 'The DRIVER has taken John away,' the stress is on 'DRIVER.' Therefore, the corresponding question must ask for the identity of the person who took John away. Option A ('Who took John away?') is the only question that identifies 'The DRIVER' as the specific piece of information being emphasized.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose an option that asks about a different part of the sentence (such as the object 'John' or the location 'away') instead of focusing on the word written in capital letters.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The judge blames the plaintiff for misleading the court
questions.instruction: In this question, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe judge blames the plaintiff for misleading the court
questions.explanation: In legal terminology, the 'plaintiff' is the party who initiates a lawsuit by filing a complaint against another party. The 'defendant' is the individual or entity being sued or accused. Since the instruction asks for the word opposite in meaning, 'defendant' is the correct choice as it represents the opposing side in a legal proceeding. Options (a) and (b) are near-synonyms or related terms, while (d) 'accused' is more specific to criminal law, whereas 'plaintiff/defendant' are the standard pair in civil proceedings.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'complainant' because it is closely related to the context of the sentence, forgetting that the instruction asks for the opposite (antonym) rather than the synonym.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Jumoke is just being Facetious about her marrying a soldier
questions.instruction: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsJumoke is just being Facetious about her marrying a soldier
questions.explanation: The word 'facetious' describes a situation where someone is treating serious issues with inappropriate humor or is being flippant rather than serious. In the context of the sentence, Jumoke is making light of the idea of marrying a soldier. Therefore, 'unserious' is the nearest in meaning. While it specifically implies a joking or tongue-in-cheek tone, 'unserious' captures the essence of not being earnest about the matter.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse 'facetious' with 'serious' (its antonym) or assume it means 'crazy' (option A) because the behavior might seem irrational, but facetious specifically refers to the lack of serious intent.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The ministry of education is making determined efforts to eradicate examination malpractice.
questions.instruction: In this question, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe ministry of education is making determined efforts to eradicate examination malpractice.
questions.explanation: In the context of the sentence, 'determined' is an adjective used to describe efforts that are resolute, firm, purposeful, and intense. To find the opposite, we need a word that describes efforts that lack impact, strength, or the ability to achieve the desired result. 'Ineffective' means not producing any significant or desired effect, making it the most appropriate antonym for 'determined' in this context. While 'unreliable' means inconsistent, 'ineffective' directly counters the potency of a 'determined effort'.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often mistakenly choose a synonym (a word with a similar meaning) instead of an antonym, or they choose an option like 'unreliable' which describes a person's character rather than the quality of the 'effort' itself.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The principal flogged the girl reluctantly
questions.instruction: In this question, choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italicsThe principal flogged the girlreluctantly
questions.explanation: The word 'reluctantly' is an adverb that describes an action done unwillingly, with hesitation, or without enthusiasm. To find the opposite, we look for a word that describes doing something with readiness and enthusiasm. 'Eagerly' means doing something with a keen interest or intense desire, making it the direct antonym of 'reluctantly'. Options like 'calmly' and 'furiously' relate to the emotional state but do not address the level of willingness.
questions.common_mistake: Students may mistakenly choose 'furiously' because they associate reluctance with a lack of intensity, or they might pick a synonym if they fail to read the instruction asking for the opposite meaning.

questions.subject: english

questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERHow old is Bint?

This detail is crucial to understanding her role in the story, particularly in scenes where her innocence and vulnerability contrast with the adult themes of the plot. The text provides direct references to her age during interactions with other characters, making option C the accurate choice.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing Bint's age with another character's or misinterpreting contextual clues about her developmental stage.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The superiority of democracy over other forms of government has long been established. From its Greek origins, the term democracy has been defined as a political ______ based on fair representation and liberty for the individual.
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERThe superiority of democracy over other forms of government has long been established. From its Greek origins, the term democracy has been defined as a political ______ based on fair representation and liberty for the individual.
questions.explanation: The sentence defines democracy as a political structure emphasizing fair representation and individual liberty. 'System' (option C) is the most appropriate noun to describe an organized framework of governance. 'Hegemony' (A) implies dominance, which contradicts democracy's principles. 'Pattern' (B) refers to a recurring design, not a governance structure. 'Influenced' (D) is a verb/adjective, not a noun, making it grammatically incorrect.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'hegemony' with democratic principles due to a misunderstanding of political terminology.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The ______ of liberty and equitable re-presentation are rooted in the definition given by Aristotle of Greece about 2500 years ago.
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERThe ______ of liberty and equitable re-presentation are rooted in the definition given by Aristotle of Greece about 2500 years ago.
questions.explanation: The sentence discusses foundational concepts ('principles') of liberty and equitable representation being rooted in Aristotle's definition. 'Principles' (B) refers to fundamental truths or rules, aligning with the historical and philosophical context. 'Example' (A) is incorrect as it implies a single instance, not foundational ideas. 'Statements' (C) and 'purposes' (D) lack the conceptual depth required for the context.
questions.common_mistake: Choosing 'example' (A) due to its literal interpretation, ignoring the abstract nature of the sentence.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: In the worlds of Aristotle, “The basis of a democratic _______ is liberty”.
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERIn the worlds of Aristotle, “The basis of a democratic _______ is liberty”.
questions.explanation: The quote is a direct excerpt from the recommended JAMB novel 'The Life Changer' by Khadija Abubakar Jalli. In the book, the author references Aristotle's famous philosophical assertion: 'The basis of a democratic state is liberty.' This quote is used to reflect on the themes of freedom, choice, and the transition into the independent life of a university student, which is the core setting of the story.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'law' because democracy is closely associated with legal frameworks, but in the context of Aristotle's quote and the text of the novel, 'state' is the specific word used.

During discussions involving philosophical concepts and general studies, the text refers to Aristotle's perspective on democracy. Specifically, it highlights that Aristotle emphasized the democratic 'idea' of freedom based on equality. While words like 'form' or 'law' might logically fit in a general political context, the specific vocabulary used in the prescribed text for JAMB is 'idea'.
questions.subtopic: The Life Changer by Khadija Abubakar Jalli
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'law' or 'form' because they associate democracy with legal structures or governmental systems, rather than recalling the specific phrasing used in the novel.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: More than 2000 years after Aristotle, the tenets of liberty, justice and equitable representation continue to ______
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERMore than 2000 years after Aristotle, the tenets of liberty, justice and equitable representation continue to ______
questions.explanation: This question is a direct reference to a statement in the JAMB recommended text, 'The Life Changer' by Khadija Abubakar Jalli. The sentence refers to the enduring influence of Aristotle's political and social philosophies. The idiomatic expression 'hold sway' means to have a great influence or to be dominant in a particular area or over a period of time. Therefore, it is the most appropriate phrase to describe how the tenets of liberty and justice remain powerful and relevant thousands of years later.
questions.subtopic: Analysis of 'The Life Changer' by Khadija Abubakar Jalli
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose 'move on' because they associate the mention of '2000 years' with the passage of time, failing to recognize that the sentence describes the continued influence of the ideas, not just their movement through history.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: “What’s is wrong” asked Clare.
questions.instruction: From the options labelled A to D , choose the option that is the most appropriate after the underlined portion of the given sentence“What’s is wrong” asked Clare.
questions.explanation: The sentence inside the quotation marks, 'What’s wrong', is an interrogative sentence (a direct question). According to the rules of direct speech, when the quoted words constitute a question, a question mark must be placed inside the quotation marks before the reporting verb (in this case, 'asked Clare'). Unlike declarative sentences where a comma might replace a full stop when the sentence continues, a question mark is never replaced by a comma in dialogue tags.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often mistakenly choose a comma because they believe that the continuation of the sentence with 'asked Clare' requires it, or they overlook the fact that the quoted text is a direct question.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The dominant narrative technique in the passage is ________
questions.instruction: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.The dominant narrative technique in the passage is ________
questions.passage: In my earlier year growing up in Nigeria, very many young people in my age category had many dreams. Some of the dreams were lofty; others were lousy. The lofty and lousy dreams were etched in the spine of youthful thinking and immature imaginations and mindsets. We dreamt about building, wealth and making ostentatious marks in all of our paths. We dreamt about conquering the world and counter-colonising our British colonial masters. We dreamt that our generation would be the First to take Nigeria to to the moon and unto all imaginable galaxies. We kept on dreaming until a certain age range when we inevitably stumbled on the illuminator called reality.
questions.explanation: The dominant narrative technique is the 'first person' because the narrator is a character within the story, recounting personal experiences and collective memories. This is evident through the consistent use of first-person pronouns such as 'I', 'my', 'we', and 'our' (e.g., 'In my earlier year...', 'We dreamt about building...'). In literature, when the story is told from the perspective of 'I' or 'we', it is classified as a first-person narrative.
questions.subtopic: Narrative Techniques and Point of View
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'subjective narrative' with 'first person'. While this passage is indeed subjective (reflecting personal feelings), 'first person' is the specific grammatical and literary technique used to describe the point of view based on pronoun usage.

We dreamt about conquering the world and counter-colonising our British colonial masters. We dreamt that our generation would be the First to take Nigeria to to the moon and unto all imaginable galaxies. We kept on dreaming until a certain age range when we inevitably stumbled on the illuminator called reality.

options.option_b: the youth in the writer’s environment
options.option_c: . the aspired young men and the writer
options.option_d: the young people and the writer

questions.explanation: In the passage, the writer begins by mentioning 'very many young people in my age category'. By using the first-person plural pronoun 'we' throughout the subsequent sentences, the writer explicitly includes themselves as part of that specific group of youths. Therefore, 'we' collectively refers to the speaker and the other young people of their generation who shared those same dreams.
questions.common_mistake: Students often pick option A or B because they identify the group but forget that the author is a member of that group, making option D the most inclusive and grammatically accurate reference.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Omar was offered admission to study __________
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGEROmar was offered admission to study __________
questions.explanation: In 'The Life Changer', Omar is the eldest child of the family. After successfully passing his matriculation examinations, he is offered admission to study Law at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria. This achievement is a significant plot point that initiates the family's discussions regarding university life.
questions.subtopic: The Life Changer by Khadija Abubakar Jalli
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the courses studied by the different children of the family. For instance, Bint is in secondary school, while Omar's siblings are at different stages of their education; students sometimes mistakenly attribute Law to one of the younger siblings.
related_topics: Plot summary of The Life Changer

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: According to Ummi, the story of Talle was more relevant to Omar because ___________
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERAccording to Ummi, the story of Talle was more relevant to Omar because ___________

options.option_a: he was leaving to the city

questions.explanation: In 'The Life Changer', Ummi narrates the story of Talle, a quiet and lonely man in the village, to her children. She explicitly points out that the story is relevant to Omar because, like Talle, Omar is a very quiet person. Ummi uses this analogy to highlight the potential social consequences of being overly reticent or reclusive, aiming to encourage Omar to be more expressive and social.
questions.subtopic: The Life Changer by Khadija Abubakar Jalli (Character Analysis)
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the reason for the story's relevance with external factors like travel plans, failing to recognize that the comparison is based purely on a shared personality trait (being quiet).
related_topics: Thematic analysis of The Life Changer
Characterization and literary devices in prose

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Whom did Salima compare the University lecturers to?
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERWhom did Salima compare the University lecturers to?
questions.explanation: In Khadija Abubakar Jalli's 'The Life Changer', during a discussion about the challenges and the nature of university lecturers, Salima compares them to 'thieves'. She uses this metaphor to describe how lecturers can unexpectedly fail students or deprive them of success in their courses, much like a thief who steals one's belongings without warning.
questions.subtopic: Character Analysis and Textual Comprehension of 'The Life Changer'
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the various metaphors used by the characters in the book to describe university life, mistakenly choosing 'police' or 'soldiers' because of the authoritative nature of lecturers, rather than the specific comparative term used by Salima.
related_topics: Literary Devices in The Life Changer
Themes and Characterization in African Prose

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: What killed Talle’s father?
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERWhat killed Talle’s father?
questions.explanation: In Khadija Abubakar Jalli's 'The Life Changer', Talle (also known as 'Tallest') lived a reclusive life after the death of his father. His father died from food poisoning, an incident that deeply affected Talle, causing him to become more withdrawn and fearful of consuming food prepared by others, which ultimately contributed to his peculiar social behavior in the narrative.
questions.subtopic: Character and Plot Analysis (The Life Changer)
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake his father's death for a natural cause like old age because of Talle's detached and quiet nature, but the book explicitly links the tragedy to food poisoning.
related_topics: Character motivation in The Life Changer
Themes of tragedy and social isolation in literature

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: What was Habib’s profession?
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERWhat was Habib’s profession?
questions.explanation: In 'The Life Changer', Habib is introduced as a prominent and wealthy businessman who eventually ventures into politics. He is known for his influence and his interaction with other characters, such as the protagonist's family. While he is involved in corrupt practices like bribery and extortion, his formal professional identity and ambition throughout the narrative are centered around his political aspirations.
questions.subtopic: Character Analysis in 'The Life Changer' by Khadija Abubakar Jalli
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse Habib's corrupt actions (like extortion) with his profession. While he engages in unethical behavior, 'extortion' is an act he commits, not his official profession.
related_topics: Thematic analysis of corruption in The Life Changer

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: ___________ was one of the charges filed against Talle
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGER___________ was one of the charges filed against Talle
questions.explanation: In the novel 'The Life Changer', Talle (often referred to as 'the quiet one') was accused of kidnapping a young girl. The community suspected him because he was a recluse, and his arrest for kidnapping became a central plot point that highlighted the dangers of social stereotyping and the consequences of being misunderstood in a society.
questions.subtopic: The Life Changer by Khadija Abubakar Jalli
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the charges against Talle with other crimes mentioned in the book or mistake the nature of his isolation for guilt, assuming he was involved in violent crimes like murder or armed robbery, which were not part of his specific charges.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: ___________ was the most common factor that strengthened the friendship between Salma and her roommates.
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGER___________ was the most common factor that strengthened the friendship between Salma and her roommates.
questions.explanation: In 'The Life Changer', the friendship between Salma and her roommates (Naima, Tomiwa, and Ada) is frequently cemented through their shared meals. The text highlights how they often ate together, shared snacks, and bonded over food, which served as a social lubricant and a central point of their communal life in the hostel.
questions.subtopic: The Life Changer by Khadija Abubakar Jalli
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'fashion' as the answer because the girls are described as stylish; however, the text emphasizes that their dining habits and the act of sharing food were the primary activities that solidified their bond.
related_topics: Thematic Development in Contemporary Nigerian Literature

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: What made Salma cry when she face the committee?
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERWhat made Salma cry when she face the committee?

options.option_b: because she mentioned Kolawale’s name by mistake
options.option_c: because Dr. Kabir and the man who introduce her to him were not there

questions.explanation: In the novel 'The Life Changer', Salma was caught in an examination malpractice case and attempted to influence the outcome by paying a bribe to Dr. Kabir through a middleman. When she finally appeared before the Examination Malpractice Disciplinary Committee (EMDC), she looked around the room expecting to see her 'benefactors.' Upon realizing that Dr. Kabir and the man who introduced her to him were not members of the committee, she understood she had been duped and that her academic career was in jeopardy, leading her to break down in tears.
questions.subtopic: Khadija Abubakar Jalli: The Life Changer
questions.common_mistake: Many students mistake Option D as the correct answer because Salma had an earlier unpleasant encounter with Professor Dabo. While his presence as the Chairman added to her fear, the primary catalyst for her crying was the realization of the scam and the absence of her supposed helpers.
related_topics: Themes of Bribery and Corruption in The Life Changer
The consequences of Examination Malpractice in the novel

The students were humming along to the melody during their stay in the hostel.
questions.subtopic: The Life Changer by Khadija Abubakar Jalli
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'Kenny Rogers' with 'Kelly Rowland' due to the phonetic similarity between the names 'Kelly' and 'Kenny', and the commonality of the surname 'Rowland' in pop culture.
related_topics: Character Analysis in The Life Changer
Plot Summary and Setting of The Life Changer

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The leader of the gambling group was _____________
questions.instruction: This question is based on Khadija Abubakar Jalli THE LIFE CHANGERThe leader of the gambling group was _____________

Kartagi is explicitly identified as the leader of the gambling syndicate. He is a key character during the conflict that leads to the involvement of the security personnel (the vigilante group) and eventually the intervention of the police.
questions.subtopic: Character Analysis - The Life Changer by Khadija Abubakar Jalli
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the names of the minor characters in the gambling scene, particularly Labaran (who is a friend of Omar) with the antagonist Kartagi.
related_topics: Plot development in The Life Changer
Characterization and roles in Nigerian prose

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I wish I knew the pastor while I was still in Lagos. This means that:
questions.instruction: Choose the most appropriate option from the list of words lettered A – DI wish I knew the pastor while I was still in Lagos. This means that:

options.option_a: I knew the pastor while I was in Lagos
options.option_b: I didn’t know the pastor and I wasn’t in Lagos
options.option_c: I knew the pastor but I was not in Lagos
options.option_d: I didn’t know the pastor but I was in Lagos

questions.explanation: In English grammar, the construction 'I wish + past perfect' (e.g., 'I wish I had known') is used to express regret about a past situation that did not happen. However, when 'I wish' is followed by a simple past tense (e.g., 'I wish I knew'), it describes a state of affairs in the present that is contrary to reality. In this specific context, the sentence 'I wish I knew the pastor while I was still in Lagos' uses the past tense to signify a missed opportunity. It implies that at the time the speaker was in Lagos, they did not have the acquaintance of the pastor. Therefore, the speaker was in Lagos, but the knowledge/acquaintance was absent.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistakenly choose Option A, confusing the wish for a reality. The structure 'I wish' implies that the action did not occur; therefore, if one wishes they had known someone, it is logically certain that they did not know them.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: A: Do you mind going for the programme? B: No! The response of speaker B indicates that:
questions.instruction: Choose the most appropriate option from the list of words lettered A – DA: Do you mind going for the programme? B: No! The response of speaker B indicates that:

options.option_a: He or She will attend the programme
options.option_b: He/She will not attend the programme because the idea behind it is bad
options.option_c: He/She will attend the programme because the idea behind it is not bad

questions.explanation: The response of speaker B, 'No!', indicates that they do not mind going for the programme. This implies that they are willing or agree to attend the programme. Therefore, the correct answer is D: 'He/She will attend the programme'.
questions.common_mistake: Some candidates may misinterpret the response 'No!' as a negative answer, leading them to choose option B. However, in this context, 'No!' is a positive response indicating that speaker B does not mind attending the programme.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Corruption has been a clog in the wheel of progress in Nigeria. This means that corruption is _________
questions.instruction: Choose the most appropriate option from the list of words lettered A – DCorruption has been a clog in the wheel of progress in Nigeria. This means that corruption is _________

options.option_a: blessing to the economy of Nigeria
options.option_b: a hindrance to the economy of Nigeria
options.option_d: a clog inside the wheel of the economic system in Nigeria

questions.explanation: The idiom 'a clog in the wheel of progress' metaphorically means something that obstructs or hinders advancement. Corruption is described as this 'clog,' indicating it impedes Nigeria's development. Option B ('a hindrance to the economy of Nigeria') best captures the figurative meaning, as it directly addresses the obstruction caused by corruption. Options C and D are overly literal, while Option A contradicts the negative connotation of the idiom.
questions.common_mistake: Selecting Option D due to its literal reference to the 'economic system,' which narrows the broader context of 'progress' implied in the idiom.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: A: How are you doing? B: I have never been better, The response of speaker B means that
questions.instruction: Choose the most appropriate option from the list of words lettered A – DA: How are you doing? B: I have never been better, The response of speaker B means that

options.option_a: Speaker B is a little bit indisposed
options.option_b: Speaker B is not in his or her right sense
options.option_c: Speaker B is enjoying his/her day

questions.explanation: The idiom 'I have never been better' is a superlative expression used to communicate that the speaker is currently in the best possible state of health, happiness, or fortune they have ever experienced. Therefore, it indicates that speaker B is feeling excellent or enjoying their day thoroughly.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake this phrase for irony or confusion because of the word 'never,' failing to realize that it is a positive comparative structure indicating peak performance or satisfaction.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: about
questions.instruction: From the word A-D, choose the word that have the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlinedabout
questions.explanation: The underlined letter 'a' in the word 'about' represents the weak, unstressed vowel sound known as the schwa /ə/. Looking at the options: 'nurse' /nɜːs/ (long vowel), 'ad hoc' /æd hɒk/ (short 'a' sound), 'afar' /əˈfɑː(r)/ contains the schwa sound in its first syllable. However, in standard phonetics for JAMB examinations, 'aghast' /əˈɡɑːst/ is the most distinct example of the unstressed schwa /ə/ at the beginning of the word, functioning identically to the initial syllable of 'about'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the schwa sound /ə/ with the short /æ/ sound (as in 'cat') or the long /ɑː/ sound, especially when they see the letter 'a' in various positions within a word.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Village
questions.instruction: From the word A-D, choose the word that have the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlinedVillage
questions.explanation: In the word 'village' (/ˈvɪlɪdʒ/), the underlined letter 'i' represents the short vowel sound /ɪ/. Let's analyze the options: (A) 'knowledge' contains /ɪdʒ/ at the end but the target vowel is in the first syllable, which is /ɒ/; (B) 'stipend' contains /ɪ/ in the first syllable (/ˈstɪpɛnd/), which matches the /ɪ/ sound in 'village'; (C) 'compass' contains /ʌ/; and (D) 'lawyer' contains /ɔː/. Therefore, 'stipend' is the correct match.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake the unstressed vowel sounds in words like 'village' for a schwa (/ə/), failing to distinguish between the short /ɪ/ sound and the neutral /ə/ sound.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Lamb
questions.instruction: From the word A-D, choose the word that have the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlinedLamb
questions.explanation: In the word 'Lamb', the final 'b' is silent. However, the question asks for the consonant sound represented by the underlined letter(s). In 'Lamb', the letter 'b' is silent, but usually, in such phonetic tasks, we analyze the phonetic representation /læm/. However, checking the options provided, 'plumber' also contains a silent 'b' at the end of the root/morpheme. If the focus is on the letter 'b', 'plumber' is the only word where the 'b' is also silent (in the context of the root 'plumb'). If the focus is on the presence of the /b/ sound, all other options (land, band, baby) contain the /b/ sound, whereas 'plumber' does not. Therefore, A is the correct answer as it shares the specific orthographic-phonetic property of having a silent 'b'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often try to pronounce the 'b' in words like 'lamb', 'plumber', 'crumb', or 'debt', failing to recognize that they are silent letters.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Breathe
questions.instruction: From the word A-D, choose the word that have the same consonant sound(s) as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined.Breathe
questions.explanation: The underlined letters in 'breathe' represent the voiced dental fricative consonant sound /ð/. In 'those', the 'th' also represents the voiced dental fricative sound /ð/. Conversely, 'breath' and 'cloth' contain the voiceless dental fricative /θ/, and 'bleed' contains the voiced alveolar lateral approximant /l/.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the voiced dental fricative /ð/ (as in 'breathe', 'these', 'mother') with the voiceless dental fricative /θ/ (as in 'breath', 'think', 'bath'). The distinction is that /ð/ is produced with vocal cord vibration, while /θ/ is not.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Horde
questions.instruction: From the word lettered A to D, choose the word that rhymes with the given word.Horde
questions.explanation: To determine a rhyme, we look at the phonetic sound of the words. The word 'horde' is transcribed as /hɔːd/. Looking at the options: 'bud' (/bʌd/) rhymes with none; 'horse' (/hɔːs/) ends in a different consonant sound; 'surd' (/sɜːd/) has a different vowel sound. 'Sword' is transcribed as /sɔːd/. Since both 'horde' and 'sword' share the exact same vowel /ɔː/ and final consonant sound /d/, they constitute a perfect rhyme.
questions.common_mistake: Students often make the mistake of looking at the spelling rather than the sound (e.g., assuming 'horse' rhymes because it shares four letters with 'horde'). Always rely on phonetic transcription rather than orthography.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Treasure
questions.instruction: From the question lettered A to D, choose the appropriate question for the given statement.Treasure
questions.explanation: To answer this question, one must identify the phonetic sound of the underlined or highlighted consonant cluster. In the word 'Treasure', the 's' produces the voiced postalveolar fricative sound /ʒ/. Analyzing the options: 'Measure' (/ˈmɛʒə/) contains the same /ʒ/ sound. In contrast, 'pressure' (/ˈprɛʃə/) and 'mission' (/ˈmɪʃən/) contain the voiceless postalveolar fricative /ʃ/, while 'sure' (/ʃʊə/) also contains the /ʃ/ sound. Therefore, 'measure' is the only word that shares the same phonetic consonant sound as 'treasure'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the voiced /ʒ/ sound (found in treasure, measure, pleasure, vision) with the voiceless /ʃ/ sound (found in pressure, sugar, mission, sure), leading them to select options that look similar in spelling rather than sound.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Jonathan visited Ilorin LAST WEEK
questions.instruction: From the question lettered A to D, choose the appropriate question for the given statement.Jonathan visited Ilorin LAST WEEK

options.option_b: Did Jonathaan aarrive Ilorin last week?
options.option_d: . Did Jonathan visit Ibadan last week?

questions.explanation: In English grammar, when a specific time phrase (in this case, 'last week') is provided as the focus of an answer, the appropriate question word to elicit that information is 'When'. By asking 'When did Jonathan visit Ilorin?', the responder is expected to provide the temporal information ('last week') present in the original statement. Options A, B, and D do not correctly elicit the specific information contained in the temporal adverbial phrase.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose option A ('Who...') because it addresses the subject of the sentence, but in this specific exercise, the focus is on identifying the appropriate question word for the specific information provided (the time).

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The electron result will be announced NOW.
questions.instruction: In the following sentence, the word that receives the emphatic stress is in capital letters. From the question lettered A to D, choose the one to which the given sentence is the appropriate answer.The electron result will be announced NOW.

options.option_b: When will the election result be announced?
options.option_c: Why will the election be announced now?
options.option_d: Who will announce the election result?

questions.explanation: In English, emphatic stress is placed on a word to highlight new or contrasting information. When a word is capitalized in this context, it serves as the focus of the sentence, meaning the sentence acts as a direct answer to a question seeking that specific information. Since the word 'NOW' (which indicates time) is stressed, the corresponding question must ask for the time of the event. Option B, 'When will the election result be announced?', directly seeks the information provided by the stressed word 'NOW'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often choose options based on the general subject matter (the election) rather than identifying the specific element being emphasized. If the stress were on 'ELECTION', the answer would be 'What will be announced now?', not 'When'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: “The Judge, with his son ………. Travelling to Lagos now”.
questions.instruction: Fill in the gap in the following sentence with an appropriate option.“The Judge, with his son ………. Travelling to Lagos now”.
questions.explanation: In English grammar, when a subject is joined to another noun or pronoun by phrases such as 'with', 'together with', 'along with', 'as well as', or 'in addition to', the verb must agree with the first (main) subject. In this sentence, the main subject is 'The Judge' (singular). The phrase 'with his son' is an intrusive prepositional phrase that does not change the number of the subject. Therefore, the singular verb 'is' is the only grammatically correct option.
questions.common_mistake: Many candidates mistakenly choose 'are' because they incorrectly assume that 'The Judge' and 'his son' collectively form a plural subject (as if using 'and').

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: If ………. Wants to succeed in life, ………. Must be hardworking because ………. Success relies on ………. Hands.
questions.instruction: Fill in the gap in the following sentence with an appropriate option.If ………. Wants to succeed in life, ………. Must be hardworking because ………. Success relies on ………. Hands.
questions.explanation: The sentence requires consistent pronoun usage. When using the indefinite pronoun 'one' as the subject of a sentence, all subsequent references to that person must maintain agreement with 'one'. Therefore: 'one' (subject), 'one' (subject of the next clause), 'one's' (possessive adjective for the person), and 'one's' (possessive adjective for the hands). Option C provides this necessary consistency, whereas other options introduce unnecessary shifts in person (e.g., mixing 'anyone' with 'one' or 'they').
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is mixing pronouns within the same sentence (e.g., starting with 'one' and switching to 'he' or 'they'), which violates the rule of pronoun consistency.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: I did ………. To school when I was in Ibadan ……….
questions.instruction: Fill in the gap in the following sentence with an appropriate option.I did ………. To school when I was in Ibadan ……….
questions.explanation: The first gap requires the base form of the verb after the auxiliary verb 'did'. In English, when 'did' is used to form a past tense statement (often for emphasis or in interrogative/negative structures, though here it functions as part of a habitual action construction), it must be followed by the bare infinitive 'go'. The second gap requires the adverbial phrase 'every day' (two words), which means 'each day', as opposed to the adjective 'everyday' (one word), which means 'common' or 'ordinary'.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse the adjective 'everyday' (meaning commonplace) with the adverbial phrase 'every day' (denoting frequency), and they often incorrectly use the past tense 'went' after the auxiliary 'did'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: 51. The incorrigible driver was warned for the last time by the FRSC personnel to get a ………. For his car.
questions.instruction: Fill in the gap in the following sentence with an appropriate option.51. The incorrigible driver was warned for the last time by the FRSC personnel to get a ………. For his car.
questions.explanation: In standard English, particularly within the Nigerian context regarding vehicular identification, the correct term for the identification tag displayed on a vehicle is a 'number plate'. While 'plate number' is frequently used in colloquial Nigerian English, 'number plate' is the formally accepted term in standard British English, which is the basis for most JAMB examinations.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is choosing 'plate number' (Option A). While it is widely used in casual conversation in Nigeria, 'number plate' is the recognized standard term in formal examination contexts.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: There shall be a ………. Meeting tomorrow.
questions.instruction: Fill in the gap in the following sentence with an appropriate option.There shall be a ………. Meeting tomorrow.
questions.explanation: In English compound nouns acting as modifiers, the noun acting as the attribute is typically used in its singular form. 'Parent' and 'teacher' modify the noun 'Association'; therefore, they should not be pluralized. The correct term is 'Parent-teacher association' (PTA). Option D correctly maintains the singular form for both components, which is the standard convention for compound nouns of this nature.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is assuming that because there are many parents and many teachers, the words must be pluralized (e.g., 'Parents-teachers-association'). However, when nouns act as adjectives to modify another noun, they retain their singular form.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Moni says, “I am a Christian”.
questions.instruction: Fill in the gap in the following sentence with an appropriate option.Moni says, “I am a Christian”.

options.option_a: Moni said (that) I am a Christian
options.option_b: Moni said (that) she was a Christian
options.option_c: Moni said (that) she was a christain
options.option_d: Moni said (that) she is a christain.

questions.explanation: When converting direct speech to indirect speech, we observe the reporting verb. Since the reporting verb 'says' is in the present tense, the tense within the reported clause does not change (it remains in the present tense). Additionally, the pronoun 'I' must change to 'she' to agree with the subject 'Moni'. Option D correctly maintains the present tense ('is') and the third-person feminine pronoun ('she'), and correctly spells 'Christian'. Options B and C are incorrect because they change the tense to past ('was'), which is only required if the reporting verb were in the past tense ('said').
questions.common_mistake: Students often automatically change the verb to the past tense (backshifting) regardless of whether the reporting verb is in the present or past tense. Always check if the reporting verb (e.g., 'says' vs 'said') dictates a tense shift.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The man was castigated by villagers for revealing the secret behind the black pot.
questions.instruction: From the list of words lettered A to D, choose the one that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word.The man was castigated by villagers for revealing the secret behind the black pot.
questions.explanation: To 'castigate' means to reprimand, scold, or criticize someone severely for their actions. To find the opposite, we look for a word that implies approval or commendation. Option A (scolded) and Option B (criticized) are synonyms of castigated. Option C (justified) means to show or prove to be right, which does not directly contrast with the act of castigating. Option D (praised) is the most direct antonym, as it means to express approval or admiration, which is the complete opposite of reprimanding someone.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'justified' because they interpret the sentence context as the man's actions being wrong, failing to realize that 'praised' is the direct functional opposite of the act of verbal castigation.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The lady is always punctilious in attending to customers despite the over-crowding condition of the environment.
questions.instruction: From the list of words lettered A to D, choose the one that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word.The lady is always punctilious in attending to customers despite the over-crowding condition of the environment.
questions.explanation: The word 'punctilious' means showing great attention to detail or correct behavior; it implies being very careful, precise, and diligent. To find the opposite, we look for a word that suggests a lack of care or attention. 'Carefree' (or unconcerned/negligent) is the most suitable antonym among the options. 'Meticulous' and 'painstaking' are synonyms of punctilious, while 'serious' is distantly related but does not capture the specific nature of precision implied by punctilious.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'punctilious' for 'punctual' (being on time). While punctilious people are often punctual, the word primarily refers to attention to detail and rigid observance of formalities, not just time-keeping.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Some of the students expressed divergent opinion about the ongoing protest in the nation
questions.instruction: From the list of words lettered A to D, choose the one that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word.Some of the students expressed divergent opinion about the ongoing protest in the nation
questions.explanation: The word 'divergent' means differing, deviating, or moving in different directions, especially concerning opinions. To find the opposite, we look for a word that signifies agreement or a single common perspective. 'Unanimous' means being in complete agreement or having the consent of all, which is the direct opposite of holding conflicting or divergent views. While 'similar' (Option A) might seem close, it suggests likeness rather than the collective consensus implied by the opposition to divergent views in a group setting.
questions.common_mistake: Candidates often choose 'different' (Option D), which is actually a synonym for 'divergent', or 'similar' (Option A), missing that 'unanimous' specifically captures the collective state of agreement that contrasts with a group expressing divergent opinions.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Regular renumerations serve as incentive to workers.
questions.instruction: From the list of words lettered A to D, choose the one that is nearly similar in meaning to the underlined word.Regular renumerations serve as incentive to workers.
questions.explanation: In this context, an 'incentive' is something that motivates or encourages a person to act in a certain way or work harder. Among the options, 'motivation' is the most direct synonym. 'Deterrent' and 'discouragement' are antonyms (opposites), while 'commendation' refers to formal praise or an award for an action already completed, rather than the driving force behind the work itself.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'incentive' with 'commendation' (praise) or 'remuneration' (payment). While payment acts as an incentive, the word 'incentive' itself describes the encouragement or drive, which is 'motivation'.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: To be qualified for admission in any of the United State of America, a candidate must be proficient in the use of English.
questions.instruction: From the list of words lettered A to D, choose the one that is nearly similar in meaning to the underlined word.To be qualified for admission in any of the United State of America, a candidate must be proficient in the use of English.
questions.explanation: The word 'proficient' means having a high degree of competence or skill in a particular area. In the context of the sentence, a candidate must be skilled or capable in the use of English to be admitted. Option C, 'competent', shares this meaning, as it denotes having the necessary ability, knowledge, or skill to do something successfully.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'trained' (Option D) for the correct answer. While a proficient person is often trained, 'trained' implies the process of instruction, whereas 'proficient' refers to the actual state of skill or competence achieved.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: When the chairman saw the shinning gun, his speech was incoherent due to the fear of being shot.
questions.instruction: From the list of words lettered A to D, choose the one that is nearly similar in meaning to the underlined word.When the chairman saw the shinning gun, his speech was incoherent due to the fear of being shot.
questions.explanation: The word 'incoherent' describes speech that is unclear, disorganized, or difficult to understand, often caused by extreme emotion or trauma. In this context, the chairman's fear of being shot caused him to stammer or lose the ability to speak clearly. 'Inarticulate' is the most similar synonym, as it refers to the inability to speak distinctly or express oneself clearly. The other options (derogatory, cogent, and logical) are antonyms or unrelated to the lack of clarity in speech.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'incoherent' for being 'afraid' or 'silent'. While fear is the cause of the incoherence in this sentence, the word itself specifically qualifies the quality of the speech, not the emotion of the speaker.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The politician usually plays an ignominious role in any national issue.
questions.instruction: From the list of words lettered A to D, choose the one that is nearly similar in meaning to the underlined word.The politician usually plays an ignominious role in any national issue.
questions.explanation: The word 'ignominious' describes something that causes public disgrace or shame. When a politician plays an 'ignominious' role, they are participating in a way that is shameful, dishonorable, or humiliating. Option A ('embarrassing') is the closest in meaning as it captures the sense of public shame and loss of dignity associated with 'ignominious'. Options B and C describe states of dissatisfaction, and option D implies deadliness, none of which fit the context of the sentence.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'ignominious' for words related to 'ignorance' due to the prefix 'igno-', or confuse it with 'ignite' because of the spelling. Additionally, some candidates guess 'lethal' (D) assuming the sentence refers to a 'dangerous' political role, ignoring the nuance of shame and dishonor.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Why did the merchant offer to buy Nandu’s horse?
questions.instruction: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.Why did the merchant offer to buy Nandu’s horse?
questions.passage: One day Nandu rode his horse to the village fair. On his way back he met Somendra, the merchant. The mer­chant was a crafty man, ready to do anything to earn some money. The villages knew this. In fact, no one knew what trick he would be up to next. Now, Nandu was poor and had no one in the world to call his own except a beautiful, white horse. He loved it more than anything else in the world. The merchant had his eye on the horse for a long time and tried to think of a way to get it for himself. Seeing Nandu, the merchant thought, Nandu is a simpleton. Let me see if I can trick him out of his horse. So he said to Nandu, You live all alone. How do you manage? What does a young boy like you need with a horse? Sell it to me and I shall make you rich in return. Nandu replied, “No I don’t want to sell my horse.”But the merchant refused to give up so easily. He offered Nandu more money. Finally, when the of­fer reached five hundred gold coins, Nandu paused and said. Five hun­dred gold coins seems like a good price. But I have a condition. If you agree to it, I shall give you my horse. “What is it?”, the merchant asked im­patiently. “Give me the money right now and I shall give you my horse when I have given you ten lashes.” After all he would resell the horse for over a thousand gold coins in the market. He would take twenty lashes for such a gain. He agreed instantly. He ran home and got the money for Nandu and brought along his whip as well. Nandu counted the money care­ fully. He then took the whip and the lashes fell on the merchant’s back in quick succession. By the eighth lash the merchant was almost in tears but he told himself that there were only two lashes to go and the horse would be his. The merchant held his breath waiting for the final lashes. Bui Nan­ du had mounted his horse and was riding off. “Wait!”, shouted the mer­chant in anger. “What about the last lashes? Where are you going with the horse? We had a deal.Nandu stopped and said, “1 agree to give you the horse only after 1 had given you ten lashes. But it is up­ setting my hoise. I’ll give you the last lashes later. Till then goodbye! “Come back you cheat!”, the merchant shouted. But the crowd that had gathered around agreed with Nandu. A deal was a deal. Till the last lash was given, the horse could not belong to the merchant. Nandu rode away richer by five hundred gold coins and Somendra waited in vain for several days for the final lash which never came.

options.option_a: He was very fond of the horse and wanted it for him­ self
options.option_b: It was his way of helping Nandu who was poor
options.option_c: The horse would be useful for carrying goods to the market.
options.option_d: He hated Nandu and wanted to deprive him of some­ thing he loved.

questions.explanation: The merchant offered to buy Nandu's horse because he was a crafty man who wanted to earn some money by tricking Nandu out of his horse. The passage states that 'The merchant had his eye on the horse for a long time and tried to think of a way to get it for himself.' and 'Seeing Nandu, the merchant thought, Nandu is a simpleton. Let me see if I can trick him out of his horse.' This indicates that the merchant's intention was to deceive Nandu and acquire the horse for himself, not because he was fond of the horse, wanted to help Nandu, or needed it for carrying goods.
questions.common_mistake: Students may choose option A, thinking that the merchant was genuinely fond of the horse, or option B, assuming that the merchant was trying to help Nandu. However, the passage clearly shows that the merchant's motive was to trick Nandu and gain something for himself.

questions.instruction: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.Why did Nandu set the condition of giving the merchant ten lashes?
questions.passage: One day Nandu rode his horse to the village fair. On his way back he met Somendra, the merchant. The mer­chant was a crafty man, ready to do anything to earn some money. The villages knew this. In fact, no one knew what trick he would be up to next. Now, Nandu was poor and had no one in the world to call his own except a beautiful, white horse. options.option_a: To discourage the merchant from buying his horse.
options.option_b: To demonstrate how painful a whipping was so that the merchant would never hit the horse
options.option_c: To bargain with the mer­chant to offer more money.
options.option_d: To outwit the merchant who was trying to cheat him.

questions.explanation: In the broader context of the story from which this passage is taken, Nandu realizes that the merchant is a crafty individual trying to cheat him. By setting a seemingly absurd or painful condition (ten lashes), Nandu is turning the tables on the merchant. The condition is not meant to be a literal trade but a clever maneuver to reveal the merchant's greed and outwit him by making the price of the horse effectively impossible or undesirable for someone who lacks integrity.
questions.common_mistake: Students often assume the question is about the physical horse or the literal act of whipping, failing to recognize the figurative 'battle of wits' between the protagonist and the antagonist described as a 'crafty man'.

questions.common_mistake: Students often make the mistake of choosing options based on personal assumptions or external logic (e.g., assuming the horse's welfare is the primary concern) rather than sticking strictly to the information provided within the text.

options.option_a: He was tired and not in the mood.

questions.explanation: Based on the provided passage, Nandu does not actually 'cite a reason' for not giving the final lashes. When the merchant asks why he is leaving, Nandu simply replies, 'I will give you the last lashes later. Till then goodbye!' The options provided in the question do not align with the text. In the context of the story, Nandu's action is a calculated trick to escape with his horse while keeping the money, rather than being motivated by pity, fatigue, or the horse's distress. If forced to choose based on the provided text, the question is technically flawed as none of the options are supported by the passage.
questions.common_mistake: Students often try to 'infer' a moral reason (like pity or animal rights) because they assume the character must have a virtuous reason for stopping, whereas, in this specific text, Nandu is simply outsmarting the merchant.

questions.explanation: The story is best described as 'didactic' because it follows a traditional fable-like structure intended to teach a moral lesson. Didactic literature is designed to instruct or provide a moral lesson, and this passage sets the stage for a narrative where virtue is tested against vice.
questions.common_mistake: Students often mistake 'didactic' for 'moral' (which is the content) rather than the intent of the author. Some might choose 'amoral' incorrectly because they assume a simple story lacks moral depth, or confuse 'apolitical' with a lack of social commentary.

questions.explanation: Based on the provided passage, there is no mention of music, musical instruments, or any individual possessing a 'flair for music.' The passage focuses entirely on a transaction between Nandu and a merchant regarding a horse. Therefore, none of the provided options (Tomiwa, Salma, Ada, or Ngozi) are supported by the text. In a typical examination context, this suggests an error in the question paper where the question does not align with the provided passage.
questions.common_mistake: The most common mistake is attempting to guess or externalize knowledge. Students often try to 'force' an answer based on personal assumptions when the information is absent from the text, rather than noting that the answer is not present.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: Ummi is translated in Arabic as _____
questions.instruction: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.Ummi is translated in Arabic as _____
questions.passage: One day Nandu rode his horse to the village fair. On his way back he met Somendra, the merchant. The mer­chant was a crafty man, ready to do anything to earn some money. The villages knew this. In fact, no one knew what trick he would be up to next. Now, Nandu was poor and had no one in the world to call his own except a beautiful, white horse. He loved it more than anything else in the world. The merchant had his eye on the horse for a long time and tried to think of a way to get it for himself. Seeing Nandu, the merchant thought, Nandu is a simpleton. Let me see if I can trick him out of his horse. So he said to Nandu, You live all alone. How do you manage? What does a young boy like you need with a horse? Sell it to me and I shall make you rich in return. Nandu replied, “No I don’t want to sell my horse.”
questions.explanation: The word 'Ummi' is an Arabic term derived from 'umm' (mother), followed by the possessive suffix '-i' (my). Therefore, it translates literally to 'my mother'. While the provided passage describes Nandu and the merchant, this specific question is a direct knowledge-based vocabulary question often found in JAMB English papers where candidates are expected to know the meaning of common foreign words or honorifics.
questions.common_mistake: Students often confuse 'Ummi' with 'Ummah' (community/nation) or assume it has a religious or abstract meaning like 'mentor' or 'muse' due to its common use as a term of endearment.

questions.question_text: In which examination was Salma caught cheating?
questions.instruction: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.In which examination was Salma caught cheating?

The villages knew this. In fact, no one knew what trick he would be up to next. Now, Nandu was poor and had no one in the world to call his own except a beautiful, white horse. Seeing Nandu, the merchant thought, Nandu is a simpleton. Let me see if I can trick him out of his horse. So he said to Nandu, You live all alone. How do you manage? What does a young boy like you need with a horse? Sell it to me and I shall make you rich in return. Nandu replied, “No I don’t want to sell my horse.”
questions.explanation: This question is an 'extraneous' or 'mismatched' question. Upon careful analysis of the provided passage, there is no mention of a character named 'Salma,' nor is there any reference to an examination or cheating. The passage focuses entirely on Nandu, his horse, and Somendra the merchant. In a real-world JAMB scenario, this would be classified as a 'null' or 'invalid' question because the information required to answer it is absent from the source text.
questions.common_mistake: Students often panic and try to 'guess' an answer or pick the most 'academic-sounding' option when they cannot find the information in the text, rather than recognizing that the question is faulty.

questions.subject: english
questions.question_text: The full meaning of “EMAL” is
questions.instruction: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.The full meaning of “EMAL” is

The villages knew this. In fact, no one knew what trick he would be up to next. Now, Nandu was poor and had no one in the world to call his own except a beautiful, white horse. He loved it more than anything else in the world. The merchant had his eye on the horse for a long time and tried to think of a way to get it for himself. Seeing Nandu, the merchant thought, Nandu is a simpleton. Let me see if I can trick him out of his horse. So he said to Nandu, You live all alone. How do you manage?
